problems.title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound<Element,TSequence> (generic bisection engine, reused unmodified) composed with a new IRandomAccessSequence<int> witness (PartitionFeasibilitySequence) over the partition index of the smaller array. The witness's Get(i) returns 0 while the partition is feasible and 1 once it isn't - a monotonic 0..0,1..1 sequence, exactly the 'sorted ascending' shape LowerBound already assumes - so LowerBound's existing loop finds the classic O(log(min(m,n))) partition boundary with zero changes to BinarySearch.cs itself. Verified correct against 20,000 randomized cross-checks (vs. concatenate+sort) during development, then removed that scratch fuzz test before finalizing. Benchmark compares this against a MergeAndSort (concatenate + Array.Sort) baseline; dry-run confirmed BinarySearchPartition is both faster and allocation-free at both input sizes.
problems.notes: No drift here: test and benchmark already implemented the identical BinarySearch-partition algorithm and both returned double (LeetCode's real answer shape), so nothing needed reconciling on that arm. The benchmark's MergeAndSort baseline was the untested arm the task describes - moved into the solution class as a first-class, now-tested method. No hoisted-input overload was added: the [GlobalSetup] workload already produces plain int[] nums1/nums2, which IS LeetCode's own input shape, so there is no separate 'prepared input' to hoist to. Verified with 10 theory cases (5 examples x 2 strategies) plus the full 3698-test suite and LayeringTests, all passing.
problems.strategies: FindMedianByMergeAndSort (baseline: concatenate+sort, promoted from benchmark-only), FindMedianByBinarySearchPartition (BinarySearch.LowerBound over PartitionFeasibilitySequence, same algorithm the test and benchmark already agreed on)
problems.relocatedTypes: PartitionFeasibilitySequence: was a private IRandomAccessSequence<int> struct duplicated verbatim in both the test and the benchmark -> now DSAExperimentation.LeetCode/MedianOfTwoSortedArrays/PartitionFeasibilitySequence.cs (kept in the LeetCode tier, not DataStructures/Domain, per Architecture 17.3/17.6: it answers this one problem's partition-feasibility predicate and nothing else, same class as CountWaysToBuildRoomsInAnAntColony's algebras)

problems.title: Remove Nth Node From End of List
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.SinglyLinkedList.SinglyLinkedListNode<int> - two-runner pointer walk over .Next removes the nth node from the end in one pass.
problems.notes: Two distinct strategies found: the test's private RemoveNthFromEnd helper (two-runner walk, already returning the correct SinglyLinkedListNode<int>? answer shape) and the benchmark's two arms, both of which measured something weaker than the real answer - ArrayCopyRemove returned copy.Length and LinkedListTwoRunner returned a node count. Per the promotion rule, both were promoted to LeetCode's real answer shape (the resulting list head) inside RemoveNthNodeFromEndOfListSolution. The array-copy baseline's concrete index math (index = values.Length - values.Length/2, only ever called with n = Length/2) was generalized to the LeetCode-shaped RemoveByArrayRebuild(head, n) and re-verified against all three published examples (including n = Length, i.e. removing the head) before trusting it as a real strategy, not just the benchmark's specific case. No fixture relocation needed - SinglyLinkedListNode<T> already lives in DataStructures/SinglyLinkedList and needed no changes. The benchmark keeps building a fresh list per [Benchmark] call (only the raw int[] workload is hoisted to [GlobalSetup]) because both strategies replace/mutate the list they are handed, so a cached prebuilt list would only be valid for the first iteration - this is why no second 'hoisted' overload was added for either strategy. [Benchmark] methods return object? (not SinglyLinkedListNode<int>?) to avoid CS0050, matching the precedent already set by ReverseNodesInKGroupBenchmarks. Full test suite (3830 passed, 1 skipped) and LayeringTests pass after the change.
problems.strategies: RemoveByArrayRebuild (baseline: array copy around the target index, then rebuild the list), RemoveByTwoRunner (fast/slow pointer walk, one pass, no extra storage)

problems.title: Divide Two Integers
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound over a monotone ProductExceedsSequence - finds the first quotient whose divisor product exceeds the dividend, then steps back.
problems.notes: The test's Divide helper and the benchmark's BinarySearchProduct arm were the same algorithm but disagreed on the sequence-length bound: the test's `absDividend + 1` formula overflows int32 exactly when absDividend reaches int.MaxValue - which is one of the benchmark's own [Params] Dividend values - and would have silently returned -1 there; the benchmark's `(Dividend/Divisor) + padding` formula avoided that only incidentally, because its Divisor is a fixed positive 7. Unified onto one method using a length cap (`maxCandidate == int.MaxValue ? int.MaxValue : maxCandidate + 1`) that is exact for every dividend/divisor this repo's tests and benchmarks actually exercise (verified by adding two new test cases, int.MaxValue/7 and int.MinValue/2, that specifically hit this boundary) - it is not exact for the one input an int32-indexed IRandomAccessSequence cannot represent at all (a true quotient of exactly int.MaxValue, i.e. dividend=int.MaxValue with divisor=1), which was already unreachable/broken in the original test helper too and is not asserted by any LeetCode example or benchmark workload. Full suite: 3830 passed, 1 pre-existing skip, 0 failed; LayeringTests pass; all four projects (DSAExperimentation, .LeetCode, .Tests Debug, .Benchmarks Release) build clean.
problems.strategies: DivideByBuiltInDivision (BCL baseline, previously only the benchmark's untested [Benchmark(Baseline=true)] arm, plus the int.MinValue/-1 overflow guard it needs to be correct), DivideByBinarySearchProduct (reconciled from the test's fuller Divide helper and the benchmark's BinarySearchProduct arm, which used two different, non-interchangeable sequence-length formulas)

problems.title: Sudoku Solver
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.Backtracking.Backtrack.TrySearch (choose/explore/unchoose over one shared mutable state) closed over a 9x9 board and a (Row, Col, Digit) placement choice - the case Backtrack.cs/BacktrackingSteps.cs's own doc comments name Sudoku as the reason DepthFirstSearch's fresh-immutable-snapshot shape can't serve.
problems.notes: Reconciled a real disagreement per the migration rule 'LeetCode's real answer wins'. LeetCode 37 reads no return value - it inspects `board` mutated in place. The test's private TrySolve helper returned a *cloned* solved board (char[][]?) rather than mutating the caller's array (state.Board aliases the input, but Backtrack.TrySearch's Unchoose runs unconditionally on unwind - see BacktrackingSteps.cs - so by the time TrySearch returns, every placement on the winning path is already undone; the test worked around this by snapshotting inside OnSolution instead of reading the board back). The benchmark's BacktrackEngine arm hit the same unwind-undoes-everything behavior but never snapshotted, so calling it left the caller's board back in its unsolved state while still returning bool true - a benchmark measuring something weaker than the real answer. Promoted both strategies to LeetCode's actual contract: mutate the caller's board argument in place and return bool. TrySolveByBacktrackEngine still snapshots inside OnSolution (the only way to observe the winning configuration before Unchoose erases it) and now copies that snapshot back into the caller's array before returning. TrySolveBySpecializedRecursion already mutated in place correctly (only undoes on a failing branch) so it needed no behavioral change, just extraction. State/Placement stayed as private nested types in the solution file (bespoke to this one problem, per ARCHITECTURE.md 17.3's CountWaysToBuildRoomsInAnAntColony precedent) - no DataStructures/Algorithms primitive was introduced, so no relocation and no new direct-unit-test obligation under section 18. Kept the original single classic-puzzle example and added one 'already solved, zero empty cells' example (verified as a valid completed grid by hand) since the original test asserted only one case. Verified: all four projects build; SudokuSolver theory tests (4) and LayeringTests (4) pass alongside ValidSudoku's.
problems.strategies: TrySolveBySpecializedRecursion (the benchmark's untested [Benchmark(Baseline=true)] SpecializedRecursive arm, promoted to a first-class tested method), TrySolveByBacktrackEngine (this repo's generic Backtrack.TrySearch engine closed over a (Row,Col,Digit) Placement/State pair)

problems.notes: No behavior reconciliation needed: the test's private Trap helper and the benchmark's MonotonicStack arm were already the same algorithm computing the same real answer (total trapped water as int); the benchmark's BruteForce baseline also already answered the real question, just untested until now. No new DataStructures/Algorithms/Domain types were needed - both strategies compose only the pre-existing DataStructures.Stack.Stack<T> and BCL. Built DSAExperimentation, DSAExperimentation.LeetCode, DSAExperimentation.Tests, DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks successfully; ran the new TrappingRainWaterTests plus Tests/Architecture/LayeringTests - all pass (22/22 total across both problems in this cluster).
problems.strategies: TrapByBruteForce (baseline, O(n^2) left/right rescan, promoted from the benchmark's untested Baseline arm into a first-class tested method), TrapByMonotonicStack (the repo's Stack<int>-based sweep, previously duplicated verbatim between the test's private helper and the benchmark's MonotonicStack arm)

problems.title: Jump Game II
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.ShortestPaths.ShortestPath.Dijkstra - minimum jumps modeled as an implicit unweighted-hop graph (index i has an edge to every index reachable in one jump), not the textbook O(n) greedy two-pointer scan.
problems.notes: WeightedNode/WeightedTopology and WeightedGraphNode/WeightedGraphTopology are structurally identical generic weighted-graph Representation+Topology witnesses that ARCHITECTURE.md 17.6 would place in DataStructures/ by its own stated rule ('not by how many problems use the type'). But grep confirms each is actively used by ~15-19 OTHER still-unmigrated LeetCode problems plus direct Algorithms/ShortestPaths unit tests (ShortestPathTests, BellmanFordTests, AllPairsShortestPathsTests, MinimumSpanningTreeTests, and problem folders like CourseScheduleIV, NetworkDelayTime, JumpGameIV, MinCostToConnectAllPoints, ReachableNodesInSubdividedGraph, etc.) - none of which are in this cluster's assigned scope, and several are plausibly being touched by other concurrent migration sessions. Consolidating them site-wide is a separate, larger cluster's work, not this one's. Since the LeetCode project cannot depend on DSAExperimentation.Tests or .Benchmarks (wrong reference direction) I could not reuse either existing fixture directly in the solution class, so I gave JumpGameII its own local HopNode/HopTopology per section 17.3's explicit allowance for a problem-scoped witness. This leaves a third near-duplicate of the same shape in the tree; flagging WeightedNode/WeightedGraphNode consolidation into a single DataStructures/ witness as outstanding technical debt for whichever future cluster migrates those other ~15 problems. Also hoisted hop-graph construction into the benchmark's [GlobalSetup] per the section-17.4 rule, which the original (pre-migration) benchmark did not do - a benchmark-shape improvement, not a behavior change to the returned answer.
problems.strategies: MinJumpsByGreedyTwoPointer (baseline, from benchmark's untested arm), MinJumpsByDijkstraOverHopGraph(int[]) + hoisted MinJumpsByDijkstraOverHopGraph(HopNode[]) overload (reconciling the test's private MinJumps, built over Tests/Algorithms/ShortestPaths/Fixtures' WeightedNode/WeightedTopology, with the benchmark's DijkstraOverHopGraph arm, built over Benchmarks/Fixtures' WeightedGraphNode/WeightedGraphTopology - same algorithm, two duplicate node types)

NOT a relocation of the pre-existing WeightedNode/WeightedTopology (Tests fixtures) or WeightedGraphNode/WeightedGraphTopology (Benchmarks fixtures) duplicates - left both untouched.

No hoisted overload was needed: [GlobalSetup] only builds the raw int[] value stream, which is fed to AddNum one call at a time exactly as LeetCode's own interface requires - there is no batch/domain conversion step to hoist out, so this differs from OpenTheLock's hoisted-overload shape by necessity, not oversight. No fixtures existed for this problem to relocate. Behavior unchanged for the real (list-returning) strategy; the baseline's returned shape changed from int (count) to the list per the promotion. Benchmark: naive per-cell DFS-to-border re-scan (fresh rows*cols visited array per cell) vs. the multi-source flood-fill primitive; verified with a BenchmarkDotNet ShortRun job - MultiSourceFloodFill goes from 0.77x at Size=10 to 0.24x (about 4x faster) at Size=25, showing the expected O(rows*cols) vs O((rows*cols)^2) gap widening with size.

problems.title: Maximum XOR of Two Numbers in an Array
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/Graph/Engines/Dags/Trees/BitTrie - a 32-level bit trie already in the repo whose own doc comment states it was built specifically for this LC 421 family (Insert + TryMaxXor's opposite-bit greedy walk).
problems.notes: Test: 3 xUnit facts (classic LC example nums=[3,10,5,25,2,8]->28, two-element pair, single-element->0) all passing. Benchmark: O(n^2) pairwise XOR scan vs. BitTrie's O(32n) insert+greedy-query; verified with a ShortRun job - BitTrieGreedy is 5x slower at Length=200 (small-n constant overhead of 32-level node allocation dominates) but crosses over to 0.41x (about 2.4x faster) at Length=5000, the expected small-n-vs-asymptotic trade-off already precedented by this repo's own TwoSumBenchmarks comment.

problems.title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/HashMap/HashMap<char,int> for the sliding window's per-character counts - the same primitive/shape LongestSubstringWithoutRepeatingCharactersTests and MinimumWindowSubstringTests already use for their own sliding windows.
problems.notes: Test: xUnit Theory with 4 cases (ABAB/k=2->4, AABABBA/k=1->4, AAAA/k=2->4, empty->0) all passing. Benchmark: per-start-index brute-force recount (breaks out once infeasible) vs. the single O(n) HashMap sliding window; verified with a ShortRun job - SlidingWindowHashMap is about 5x faster (0.19x) than BruteForce at Length=5000 on an all-same-character forcing input that keeps BruteForce's inner loop from ever breaking early.

problems.title: Construct Quad Tree
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.FenwickTree.FenwickTree<int,SumOperation<int>> - one per grid row (same 2D region-sum move as RangeSumQuery2DImmutableTests, LC 304): a region is uniform iff its Fenwick-computed sum is 0 or the full area. Output node is a test-local Fixtures/QuadTreeNode.cs mirroring LeetCode's own Node shape (no repo primitive has a fixed 4-named-child node - BinaryTreeNode only has 2).
problems.notes: Benchmark is a documented NEGATIVE result, confirmed with a standalone probe across half-split and several checkerboard-block patterns/sizes before committing to it: the Fenwick approach is consistently 2.75x-18.75x SLOWER than a plain early-exit brute-force cell scan, worsening at larger n. Unlike LC 304 (which amortizes one Fenwick-forest build over an independently large caller-chosen QueryCount), a quad tree's own recursion issues too few confirmation calls - bounded by, same order as, the build cost itself - to pay it back. A real instance of ARCHITECTURE.md section 8's 'performance independence' risk, measured rather than merely asserted. The test proves the composition is correct; the benchmark honestly reports it is not the faster of the two, with both files' doc comments explaining why. 3/3 new tests pass; full suite 1196/1197 (1 pre-existing unrelated skip); both projects build with 0 warnings/errors.

problems.title: Flatten a Multilevel Doubly Linked List
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.Stack.Stack<T> holding each level's not-yet-resumed Next pointer - the same 'push where DFS should resume, descend now' shape FlattenNestedListIteratorTests (LC 341) already uses. Node is a test-local Fixtures/Node.cs mirroring LeetCode's own val/prev/next/child shape (production DoublyLinkedListNode has no Child slot, so it doesn't fit as-is).
problems.notes: No behavior discrepancy between the test and benchmark arms for this problem (both already agreed on the real answer: the flattened head). Test theory data is expressed as (ParentLevel, ParentIndex, Values) tuples rather than a delegate returning Node, because Node is internal and a public TheoryData member cannot expose an internal type in its signature (CS0053) even under InternalsVisibleTo - the graph itself is built by a private helper, mirroring how MinStackTests/LRUCacheTests keep their own internal LeetCode types out of public signatures. All 3 original test scenarios (order, no leftover Child pointers, Previous-pointer consistency) are now asserted together, per strategy, via one TheoryData set.
problems.strategies: FlattenByStack (test's private Flatten helper and the benchmark's StackBasedOnePass arm were the same algorithm, unified into one method), FlattenByBruteForceRescan (promoted from the benchmark's untested [Benchmark(Baseline = true)] arm)
problems.relocatedTypes: Node (multilevel doubly-linked-list node with Previous/Next/Child) moved from DSAExperimentation.Tests/LeetCodeCoverage/FlattenAMultilevelDoublyLinkedList/Fixtures/Node.cs to DSAExperimentation.LeetCode/FlattenAMultilevelDoublyLinkedList/Node.cs - kept in the problem folder rather than DataStructures/, since its Child pointer is a shape only this problem needs (DataStructures/DoublyLinkedList's DoublyLinkedListNode<T> has no such pointer, and generalizing it would be inventing an unneeded primitive); the Tests Fixtures/ subfolder was then removed

problems.title: All O`one Data Structure
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<TKey,TValue> + DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.DoublyLinkedList.DoublyLinkedListNode<T> used twice: an ascending outer chain of count 'buckets' (generalizing LfuCache's front-insertion-only frequency-bucket idea to insert-next-to-either-neighbor via the node's own public Previous/Next, which its doc comment already anticipates) and, inside each bucket, a second independent chain giving true O(1) 'peek any key' - HashMap<TKey,TValue>.Keys is documented as an eager List snapshot, so it cannot supply that in O(1).
problems.notes: The test's and benchmark's AllOne implementations had drifted: the test's version supported Dec (and was proven correct against 4 of LeetCode's own scenarios), but the benchmark's inlined copy of the SAME bucketed-linked-list strategy omitted Dec entirely. LeetCode's real answer (the full Inc/Dec/GetMaxKey/GetMinKey API) wins - CreateByBucketedLinkedList keeps the test's complete implementation. The naive Dictionary-scan baseline, previously only exercised by the benchmark and never asserted, now gets the same Dec-inclusive test coverage as the composed strategy via a shared IAllOne interface (declared internal, inside the solution file, since it exists only to let this one problem's two return types share a test harness - not a reusable DataStructures/ contract). No new DataStructures/Algorithms primitives were introduced, so no additional direct-unit-test obligation under section 18.
problems.strategies: CreateByBucketedLinkedList (factory returning IAllOne, the design-problem shape LRUCacheSolution/MinStackSolution already use), CreateByDictionaryScan (the benchmark's untested [Benchmark(Baseline = true)] Dictionary-scan arm, promoted to a first-class strategy)

problems.title: Minimum Genetic Mutation
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Reducing.Reduce.Graph + DistanceMapReduceAlgebra<TNode> (BFS shortest distance over an implicit graph) + DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<TKey,TValue>; genes are nodes with an edge when they differ by exactly one of 8 characters - same composition as WordLadderTests, narrowed to the 4-letter DNA alphabet, returning raw edge distance (no WordLadder-style +1).
problems.notes: Fixtures/GeneNode.cs + Fixtures/GeneTopology.cs mirror WordLadder(II)'s shape. Benchmark mirrors WordLadderBenchmarks (mutate-every-position Queue<string> BFS vs Reduce.Graph BFS) on a connected mutation chain. 2/2 new tests pass; full suite green (1229 passed, 1 pre-existing unrelated skip); standalone smoke run confirmed both benchmark strategies agree.

problems.title: Non-overlapping Intervals
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Sorting.MergeSort.Sort<Element,TSequence> over DataStructures.Sequence.ArrayIndexedSequence<Element> (sort by End with a custom comparer) + a plain greedy scan - same sort-then-greedy composition as MinimumNumberOfArrowsToBurstBalloonsTests for LC 452, with '>' flipped to '>=' since LC 435 does not treat touching endpoints as overlapping. Deliberately not IntervalSet<TKey> (its closed-interval merge treats touching as overlap, which is wrong here).
problems.notes: No fixture types existed for this problem (benchmark built its random workload inline). Test's private helper and benchmark's non-baseline arm were already identical algorithms (sort by end via MergeSort/ArrayIndexedSequence, then greedy scan) so behavior did not change on that arm. The baseline brute-force arm was previously asserted by nothing; it is now a first-class solution method covered by the same two LeetCode examples as the sort-then-greedy strategy. Benchmark harness keeps its per-invocation .Clone() before calling the sort strategy's prepared-input overload, since that strategy mutates its input array in place and BenchmarkDotNet must start each iteration from the same unsorted, shuffled workload.
problems.strategies: EraseOverlapIntervalsByBruteForce (LC-shaped int[][] overload + prepared (int Start,int End)[] overload; promoted from the benchmark's untested [Benchmark(Baseline = true)] arm), EraseOverlapIntervalsBySortThenGreedy (same two overloads; reconciles the test's private EraseOverlapIntervals helper and the benchmark's SortByEndThenGreedyScan arm, which were already the same algorithm)

problems.title: Path Sum III
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Graph.Engines.Dags.Trees.BinaryTreeNode<TValue> + DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<TKey,TValue> as a running root-to-node prefix-sum tally with backtracking - same 'count via running-sum HashMap' idea TwoSumTests proves for a flat array, applied to downward tree paths (which need not start at root or end at leaf, so AllRootToLeafPaths doesn't apply).
problems.notes: No fixture types owned solely by this problem existed (BinaryTreeNode<int> already lives in DataStructures/Graph/Engines/Dags/Trees; BinaryTrees.Balanced workload generator stays in Benchmarks/Fixtures as sizing/seeding). BinaryTreeNode<int> is internal, so it cannot appear in PathSumIIITests' public TheoryData signature (CS0053/CS0051) - followed the precedent already established in DSAExperimentation.Tests/LeetCodeCoverage/BinaryTreeLevelOrderTraversal/BinaryTreeLevelOrderTraversalTests.cs: TheoryData carries LeetCode's own level-order int?[] array plus target, with a local BuildTree helper (same shape as that reference file) reconstructing the tree per example. Target is now a solution parameter rather than a benchmark-only constant; the benchmark keeps Target = -1 as its own workload-sizing constant matching BinaryTrees.Balanced's non-negative values, unchanged from before. Behavior unchanged on both arms.
problems.strategies: PathSumByDoubleDfs(BinaryTreeNode<int>?, int) - promoted from the benchmark's untested [Benchmark(Baseline = true)] arm (CountFromEveryNode/CountDownwardFrom); PathSumByPrefixSumHashMap(BinaryTreeNode<int>?, int) - reconciles the test's private PathSum/CountPaths helper and the benchmark's PrefixSumHashMap arm, which were already the same running-sum HashMap<long,int> algorithm with backtracking

problems.title: Find All Anagrams in a String
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<char,int> (same frequency-map shape ValidAnagramTests uses), composed into a fixed-size sliding window over s: two frequency maps (window vs. target) plus a running 'matched distinct characters' counter, so each character enters/leaves the window exactly once - O(n+m).
problems.notes: Two strategies, not three: the test's private FindAnagrams helper and the benchmark's SlidingWindowFrequencyMap were the same sliding-window algorithm, unified into one FindAnagramIndicesBySlidingWindow that returns LeetCode's real answer shape, List<int> of start indices. The benchmark's baseline arm (PerWindowFrequencyRebuild) previously returned a match COUNT (int) instead of indices - a weaker result than the real answer - so per the promote-don't-preserve-a-weaker-arm instruction I promoted it to return the actual List<int> of indices as FindAnagramIndicesByBruteForceRebuild; both [Benchmark] methods now return List<int>. Per section 17.5, the baseline's internals were switched from this repo's HashMap<char,int> to a plain BCL Dictionary<char,int> (the sliding-window strategy keeps the repo HashMap) since a baseline must stay BCL internally, only the input container a caller hands it may be a repo type - here the input is just two strings, so no hoisted-overload split was needed. No Fixtures/ folder existed for this problem, nothing to relocate. Verified: DSAExperimentation.LeetCode and DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks both build clean in the live repo. DSAExperimentation.Tests currently fails to build in the live repo, but only due to an unrelated, concurrent session's in-flight edit to DSAExperimentation.Tests/LeetCodeCoverage/PathSumIII/PathSumIIITests.cs (CS0053/CS0051 accessibility errors, a file this migration never touched - confirmed via git status showing it modified/untracked independently). Built and ran the full Tests project in an isolated scratch copy of the repo with only that one unrelated file excluded: build succeeded, and all 16 relevant tests passed (6 for this problem's two strategies x 3 examples, 6 for LC 440, plus all 4 Tests/Architecture/LayeringTests.cs tests), confirming tier order is intact and behavior is unchanged.
problems.strategies: FindAnagramIndicesByBruteForceRebuild (baseline, was benchmark's PerWindowFrequencyRebuild), FindAnagramIndicesBySlidingWindow (was the test's private FindAnagrams helper, same algorithm as benchmark's SlidingWindowFrequencyMap)

problems.title: K-th Smallest in Lexicographical Order
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Traversal.DepthFirst.DepthFirstSearch.Traverse - the same successor-function primitive LexicographicalNumbersTests (LC 386) already uses to walk the implicit 10-ary 'next digit' tree in lexicographical order; the k-th smallest is the (k-1)-th element of that order.
problems.notes: Simplest of the two: test helper and benchmark's non-baseline arm already agreed exactly (same algorithm, same int return), and the baseline already returned the real answer too, so this was mechanical extraction with no shape drift to fix. GlobalSetup only derives k = N/2 (trivial arithmetic, no domain object construction), so no hoisted-overload pair was needed per the 17.4 rule - both strategies take plain (n, k) ints. No Fixtures/ folder existed, nothing to relocate. Verified the same way as LC 438: DSAExperimentation.LeetCode and DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks build clean live; DSAExperimentation.Tests was verified in an isolated scratch copy (with only the unrelated in-flight PathSumIII test file from another session excluded) - build succeeded and all 6 tests for this problem's two strategies passed, alongside LayeringTests.
problems.strategies: FindKthNumberByGenerateAndSort (baseline, was benchmark's GenerateAndSortStrings), FindKthNumberByDepthFirstTraversal (was both the test's private FindKthNumber helper and the benchmark's DepthFirstTraversalOrder - already identical and already returning the real int answer, so no reconciliation of shape was needed here)

problems.title: Add Two Numbers II
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.SinglyLinkedList.SinglyLinkedListNode<int> + DataStructures.Stack.Stack<int> (aliased NumberStack, same Stack<T>/BCL-namespace-collision workaround ReverseIntegerTests uses). Digits are MSB-first here (opposite LC2's AddTwoNumbersTests), so Stack<T> reverses each list's digit order by pushing while walking .Next once, then popping both stacks in lockstep with a running carry, prepending each result digit - no input-list mutation/reversal.
problems.notes: The test's private helper and the benchmark's TwoStacksDigitwiseAdd were the same algorithm and already agreed on behavior (build the summed list); only the benchmark's baseline (BigIntegerConvertAndBack) measured something weaker (a digit count) than LeetCode's real answer (the summed list) - promoted it to AddByBigInteger, which now builds and returns the actual SinglyLinkedListNode<int> chain. Benchmark [Benchmark] methods wrap the solution calls with a CountDigits helper (mirrors the reference SerializeAndDeserializeBinaryTreeBenchmarks/CountNodes pattern) since [Benchmark] methods must be public and SinglyLinkedListNode<int> is internal. No fixture types existed to relocate. No hoisted-input overloads were needed: GlobalSetup's _first/_second are already the domain-shaped input the solution methods take directly, matching the AddBinary reference pair's shape.
problems.strategies: AddByBigInteger (naive baseline: BigInteger conversion + digit unpack, BCL-only internals, promoted from the benchmark's weaker digit-count measurement to build and return the real sum list), AddByTwoStacks (repo Stack<int> digitwise add with carry, the algorithm previously duplicated in the test's private AddNumbers/CombineDigitStacks helpers and the benchmark's TwoStacksDigitwiseAdd)

problems.title: Serialize and Deserialize BST
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Graph.Engines.Dags.Trees.BinaryTreeNode<TValue> + BinarySearchTree<TValue>.Insert. A BST's ordering invariant means a pre-order VALUE sequence alone (no null markers) round-trips: re-inserting those values in the same order into a fresh BinarySearchTree<int> re-derives the identical shape, since Insert's comparison walk is exactly the walk that produced pre-order in the first place. Serialize is a thin local pre-order walk (same shape SerializeAndDeserializeBinaryTreeTests/LC297 already uses, minus the null-marker token).
problems.notes: The test only ever exercised the preorder-value/BST-insert strategy; the benchmark's NullMarkerQueueRoundTrip baseline was a second, real, previously-untested LC 449 strategy (correct but not BST-invariant-exploiting) that is now under test via SerializeByNullMarkerQueue/DeserializeByNullMarkerQueue. Its internals were changed from the benchmark's original repo Queue<string> to a plain BCL Queue<string> to satisfy the 'naive baseline stays BCL internally' rule (matching the OpenTheLock/AddBinary/AddTwoNumbersII baseline precedent) - behavior is identical since both Queue types expose the same Enqueue/TryDequeue surface used here. The benchmark's original per-iteration BuildManual(...) call (inside the timed [Benchmark] method) was hoisted into [GlobalSetup] so both arms are handed the same prebuilt tree and construction is not charged to either measured strategy - this changes what is timed but not what either strategy returns. BuildManual/InsertManual stayed as private workload-construction helpers in the benchmark class (workload sizing/seeding, not an algorithm strategy), matching the RecoverBinarySearchTreeWorkloads precedent of building trees directly via BinaryTreeNode rather than through a strategy under test. No fixture types existed to relocate.
problems.strategies: SerializeByNullMarkerQueue/DeserializeByNullMarkerQueue (naive baseline: LC 297-style null-marker preorder grammar replayed through a plain BCL Queue<string>, ignoring the BST invariant), SerializeByPreOrderValues/DeserializeByBstInsert (the test's original algorithm: value-only preorder replayed through repo BinarySearchTree<int>.Insert)

problems.title: Delete Node in a BST
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Graph.Engines.Dags.Trees.BinarySearchTree<TValue>.TryDelete is exactly this problem's target API (leaf/one-child/two-child cases, the two-child case via in-order-successor promotion, all handled internally). Verified via Has plus InOrderTraversal/IInOrderHooks (same composition KthSmallestElementInABSTTests already uses) to confirm the result stays a validly ordered BST.
problems.notes: Reconciled both arms onto (BinarySearchTree<int> tree, int key) -> BinarySearchTree<int>, this repo's own tree type being the pre-existing convention for this problem's LeetCode input shape (the test file already committed to it). The benchmark baseline (CollectFilterRebuild) previously returned only a node count via CountNodes, never asserted anywhere; promoted to actually build and return a real, correct BinarySearchTree<int> from the filtered in-order values, inserted root-first so height stays O(log n). BinarySearchTree<TValue> has no public way to replace its private _root field, so the baseline returns a freshly rebuilt tree rather than mutating the input tree in place (the composed strategy, DeleteByBinarySearchTreeDelete, mutates and returns the same instance via TryDelete, which needs no such workaround since it's internal to the class). This sidesteps the encapsulation limit without adding any new DataStructures capability. Behavior on all original test inputs and the original benchmark's random shuffled-insertion workload is unchanged; only the answer shape and the baseline's returned artifact changed, per the instructions' 'promote a weaker measurement to the real answer' allowance.
problems.strategies: DeleteByCollectFilterRebuild, DeleteByBinarySearchTreeDelete

problems.title: Sort Characters By Frequency
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<char,int> counts occurrences, then DataStructures.Heap.Heap<T,TOrder> ordered by Graph.ShortestPaths.ByPriorityOrder<TNode,TWeight> - the same (node, priority) projection TopKFrequentElementsTests uses for LC347 - with frequency negated so the heap's only order (ascending priority) pops characters back out in descending-frequency order, popped to completion instead of capped at k.
problems.notes: The test's private FrequencySort helper and the benchmark's HashMapThenHeapDescendingPop arm were the same count-then-heap algorithm duplicated verbatim across both files; consolidated into FrequencySortByHashMapHeap. The benchmark's DictionaryThenOrderByDescending baseline was never asserted anywhere; promoted to a first-class, now-tested strategy (FrequencySortByDictionaryOrderBy). Both take/return plain string, matching real LeetCode's signature exactly (no repo domain type needed for this problem). Rewrote the assertion as a general 'characters grouped into runs of non-increasing length, same multiset as input' check shared by both strategies via one Examples table, replacing the original's hardcoded 'result is "eert" or "eetr"' enumeration - this matches LeetCode's actual 'any valid ordering' contract and generalizes cleanly to both algorithms' outputs instead of hand-enumerating tie-break orderings.
problems.strategies: FrequencySortByDictionaryOrderBy, FrequencySortByHashMapHeap

problems.title: Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons
problems.primitivesUsed: MergeSort.Sort<Element,TSequence> over ArrayIndexedSequence<(int Start,int End)> (Algorithms/Sorting) sorted by End via a custom comparer, then a single greedy scan. Deliberately NOT IntervalSet: its transitive overlap-merge (e.g. [1,2],[2,3],[3,4] merging into one interval) is not the same quantity as minimum stabbing points, which the test explicitly documents/asserts against.
problems.notes: Both the test's private helper and the benchmark's non-baseline arm already agreed on the answer shape (count of arrows, int) and algorithm, so no reconciliation was needed - just consolidation. Added a hoisted (int Start,int End)[] overload for each strategy since the benchmark's GlobalSetup already built points in that tuple shape (not int[][]); the two overloads can never collide since int[][] and (int,int)[] are distinct, non-convertible array element types. No fixtures existed to relocate. Verified: DSAExperimentation.LeetCode, .Tests, and .Benchmarks all build clean; full test suite (5801 passed/1 pre-existing skip) and LayeringTests pass.
problems.strategies: FindMinArrowShotsByBruteForceRescan(int[][]) + hoisted overload((int Start,int End)[]); FindMinArrowShotsBySortEndsThenGreedyScan(int[][]) + hoisted overload((int Start,int End)[])

problems.title: Assign Cookies
problems.primitivesUsed: MergeSort.Sort<int,ArrayIndexedSequence<int>> (Algorithms/Sorting) applied to both the greed-factor and cookie-size arrays, followed by a two-pointer greedy pass - same shape HIndexTests already exercises for a single array.
problems.notes: Both arms already agreed on shape (count of content children, int); consolidated as-is, behaviour unchanged. No hoisted overload needed - the benchmark's GlobalSetup already produces plain int[] arrays identical to LeetCode's own parameter shape, so there was nothing extra to hoist. No fixtures existed to relocate. Verified: all four projects build clean; full test suite (5801 passed/1 pre-existing skip) and LayeringTests pass.
problems.strategies: FindContentChildrenByBruteForceScan(int[] greed, int[] sizes); FindContentChildrenBySortThenTwoPointer(int[] greed, int[] sizes)

problems.title: 132 Pattern
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Stack.Stack<int> (aliased as OneThreeTwoStack) as a decreasing monotonic stack in a right-to-left sweep tracking a running 'third' candidate - same precedent as LargestRectangleInHistogramTests/TrappingRainWaterTests.
problems.notes: No return-shape disagreement between test and benchmark arms (both bool, matching LeetCode's real answer) - straightforward consolidation, no reconciliation needed. No hoisted overload needed (GlobalSetup only builds the raw int[] input, same as the AddBinary reference shape). No new DataStructures/Algorithms types introduced, so no Section 18 obligation.
problems.strategies: HasPatternByBruteForce (baseline, O(n^2) prefix-min rescan, promoted from benchmark's untested [Benchmark(Baseline=true)] arm), HasPatternByMonotonicStack (repo Stack<int> right-to-left sweep, was duplicated identically in both the test's private helper and the benchmark's non-baseline arm; consolidated to one)

problems.title: Circular Array Loop
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.SinglyLinkedList.SinglyLinkedListNode<int> + SinglyLinkedList.CycleDetection.HasCycle (Floyd's tortoise-and-hare) - the array's (i + nums[i]) mod n jump rule is built once as a functional graph of node links (edges left null for same-index self-loops and direction-mismatched adjacent steps, both of which disqualify a LeetCode cycle), then HasCycle is run from every start index.
problems.notes: No return-shape disagreement (both bool, matching LeetCode's real answer). DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks/Fixtures/CircularArray{Graphs,Node,Topology}.cs looked related by filename but belong to a different problem (LC 2515, Shortest Distance to Target String in a Circular Array) and were left untouched - not this problem's fixtures. Kept GlobalSetup's random-value construction inline unchanged rather than adding a hoisted-input overload, per step 7's 'preserving the original GlobalSetup workload' - the pre-migration benchmark already charged graph construction to the measured LinkedListFloyd method itself, and no fixture needed relocating. No new DataStructures/Algorithms types introduced, so no Section 18 obligation.
problems.strategies: HasLoopByHashSetWalk (baseline, BCL HashSet per-start walk, promoted from benchmark's untested [Benchmark(Baseline=true)] arm), HasLoopByLinkedListFloyd (repo SinglyLinkedListNode<int> functional graph + CycleDetection.HasCycle, was duplicated identically in both the test's private helper and the benchmark's non-baseline arm; consolidated to one)

problems.title: Poor Pigs
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound + DataStructures.Sequence.ArraySequence<long> - (rounds+1)^pigs is monotonic in pigs, so the minimum pig count is the lower bound of `buckets` over an ArraySequence<long> of precomputed powers.
problems.notes: Test's helper and benchmark's non-baseline arm both computed basis=(minutesToTest/minutesToDie)+1 then binary-searched precomputed powers - no drift there. The baseline arm (LinearRecompute) had drifted to a narrower signature (Buckets only, Basis hardcoded to 2) since it lived only in the benchmark; reconciled onto LeetCode's real 3-parameter signature (buckets, minutesToDie, minutesToTest) so both strategies answer the same question and the baseline is now under test. Benchmark calls both with MinutesToDie=MinutesToTest=15 (basis 2) to preserve the original measured workload exactly.
problems.strategies: MinPigsByLinearRecompute (naive baseline, promoted from the benchmark's untested [Benchmark(Baseline=true)] arm), MinPigsByBinarySearch (test's private helper + benchmark's BinarySearchOverPowers, which were already the same algorithm)

problems.title: Repeated Substring Pattern
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.StringMatching.PrefixFunctionSearch.ComputeFailureFunction (existing KMP) - s repeats iff failure[^1] is nonzero and s.Length % (s.Length - failure[^1]) == 0; this exact reuse beyond FindAll is called out in that primitive's own doc comment.
problems.notes: No drift between the test's private helper and the benchmark's KmpFailureFunction arm - both already returned bool via PrefixFunctionSearch.ComputeFailureFunction. The DivisorBruteForce baseline was untested before this migration; it is now a first-class method with its own theory cases. The benchmark's random-string GlobalSetup workload is left inline (workload sizing/seeding of a raw string, not a domain object) rather than hoisted into a second overload, since the LeetCode-shaped parameter (string) already is the prepared input.
problems.strategies: HasRepeatedSubstringPatternByDivisorBruteForce (naive baseline, promoted from the benchmark's untested [Benchmark(Baseline=true)] arm), HasRepeatedSubstringPatternByKmpFailureFunction (test's private helper + benchmark's non-baseline arm, which were already identical)

problems.title: LFU Cache
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.Cache.LfuCache.LfuCache<TKey,TValue> - existing HashMap + frequency-bucket linked-list cache directly models get/put LFU eviction.
problems.notes: This pair didn't match the literal 'inline helper vs inline benchmark arm' defect: the old test called DataStructures.Cache.LfuCache.LfuCache<int,int> directly (one Fact, no algorithm inlined), and the old benchmark was a placeholder stub (Baseline()=>1, PrimitiveComposed()=>1) measuring nothing. Followed the already-migrated LRUCacheSolution/LRUCacheTests/LRUCacheBenchmarks pattern (LC 146, the exact peer problem) as the template: added a genuine textbook baseline (CreateByDictionaryLinearScan) as a first-class strategy so it's finally under test, both factories return ICache<int,int>. Test now states LeetCode's official worked example (including the frequency-tie-broken-by-LRU case) plus the original coverage entry's thinner example as LFUCacheOp scripts (Get/Put with LeetCode's -1-on-miss convention), one Theory per strategy. Benchmark rebuilt as a script-replay harness (GlobalSetup builds a fixed put/get script sized by [Params(200, 2000)], Replay sums returned values so the JIT can't dead-code it) mirroring LRUCacheBenchmarks exactly. Both benchmark arms previously returned int (count of non-null parts) instead of the real ListNode[] answer; the test's helper already returned the real SinglyLinkedListNode<int>?[] answer, so that shape wins per LeetCode's actual signature. Could NOT literally 'promote' the benchmark arms to return the array itself: SinglyLinkedListNode<T> is a top-level internal class, and the [Benchmark] methods live on a public Benchmarks class, so returning it triggers CS0050 (a public member cannot expose a less-accessible type) - the same constraint the existing OddEvenLinkedListBenchmarks precedent hits and resolves the same way, by counting non-null parts via a small CountNonNullParts helper instead. Both [Benchmark] methods still call straight into the real SplitListToPartsBy* methods (which do return the real array), so the algorithm under measurement is now the one the test proves correct, and the baseline arm is asserted by the test. Clone/Build helpers stay duplicated in the test and benchmark harnesses (matches OddEvenLinkedListBenchmarks/Tests precedent - pure fixture plumbing, not the algorithm). No fixture types to relocate.
problems.strategies: SplitListToPartsByArrayRebuild (baseline: materializes values into a BCL List<int>, allocates k new node chains), SplitListToPartsByInPlaceRewire (test's original algorithm and the benchmark's former InPlaceSplit: walks the input chain once and cuts existing Next pointers in place)

problems.title: My Calendar I
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.IntervalSet.IntervalSet<int> (HasOverlap + Add). IntervalSet's own doc comment states it models CLOSED-interval merge semantics, explicitly NOT My Calendar's half-open [start,end) semantics, and says callers must adjust - so each event is stored as the closed pair (start, end - 1), which makes IntervalSet's closed-interval overlap rule exactly equivalent to half-open booking overlap for integer endpoints. Same encoding idiom this repo's DataStreamAsDisjointIntervalsTests (LC 352) already establishes in the mirror (+1) direction.
problems.notes: LC 729 is a stateful 'design' problem (Book() called repeatedly against one object), so - following the already-migrated DataStreamAsDisjointIntervalsSolution (LC 352) precedent for exactly this shape - the strategies are factory methods (CreateByIntervalSet/CreateByLinearScan) returning a public nested ICalendar interface implemented by two private classes, rather than static pure functions. The test's private nested MyCalendarI wrapper class became CreateByIntervalSet's IntervalSetCalendar; the benchmark's LinearScan baseline became CreateByLinearScan's LinearScanCalendar - previously two independent implementations of the same booking check, now one interface with two implementations both harnesses call into. No behavior change: same encoding, same overlap predicate, same accepted-count metric in the benchmark. No fixture types to relocate.
problems.strategies: CreateByIntervalSet (real answer: wraps this repo's IntervalSet<int>, encoding each half-open [start,end) booking as the closed pair (start, end-1) so IntervalSet's closed-interval overlap check is equivalent to half-open booking semantics), CreateByLinearScan (baseline: BCL List<(int,int)> scanned linearly per Book call)

problems.title: My Calendar II
problems.primitivesUsed: Two DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.IntervalSet.IntervalSet<int> instances - one merging all accepted bookings (_covered), one merging all double-booked territory (_doubled) - composed only via IntervalSet's public Get/Count/HasOverlap/Add surface (the same 'scan Get/Count directly, never reach into private storage' idiom RangeModuleTests.RemoveRange already uses), plus the same half-open-to-closed (end - 1) encoding used for My Calendar I. A new event is rejected only if it touches _doubled (would make a triple); otherwise its intersection with each interval already in _covered becomes new _doubled territory before the event itself is added to _covered.
problems.notes: Test's private MyCalendarII helper and benchmark's TwoIntervalSetScan were already the same algorithm (both bool-returning, half-open-to-closed encoding) - no drift to reconcile. Only defect was the untested TwoListScan baseline, now promoted into the solution class and covered by the same TheoryData examples as the real answer. Design-shaped (stateful ICalendar), matching MyCalendarISolution's established pattern.
problems.strategies: CreateByTwoIntervalSetScan (real answer, matches original test+benchmark IntervalSet arm), CreateByTwoListScan (benchmark's untested baseline, promoted to a tested first-class strategy)

problems.title: My Calendar III
problems.primitivesUsed: HashMap<int,int> as a delta/event-count accumulator (+1 at each booking's start, -1 at its end) plus MergeSort.Sort over an ArrayIndexedSequence<int> to walk the delta keys in ascending order on every Book() call - the standard 'sort the event points, sweep for the running-sum max' technique, substituting for the ordered-map primitive (TreeMap/NavigableMap) this repo doesn't have. Implemented as an incremental MyCalendarThree.Book(start,end) class matching LeetCode's real design-problem shape (same convention as RangeModuleTests), not an offline batch function.
problems.notes: Test helper and benchmark's non-baseline arm were verbatim duplicates (both int-returning max-overlap sweeps) - no drift to reconcile. Only defect was the untested BruteForceEventRescan baseline, now promoted and covered by the same TheoryData examples as the real answer. Design-shaped (stateful ICalendar returning int), matching MyCalendarISolution/MyCalendarIISolution's pattern.
problems.strategies: CreateByHashMapMergeSortSweep (real answer, matches original test's MyCalendarThree helper and benchmark's duplicate HashMapMergeSortSweep arm), CreateByBruteForceEventRescan (benchmark's untested baseline, promoted to a tested first-class strategy)

problems.title: Asteroid Collision

No new DataStructures/Algorithms types introduced (Stack<int> already existed), so no §18 obligation.

problems.title: Network Delay Time
problems.notes: Reconciled: the test's private helper (Dijkstra distances, max-or-(-1)) is now MinutesToReachAllByDijkstra. The benchmark's three arms (Dijkstra/BellmanFord/FloydWarshall) previously returned distances.Count (a weaker measurement than LC743's real answer, per the migration brief's allowance) - promoted all three to the real answer (max distance from source across all n nodes, or -1 if unreachable), consistent with the test's own semantics; FloydWarshall's arm reads its all-pairs matrix down to just the source row. All three strategies verified equal on LeetCode's own examples plus the original test's two cases (12 assertions total, up from 2). Full test suite (6120 tests) and LayeringTests pass; all four projects build clean.
problems.strategies: MinutesToReachAllByDijkstra, MinutesToReachAllByBellmanFord, MinutesToReachAllByFloydWarshall - each with a LeetCode-shaped overload (int[][] times, int n, int k) and a generic hoisted overload <TNode,TTopology>(List<TNode> vertices, TNode source) over IEdgeTopology<TNode, ListEdges<TNode,int>, int>
problems.relocatedTypes: None relocated. Added new problem-local witnesses NetworkNode/NetworkTopology to DSAExperimentation.LeetCode/NetworkDelayTime/ (used by this problem alone in the migrated tier). The pre-existing WeightedNode/WeightedTopology (Tests) and WeightedGraphNode/WeightedGraphTopology/RandomWeightedGraphs (Benchmarks) fixtures were deliberately left untouched: they are shared by a dozen other still-unmigrated LeetCode problems (JumpGameIV, CourseScheduleIV, ModifyGraphEdgeWeights, ReachableNodesInSubdividedGraph, etc.), not carried uniquely by this pair, so relocating/renaming them is out of this migration's scope and would risk colliding with other in-flight migrations. To let the benchmark keep using its existing WeightedGraphNode workload without a new duplicate representation, the three strategies' prepared-input overloads are generic over TNode/TTopology (the reduction itself - 'every node reached? take the max; else -1' - is exactly as generic as ShortestPath.Dijkstra), so the benchmark instantiates them with WeightedGraphNode/WeightedGraphTopology directly.

problems.title: Prefix and Suffix Search

The baseline (previously asserted nowhere) is now covered by the harness. Improved the benchmark per the hoisted-overload rule: the HashMap precompute was previously rebuilt inside the measured PrecomputedHashMapLookup benchmark method on every iteration rather than in [GlobalSetup]; added the hoisted HashMap-taking overload and moved the one-time precompute into Setup so only the O(1)-per-query lookup is charged to that arm now, matching what the strategy is meant to demonstrate. Verified against LeetCode's published examples plus both original test cases (10 assertions across both strategies, up from 5 for one strategy). Full test suite (6120 tests) and LayeringTests pass; all four projects build clean.
problems.strategies: SearchByLinearScan(words, prefix, suffix); SearchByPrecomputedHashMap(words, prefix, suffix) and its hoisted overload SearchByPrecomputedHashMap(HashMap<string,int> index, prefix, suffix); plus the public builder BuildPrefixSuffixIndex(words) used by both the LeetCode-shaped overload and the benchmark's [GlobalSetup]

Benchmark follows FibonacciBenchmarks' 3-strategy shape: NaiveRecursive (O(2^n)) vs TopDownMemoized (Memoizer) vs IterativeConstantSpace (O(n)/O(1)).

All three now live as first-class methods on MinCostClimbingStairsSolution, all returning the same int (no shape disagreement existed here - both original arms already agreed on 'minimum cost' as an int). No fixtures existed to relocate; no hoisted-input overload was needed since the LeetCode input (int[] cost) is already exactly what GlobalSetup builds. Full suite (6101 tests) plus LayeringTests pass; all four projects build clean.

problems.title: Contain Virus
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Traversal.DepthFirst.DepthFirstSearch.Traverse for the per-round 4-connected infected-region flood fill (the same primitive MaxAreaOfIslandTests/NumberOfIslandsTests/SurroundedRegionsTests already use for LC 695/200/130), re-run fresh every round since quarantine/spread mutate the grid between rounds. The round-by-round region ranking (HashSet-based threatened-cell count), wall counting, and quarantine/spread bookkeeping is this problem's own bespoke simulation control flow layered on top of that reused flood-fill primitive - not a new data-structure primitive. Benchmark compares a hand-rolled recursive flood fill (baseline, mirroring MaxAreaOfIslandBenchmarks) against the DepthFirstSearch.Traverse-based one, both wrapped in the identical simulation loop.
problems.notes: The test's private simulation used only the DepthFirstSearch.Traverse-based region discovery (LeetCode-shape signature, mutates its input grid in place); the benchmark additionally had a hand-rolled recursive-flood-fill baseline arm that was never asserted against anything, plus its own duplicate copy of the exact same round-by-round simulation logic (find regions -> rank by threat -> quarantine -> spread). Reconciled onto one shared simulation loop in ContainVirusSolution with two interchangeable region-collection strategies (mirrors MaxAreaOfIslandSolution's NaiveFloodFill/DepthFirstSearch pair for LC 695), both now returning LeetCode's real answer (int wall count) and both cloning their input grid internally so callers' arrays are never mutated - previously the test mutated the caller's array while the benchmark cloned via a private CloneGrid() before each call; unifying on 'always clone' matches the already-migrated MaxAreaOfIsland convention and fixes the latent mutation risk from theory data reuse across the two per-strategy test methods. The problem-local Region class (plain class, not record, for MaxBy reference-identity reasons) stayed a private nested type inside the solution per section 17.3 (a witness used by this problem alone). No DataStructures/Algorithms primitives were invented; DepthFirstSearch.Traverse (existing tier-2 primitive) is reused as-is. Full suite (6101 tests) plus LayeringTests pass; all four projects build clean.
problems.strategies: MinimumWallsByNaiveRecursiveFloodFill, MinimumWallsByDepthFirstSearchTraversal

problems.title: Open the Lock

Also uses DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<string,LockNode> to index the ~10,000 non-deadend combinations. Benchmark compares the textbook mutate-every-wheel Queue<string> BFS against Reduce.Graph BFS, mirroring WordLadderBenchmarks' shape, with target fixed at LC's own farthest combination ('5555') to force the full 20-turn BFS radius.

problems.title: Basic Calculator IV
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<TKey,TValue> - used twice: an evalvars->evalints substitution lookup, and the term-key(sorted '*'-joined variables)->coefficient polynomial accumulator built/combined by a hand-written recursive-descent parser (+/- lowest precedence, * higher, parens override) - plus DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.Sorting.MergeSort over ArrayIndexedSequence<Term> for the final degree-desc/lexicographic-asc term ordering.

The benchmark's arms also never exercised evalvars/evalints substitution (workload always passes none); the promoted EvaluateBy* methods do support it (needed for correctness/test parity) via a known-value lookup baked into each strategy's Variable closure at construction time - functionally identical to the test's original values.TryGetValue substitution. problems.title: Swim in Rising Water

problems.title: Cheapest Flights Within K Stops
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.ShortestPaths.ShortestPath.Dijkstra<TNode,TTopology,TEdges,TWeight> (unmodified) run over a layered (city, edgesUsed) state-space expansion of the flight list, rather than over the raw flight graph directly. Dijkstra itself has no 'bound the number of edges used' parameter, and the repo's BellmanFord likewise hardcodes its own round count (|V|-1) with no caller-controlled bound - so the K<=stops constraint is expressed as graph SHAPE instead: new Fixtures/FlightState.cs (city, stopsUsed pair) + FlightStateTopology.cs, where an edge only ever moves a state from stop-layer L to L+1. The answer is then the minimum distance to any (dst, layer<=K+1) node - a read-only post-processing step, zero changes to ShortestPath.cs.
problems.notes: Two strategies existed but only one was tested: the test's private FindCheapestPrice helper was the Dijkstra-over-stop-layers arm, and the benchmark's [Benchmark(Baseline = true)] NaiveDfs arm (unmemoized DFS over every path with at most K+1 edges) was asserted by nothing - it is now a first-class method under the same TheoryData. No behaviour change: both arms return LeetCode's answer (cheapest price, -1 via LeetCodeAnswer.None when unreachable), the baseline keeps BCL internals (recursion over List<(int To,int Price)>), and the benchmark keeps [Params(15, 40)] with the identical K = max(2, CityCount/6) stop bound, seed 7 and the same flight-generation draw order, so the measured workload is byte-identical. Test coverage went from 3 single-[Fact] cases (one strategy) to 6 examples x 2 strategies = 12 assertions: LC's own examples 1-3 (including n=4 K=1 -> 700), the same n=4 network with K=2 -> 400, the original unreachable case -> -1, and src == dst -> 0.
problems.strategies: FindCheapestPriceByNaiveDfs(int n, int[][] flights, int src, int dst, int k) + hoisted overload (FlightNetwork, int src, int dst, int k); FindCheapestPriceByDijkstraOverStopLayers(int n, int[][] flights, int src, int dst, int k) + hoisted overload (FlightStateGraph, int src, int dst)
problems.relocatedTypes: FlightState and FlightStateTopology moved from DSAExperimentation.Tests/LeetCodeCoverage/CheapestFlightsWithinKStops/Fixtures/ (and their duplicate private copies deleted from the benchmark) into DSAExperimentation.LeetCode/CheapestFlightsWithinKStops/ - a witness that answers this problem alone, per ARCHITECTURE.md 17.3, so no DataStructures/Algorithms type was created and no section 18 obligation arises. Two new problem-local containers added beside them for the hoisted overloads: FlightStateGraph.cs (the layered (city, edgesUsed) expansion, previously built inline in both the test and the benchmark) and FlightNetwork.cs (plain adjacency for the naive DFS, previously the benchmark's private BuildAdjacency). Workload generation moved to DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks/Fixtures/FlightWorkloads.cs (BuildFlights(cityCount, seed), StopBound(cityCount)). The test's Fixtures/ subfolder is deleted.

No [GlobalSetup] hoisting was needed - the prepared inputs are two plain strings, already LeetCode's own parameter shape, so no second overload exists to make ambiguous; the s+s doubling stays inside each strategy because it is part of the algorithm, not input construction. problems.title: All Paths From Source to Target

problems.notes: Two strategies inventoried: the test's private LargestArea helper and the benchmark's ConvexHullReduction arm were the SAME algorithm written twice (they differed only in where DrainToChain's Reverse() sat), so they reconcile to one strategy, LargestAreaByConvexHullReduction. problems.title: Ambiguous Coordinates
problems.primitivesUsed: No repo primitive applies - pure string generation/validation over the digit run (split into two non-empty halves at every position, then insert a decimal point at every position within each half, discarding invalid leading-zero/trailing-zero placements). Same 'no reusable data structure needed' category already established in this repo for GasStation/Candy/MaximumProductSubarray.
problems.notes: Two strategies: the test's private FindAmbiguousCoordinates helper and the benchmark's SliceAndCheckBoundary arm are the same slice-and-check-boundary technique, reconciled into FindCoordinatesBySliceAndCheck; the benchmark's untested [Benchmark(Baseline = true)] RebuildAndRescan arm (StringBuilder-materialize each candidate, then IndexOf the dot and re-walk both sides to validate) becomes FindCoordinatesByRebuildAndRescan and is now asserted. DELIBERATE CHANGE IN WHAT IS MEASURED, following ARCHITECTURE.md 17.8's WordLadderII precedent: both benchmark arms previously only COUNTED candidates (returned int) to keep the measured return cheap, while the test built the actual coordinate strings. LeetCode's real answer is the list of "(x, y)" strings, so both strategies are promoted to return List<string> and the benchmark now measures string construction as well as enumeration - the baseline's StringBuilder-vs-slice distinction is still exactly what separates the two arms, so the comparison keeps its meaning. SIGNATURE RECONCILIATION: the strategies take LeetCode's own parenthesized input ("(123)") and strip the parens internally, as the test's helper did; the benchmark's [GlobalSetup] previously produced a bare digit run, so it now wraps the generated digits in parentheses at setup time. That means no hoisted second overload was possible or needed here - a digit-run overload would have had the identical (string) signature and been ambiguous - and setup still pays all the construction; the measured method pays only one substring slice. [Params(8, 16)], the seed-816 generator and its never-a-leading-zero first digit are preserved verbatim, and the workload stays in the benchmark file rather than moving to Benchmarks/Fixtures: the existing DigitStringWorkloads.BuildDigits draws digit 0 from 0-9 and reusing it would have silently changed the measured workload. No fixture types existed for this problem, so nothing moved and section 18 incurs no new obligation. Tests kept both original examples and added LeetCode's other two published ones ("(00011)" and "(100)"), still comparing as sets since order is not part of the answer.
problems.strategies: FindCoordinatesByRebuildAndRescan, FindCoordinatesBySliceAndCheck

problems.title: Linked List Components

problems.notes: Two arms, one question, no drift to reconcile: both already returned the component count. The test's private ComponentCounter is now a private mutable struct ComponentRuns inside the solution class, shared by both strategies (struct rather than class so the baseline keeps its zero-allocation profile under MemoryDiagnoser). No hoisted overload was added: the benchmark's [GlobalSetup] prepares exactly LeetCode's own input shape (the list head and the nums array), and the Set<int> seeding is deliberately left inside the measured method because the O(n+k)-including-build cost is the whole point of the comparison against the O(n*k) baseline — so what the benchmark measures is unchanged. No fixture types existed for this pair (both files built their linked list with a private helper); the test keeps a private BuildList/AppendAfter harness helper, matching the migrated AddTwoNumbersTests precedent, and the benchmark keeps its private workload Build. problems.title: Race Car
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Reducing.Reduce.Graph closed over DistanceMapReduceAlgebra + BreadthFirstReduceOrder (BFS shortest-distance composition, same as OpenTheLockTests for LC 752) over an implicit IGraphTopology built from (position, speed) state nodes; the otherwise-unbounded state space is pre-materialized within a generous target-scaled bound (same shape CheapestFlightsWithinKStops/JumpGameII/OpenTheLock already use).
problems.notes: No drift between the two arms' answers (both returned the fewest commands), but they disagreed on how the bound was supplied: the test computed 4*target+2 and the power-of-two speed cap inline, while the benchmark's baseline borrowed the prepared graph's key set via _nodesByState.ContainsKey. That bound is now stated once in RaceCarStateSpace (Contains is exactly equivalent to the old ContainsKey test, since speeds are always +-powers of two within the cap), so the baseline no longer needs a materialized graph — its hoisted overload takes RaceCarStateSpace (a readonly record struct, not IEnumerable, so no ambiguity with the int-target overload) and the composed arm's takes RaceCarStateGraph. Benchmark [Params(6, 25)] and the [GlobalSetup] workload are preserved; both arms are now one-line calls. Two deliberate, LeetCode-correct behaviour choices on paths the originals never hit: unreachable now reports LeetCodeAnswer.None (-1) instead of the test's int.MaxValue leak (the benchmark baseline already returned -1), and nothing else changed on any original input. Test coverage went from 4 [InlineData] cases on one inlined helper to a 10-case TheoryData x 2 strategies = 20 assertions, keeping all four original cases (1->1, 2->4, 3->2, 6->5) and adding targets 4, 5, 7, 8, 10 and 25, whose expected values were cross-checked against an independent brute-force BFS.
problems.strategies: RaceCarSolution.MinCommandsByMutationQueue(int target) + hoisted overload MinCommandsByMutationQueue(RaceCarStateSpace space, int target) — the benchmark's former untested [Benchmark(Baseline = true)] MutationQueueBfs, BCL Queue/HashSet internals; RaceCarSolution.MinCommandsByReduceGraph(int target) + hoisted overload MinCommandsByReduceGraph(RaceCarStateGraph graph, int target) — the Reduce.Graph + DistanceMapReduceAlgebra BFS that the test's private MinCommands and the benchmark's ReduceGraphBfs each re-implemented.
problems.relocatedTypes: RaceCarNode and RaceCarTopology moved (from BOTH DSAExperimentation.Tests/LeetCodeCoverage/RaceCar/Fixtures/ and DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks/Fixtures/, two near-identical copies) to DSAExperimentation.LeetCode/RaceCar/RaceCarNode.cs and RaceCarTopology.cs. The benchmark fixture RaceCarGraphs.cs (which duplicated the test's private BuildStateGraph) became DSAExperimentation.LeetCode/RaceCar/RaceCarStateGraph.cs, and its bounding rule was split out as DSAExperimentation.LeetCode/RaceCar/RaceCarStateSpace.cs. All four are tier 4, not DataStructures/ or Domain/: their content is LC 818's own (position, speed) command semantics and its target-scaled search box, used by this problem alone — the same placement CheapestFlightsWithinKStops uses for FlightState/FlightStateGraph/FlightStateTopology. Nothing new was added under DataStructures/ or Algorithms/, so section 18 owes no new direct unit tests.

problems.title: Most Common Word
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<string,int> for word-frequency counting (same shape TopKFrequentWordsTests uses) plus DataStructures.Set.Set<string> for banned-word membership checks.
problems.notes: Two strategies inventoried: the benchmark's [Benchmark(Baseline=true)] DictionaryAndHashSet arm (BCL Dictionary+HashSet, previously never asserted) and the HashMapAndSet arm, which is the same algorithm the test's private MostCommonWord/WordTally helper carried. The two agreed on answer shape (string), so nothing had to be reconciled. Answer-shape reconciliation that WAS needed: the benchmark arms were handed pre-tokenized, already-lowercase words, so neither tokenized nor lower-cased banned words; the LeetCode-shaped overloads now do both (tokenize on runs of non-letters, lower-case banned), exactly as the test helper did. The benchmark's [GlobalSetup] hoists tokenization only, so the second overload takes DynamicArray<string> (a repo container that is not IEnumerable, so it can never be bound by the (string paragraph, ...) overload); banned stays a string[] and each arm still builds its own membership structure inside the measured method (HashSet for the baseline, Set<string> for the composed arm) so the original measurement - Dictionary+HashSet vs HashMap+Set - is preserved rather than collapsed to just Dictionary-vs-HashMap. problems.title: Short Encoding of Words
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Set.Set<string> to evict every proper suffix of each word from a full-word set (test's primary primitive). Benchmark additionally showcases DataStructures.Graph.Engines.Dags.Trees.LowercaseTrie<TValue> as a second, distinct repo-primitive strategy (insert reversed words; a word needs its own encoding iff its reversed node is a trie leaf).
problems.notes: Three strategies inventoried: the benchmark's baseline NestedLoopSuffixCheck (never asserted before), SetBasedSuffixRemoval (the same algorithm the test's private MinimumLengthEncoding/Deduplicate/FindWordsThatAreNotSuffixesOfAnother helpers carried), and LowercaseTrieLeafCount (reversed-word LowercaseTrie<bool>, benchmark-only until now). Behaviour correction, per 'LeetCode's real answer wins': the two benchmark-only arms never deduplicated, because the benchmark's workload came out of a HashSet and was distinct by construction; on a real LeetCode input containing a repeated word (e.g. ["time","time"]) they would have charged the same word twice - the pairwise scan's 'other.Length > word.Length' guard never drops an equal-length duplicate. All three strategies now deduplicate first (the baseline with a BCL HashSet, so its internals stay BCL; the two composed arms share a Set<string>-based Deduplicate), and the test pins the repeated-word case that would have caught it. On the benchmark's own distinct workload the measured answers are unchanged. No hoisted overload: the benchmark's [GlobalSetup] prepares nothing beyond LeetCode's own string[] input, so there is no construction to move off the measured method. [Params(500, 5_000)], seed 820, the shared SuffixPool and the prefix generation are preserved verbatim in [GlobalSetup]. Test kept both original examples and added three (a suffix-of-a-longer-word pair, two words sharing one suffix, and the repeated-word case). No new DataStructures/ or Algorithms/ types were introduced by either problem, so nothing is owed under section 18; neither problem had a Fixtures/ folder or a Benchmarks/Fixtures entry to relocate.
problems.strategies: MinimumLengthByPairwiseSuffixScan(string[] words); MinimumLengthBySuffixEviction(string[] words); MinimumLengthByReversedTrieLeaves(string[] words)

problems.title: Making A Large Island
problems.primitivesUsed: DepthFirstSearch.Traverse (same flood-fill primitive MaxAreaOfIsland/NumberOfIslands use) labels each island with a distinct id written back into the grid; HashMap<int,int> records each island's area by id; Set<int> dedupes a water cell's up-to-4 neighboring island ids before summing their areas plus the flip itself.
problems.notes: Two strategies, both handed LeetCode's int[][] shape, so no hoisted overload was needed - the benchmark's [GlobalSetup] already builds exactly the LeetCode-shaped input and the [Params(20, 60)] sizing plus seed 7 / 0.6 land probability stayed in the harness. BEHAVIOUR CHANGE, deliberate, on the baseline arm only: NaiveRepeatedFloodFill only ever considered flipping a water cell, so on a grid that is already entirely land (no water cell to flip) it returned 0 instead of the full grid area - LC 827 allows 'at most one' flip, so the answer there is rows*cols. That arm was never asserted by anything, which is exactly the defect this migration removes; it is now promoted to LeetCode's real answer via a sawWater guard and the test's all-land example ([[1,1],[1,1]] -> 4) pins it. Every other grid is unaffected, since any grid containing a zero has a zero adjacent to its largest island, so the best flip dominates. The composed strategy's answers are unchanged. Both strategies now clone the grid internally before labeling/probing it (the benchmark previously cloned inside each measured arm, so the measurement is preserved), matching MaxAreaOfIslandSolution's precedent for LC 695. The three private record structs (GridContext, IslandGridContext, FloodFillGrid) were file-private in the old harnesses and became private nested types of the solution class - nothing moved to another tier, so no section 18 obligation. Test kept all four original examples and added two: a 3x3 checkerboard of single-cell islands (merge of two islands) and [[1,1,0],[1,0,0],[0,0,0]] -> 4, whose flip touches the same island through two neighbours, which is what the labeled strategy's Set<int> dedup exists for (without dedup it would report 7).
problems.strategies: LargestIslandByNaiveFloodFill (from the benchmark's [Benchmark(Baseline = true)] NaiveRepeatedFloodFill arm, now first-class and under test), LargestIslandByLabeledFloodFill (the test's private LargestIsland helper and the benchmark's LabeledFloodFillWithAreaLookup arm, which were the same algorithm written twice)

problems.title: Flipping an Image
problems.primitivesUsed: Stack<int> (this repo's LIFO Stack, same digit-reversal primitive ReverseInteger/RotateImage already compose) - push each row, then pop it back out while inverting each bit (1-value) in the same pass, since popping naturally reverses row order.
problems.notes: Two strategies, both taking LeetCode's int[][] and returning it, so no hoisted overload applies. Both rewrite the rows in place and return the same image, exactly as the original test's helper did; the harnesses clone before calling, which is where the old benchmark's Clone already sat (inside the measured method), so the measurement is unchanged and [Params(50, 300)] / seed 4 sizing stayed in the benchmark. No behaviour change: the test arm and the benchmark arm already agreed on LeetCode's answer shape here. No fixture types existed in either file. Test kept all three original examples (both published LC examples plus the single-column case) and added [[0,1]] -> [[0,1]], an even-width row where the flip and the inversion cancel, which the old suite had no case for.
problems.strategies: FlipAndInvertImageByTwoPointerReverse (from the benchmark's [Benchmark(Baseline = true)] TwoPointerReverseAndInvert arm, BCL-only internals, now under test for the first time), FlipAndInvertImageByStackReverse (the test's private FlipAndInvertImage helper and the benchmark's StackReverseAndInvert arm - the same Stack<int> pass written twice)

problems.title: Rectangle Overlap
problems.primitivesUsed: None in the coverage test itself - reduces to O(1) scalar arithmetic (strict per-axis interval overlap), the same 'lighter repo-primitive fit' case already precedented by RectangleArea (LC 223). The benchmark's brute-force baseline does compose DynamicArray<bool> as a unit-grid coverage scan, mirroring RectangleAreaBenchmarks.
problems.notes: Two distinct strategies existed: the test's private IsRectangleOverlap helper (closed-form axis-interval check) and the benchmark's unasserted [Benchmark(Baseline=true)] UnitGridIntersectionScan; the benchmark's non-baseline ClosedFormAxisOverlap arm was a third copy of the test helper, reconciled onto one method. Both now answer LeetCode's real shape (bool from two int[4] rectangles), so the baseline is under test for the first time. Two deliberate changes, both noted in the solution's comment: (1) the baseline's coverage grid is now a plain bool[] instead of this repo's DynamicArray<bool>, per ARCHITECTURE.md 17.5 (a baseline's internals stay BCL; only its input container may be a repo type) and following the identical call RectangleAreaSolution already made for LC 223's unit-grid arm - the scan's asymptotics and the workload are unchanged; (2) the benchmark's private Rectangle/GridFrame record structs are gone, the eight loose GlobalSetup ints now build the two int[] rectangles that are LeetCode's own input shape, so no hoisted overload was needed and construction stays in [GlobalSetup]. No fixture types existed to relocate; no new DataStructures/ or Algorithms/ types, so no section 18 obligation. One candidate example was dropped after it failed: a degenerate zero-area rectangle ([1,1,1,4]) makes the closed form report true and the grid scan false, but LC 836 constrains both inputs to non-zero area, so the input is out of spec rather than either arm being wrong.
problems.strategies: RectangleOverlapSolution.OverlapsByClosedFormAxisIntervals(int[] rec1, int[] rec2); RectangleOverlapSolution.OverlapsByUnitGridIntersectionScan(int[] rec1, int[] rec2)

problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.DisjointSet.DisjointSet (union-find over word indices) + DataStructures.Set.Set<int> (dedupe resolved roots into a group count)

The shared IsSimilar/MismatchState predicate (equal, or exactly two mismatched positions that are each other's swap) is private to the solution class and stays pure-BCL, so the baseline remains textbook. No hoisted overload: [GlobalSetup] produces a string[] word pool, which is already LeetCode's own input shape, so a second overload would only have been an ambiguous duplicate. No fixture types existed for this problem (no test Fixtures/ folder, no Benchmarks/Fixtures entries) and no new DataStructures/Algorithms type was needed, so section 18 owes nothing here. Test kept all 3 original examples and adds two thin-coverage cases (three mutually dissimilar words -> 3 groups; single word -> 1 group).
