problems.title: Guess the Word
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.DynamicArray.DynamicArray<string> (shrinking candidate pool, rebuilt fresh each round)
problems.notes: The two arms disagreed on answer shape and the benchmark's baseline was also weaker than the problem: the test helper returned the found secret word, while BOTH benchmark arms returned a guess COUNT, and the baseline arm never consulted a Master at all - it compared candidates straight against the private _secret field, so it was not even playing LC 843's interactive game. Reconciled onto LeetCode's real answer: every strategy now takes a SecretWordMaster, only learns match counts through master.Guess, and returns the secret word; the benchmark arms return string instead of int. That is a deliberate change in what is measured (per section 17.8's precedent) but not in the work done - the guess sequence, the number of rounds and the per-round filtering cost are identical. The baseline also gained the test version's empty-pool guard (while candidates.Count > 0, returning string.Empty) instead of the original benchmark's while(true), which would have thrown if the secret were absent; on every original input the behaviour is unchanged. No hoisted overload: [GlobalSetup] prepares a string[] word list, already LeetCode's input shape; only the per-run SecretWordMaster (O(1)) is constructed inside each arm, because its guess counter is per-invocation state. Test keeps both original LeetCode examples and adds three cases the original lacked - the same word list with a non-first secret so the filtering loop actually runs, a four-word list needing three rounds, and a single-word list - and now asserts the 10-guess budget for the baseline too. Benchmark keeps [Params(100, 1_000)], seed 843 and the random-word workload verbatim.
problems.strategies: FindSecretWordByInPlaceListRemoval (baseline, BCL List<string> filtered in place back-to-front, previously only the benchmark's InPlaceListRemoval arm and never asserted), FindSecretWordByShrinkingPool (DynamicArray<string> rebuilt each round, previously the test's private FindSecretWord helper and the benchmark's ShrinkingCandidatePool arm)
problems.relocatedTypes: Master (the test's private nested oracle) -> DSAExperimentation.LeetCode/GuessTheWord/SecretWordMaster.cs, renamed SecretWordMaster and keeping its GuessCount budget counter - a witness for this problem alone, so section 17.3 puts it in the problem folder, not Domain/. The MatchCount helper that was written out three times (test helper, test oracle, benchmark) -> DSAExperimentation.LeetCode/GuessTheWord/WordMatch.cs as WordMatch.ExactPositionMatches. Neither is a DataStructures/ or Algorithms/ type, so no section 18 mirrored unit tests are owed.

Both arms already agreed on the bool answer shape, so no reconciliation was needed. Baseline internals stay BCL per 17.5. It cannot change any answer (a successful sweep consumes cards in whole groups, so a non-divisible hand must fail some group anyway), and I kept it on both arms as the textbook early-out - the benchmark workload is always divisible, so the measured path is unchanged. No hoisted overload: the [GlobalSetup] workload is an int[] hand, LeetCode's own shape; counting and sorting ARE the algorithm and must stay inside the measured method. problems.title: Shortest Path Visiting All Nodes

One reconciliation: on an unreachable/disconnected graph the test helper returned int.MaxValue while the benchmark baseline returned -1. LeetCode guarantees a connected graph, so this is unobservable on any original input; the migrated ReduceGraph arm now reports LeetCodeAnswer.None (-1) like the baseline. VisitStateGraph is deliberately not IEnumerable so the two ReduceGraph overloads cannot be ambiguous. [Params(8, 11)] and the seed 847 workload are unchanged. problems.title: Cat and Mouse
problems.notes: The correct algorithm is retrograde/Zermelo-style multi-source BFS over (mousePos, catPos, turn) states, seeded from known terminal states and propagated backward with AND/OR win-loss logic - required because draws are possible, i.e. the state graph has genuine cycles. The repo's two closest primitives both explicitly rule this shape out: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer's own doc comment states its precondition as a well-founded (acyclic) state graph - a cyclic Cat-and-Mouse recurrence would stack-overflow under it, not just misanswer; Algorithms.TopologicalSort.TopologicalSort (Kahn's algorithm) is DAG-only single-outcome in-degree propagation, not a two-player AND/OR retrograde solver with a draw outcome. No production primitive here performs cycle-safe fixed-point propagation over an adversarial game graph, so solving it would mean hand-writing the entire retrograde-BFS algorithm ad hoc rather than composing existing primitives. Missing primitive: a Zermelo-style retrograde/fixed-point game-state solver that tolerates cycles by construction.

problems.title: Beautiful Array
problems.primitivesUsed: HashMap<int,int[]> as the top-down memoization cache for the standard odds/evens divide-and-conquer construction (Build((n+1)/2) -> 2x-1, Build(n/2) -> 2x).
problems.notes: No fixture types and no [GlobalSetup] - the only input is a length - so no hoisted overloads. LC 932 is checker-judged (ANY beautiful permutation of 1..n is accepted) and the two strategies legitimately return DIFFERENT valid arrays: the backtracking arm returns the lexicographically smallest, and the two first diverge at n=8 ([1,5,3,2,7,6,4,8] vs [1,5,3,7,2,6,4,8]). The harness therefore asserts the property (permutation of 1..n AND no i<k<j with 2a[k]=a[i]+a[j]) rather than pinning one array; that is strictly what LeetCode's judge checks, and pinning the D&C output would wrongly fail the equally valid baseline. The original's exact-value facts (n=1 -> [1], n=4 -> [1,3,2,4]) are subsumed: both arms do produce exactly those, verified, and both are the unique/lexicographically-first beautiful arrays there. Lengths: shared Examples = 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,10,12 for BOTH arms (keeps the original's 1,2,4,5,10 and adds 3,6,8,12). The original's n=17 case is kept as a second LargeExamples theory on the memoized arm alone (17,33,64), because the backtracking baseline is exponential - measured ~13M search nodes at n=16 and ~12x that at 17, i.e. tens of seconds - so putting 17 in the shared set would have made the suite unusable. Benchmark [Params(6,8)] preserved unchanged.
problems.strategies: ConstructByPrunedBacktracking (the benchmark's previously-unasserted baseline arm, made static over n instead of reading the [Params] field; BCL arrays only), ConstructByMemoizedDivideAndConquer (the test's private Build helper and the benchmark's second arm, which were duplicate implementations; composes DataStructures.HashMap<int,int[]> as the memo)

problems.title: Number of Recent Calls

problems.notes: Two strategies were inventoried: the test's private RecentCounter class (repo Queue<int> sliding window, duplicated as the benchmark's SlidingWindowQueue arm) and the benchmark's untested [Benchmark(Baseline = true)] FullHistoryRescan (BCL List + full rescan per ping), which is now a first-class method under test. Answer shape reconciled onto the whole stream, following the already-migrated OnlineStockSpan precedent for a design/stream problem: both take the timestamp stream and return the count produced by each ping, in order. Deliberate promotion: both benchmark arms previously returned only the LAST ping's count; they now return every ping's count (the real judge-visible answer) - the per-ping work measured is unchanged, only an int[] write per call is added to both arms equally. Baseline internals stay BCL (List<int> + linear rescan). No hoisted overload was needed: [GlobalSetup] only sizes/seeds the timestamp array (tier-5 workload sizing per 17.7) and hands it straight to the LeetCode-shaped int[] parameter, so no construction is charged to the measured method. No fixture types existed to relocate and no new DataStructures/Algorithms type was created, so 18 adds nothing. Test kept both original assertions (LeetCode's 1/100/3001/3002 example and the far-apart stream) and added five cases, including both window boundaries (a request exactly 3000ms old counts, 3001ms does not). Also dropped the vestigial `partial` on the test class. 26 tests pass across this problem and 936; Architecture/LayeringTests pass.
problems.strategies: NumberOfRecentCallsSolution.PingCountsByFullHistoryRescan(int[]), NumberOfRecentCallsSolution.PingCountsBySlidingWindowQueue(int[])

problems.title: Stamping The Sequence
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.Stack.Stack<int> - reverse-simulation stamping discovers moves in reverse chronological order; the repo Stack records them via Push then unwinds to forward order via TryPop (same explicit-repo-Stack move AsteroidCollisionTests/BasicCalculatorTests already make).
problems.notes: Two strategies: the benchmark's untested ListPrepend baseline (List<int>.Insert(0, i), O(m^2) shifting) and the repo-Stack<int> record-then-unwind arm, which the test had inlined as MovesToStamp/TryReverseStamp/ExtractMovesInOrder and the benchmark had re-inlined as StackAndReverse. The two files disagreed on answer shape: the test returned int[] start indices while both benchmark arms returned only a COUNT (order.Count / result.Length). LeetCode's real answer wins, so both strategies now return the int[] move sequence - a deliberate promotion of the benchmark arms from counting to building. That also fixed a real defect in the baseline arm: ListPrepend reported its count without ever checking turnedCount == target.Length, so on an unsatisfiable target it returned a nonzero partial count instead of the empty answer; it now returns [] like the stack arm. Both arms share the identical reverse-simulation scan (StampCanvas + TryStampWindow/WindowMatchesStamp) and differ only in the recorder, so they return the same sequence; the baseline's recorder stays BCL. No hoisted overload needed: [GlobalSetup] only builds the repeated-stamp target string (tier-5 sizing) and passes it to the LeetCode-shaped (stamp, target) parameters. The test's private StampScanState/ReplayReconstructsTarget were algorithm/assertion helpers, not fixture types - the scan moved into the solution, the replay check stayed as the harness's postcondition assertion (many move sequences are valid, so the harness pins the move count and replays the indices onto a blank canvas exactly as the judge does). Kept all three original examples and added three: stamp == target, a target shorter than the stamp, and a target whose reverse simulation gets stuck partway ('abc' -> 'abca'). No new DataStructures/Algorithms types, so 18 adds nothing.
problems.strategies: StampingTheSequenceSolution.MovesToStampByListPrepend(string, string), StampingTheSequenceSolution.MovesToStampByStackReverse(string, string)

problems.title: Range Sum of BST

The two arms did not disagree on answer shape here — the benchmark's baseline simply pinned low/high as consts; those became ordinary parameters, and the benchmark passes the same Low=0/High=20 values, so behaviour and measurement are unchanged ([Params(500, 20_000)], seed 938, Fisher-Yates shuffle + BinarySearchTree.Insert setup all preserved). problems.title: Find the Shortest Superstring
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms/DynamicProgramming/Memoizer.cs — bitmask-TSP memoized recursion over (Mask,Last) state; TResult is (Best,Prev) so the winning permutation can be reconstructed, not just its overlap total. Overlap-matrix computation and final string assembly are plain local helper logic, the same shape other coverage tests (e.g. StickersToSpellWordTests) already use around Memoizer.
problems.notes: Test arm and benchmark arm disagreed on the answer shape: the test built LeetCode's actual superstring (string), while BOTH benchmark arms only computed totalLength - bestOverlap (an int length). Promoted both strategies to LeetCode's real answer - the superstring itself - per §17.8's precedent; the brute force now tracks the winning permutation instead of just its overlap total, and the benchmark methods return string. Measured work is otherwise unchanged (the permutation search and the memoized (Mask,Last) recurrence are line-for-line the originals), and assembling the string is O(total length), negligible against n!/2^n. WordOverlaps is the prepared-input overload's parameter so the overlap matrix is still built in [GlobalSetup], never charged to the measured method; it is not a BCL collection, so the two overloads cannot be ambiguous. [Params(6, 9)] and seed 943 preserved, and the fixture reproduces the identical word list (verified). Cross-checked in a scratch console app: both strategies agree on length and containment for the exact benchmark workloads at n=6 (24) and n=9 (35), and over 300 random word sets. Test harness keeps both original examples (LC's 'alex/loves/leetcode' -> 17 and the DNA example -> 16) and adds four thin-coverage cases (single word, two-word overlap, mutual one-char overlap, and an all-a/b set whose optimum is a non-obvious order). Assertions are length + containment of every word rather than an exact string, because LC 943 accepts any minimum-length superstring and the two strategies legitimately break ties differently. Side effect: this file was the repo-wide compile break other sessions recorded in manifest.json notes (a Memoizer method-group/Func mismatch in the old test); DSAExperimentation.Tests now builds clean. 26 tests pass across both problems; Architecture/LayeringTests pass.
problems.strategies: ShortestSuperstringByPermutations(string[]) + hoisted ShortestSuperstringByPermutations(WordOverlaps) [was the benchmark's BruteForcePermutations baseline, previously untested]; ShortestSuperstringByMemoizedBitmask(string[]) + hoisted ShortestSuperstringByMemoizedBitmask(WordOverlaps) [was the test's private ShortestSuperstring helper and the benchmark's MemoizedBitmaskDp arm, which had drifted apart]
problems.relocatedTypes: New problem-local type DSAExperimentation.LeetCode/FindTheShortestSuperstring/WordOverlaps.cs - the overlap matrix + assembly rule that was written out twice (BuildOverlaps/OverlapLength in both the test and the benchmark). It is a §17.3 problem-only witness (it fixes LC 943's 'no word is a substring of another' premise and its drop-the-overlap concatenation), so it stays in the LeetCode problem folder, not Domain/ - hence no §18 DataStructures/Algorithms test obligation. Word generation (alphabet ACGT, length 5, seed 943, distinctness loop) moved verbatim out of the benchmark into DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks/Fixtures/SuperstringWordWorkloads.cs as workload sizing/seeding only (§17.7). No existing repo type was duplicated; Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer is reused as before.

problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<TKey,TValue> - groups every point-pair (candidate diagonal) by (2*midpointX, 2*midpointY, diagonalLengthSquared); two pairs sharing a key are a rectangle's two diagonals (equal-length diagonals bisecting each other is the textbook rectangle criterion), and area is the product of the two adjacent sides at the shared diagonal endpoint.
problems.notes: Two distinct strategies existed: the benchmark's [Benchmark(Baseline = true)] BruteForceQuadruples (O(n^4) over every 4-point combination, three diagonal pairings each, bisect-and-equal-length checked by hand) and the diagonal-grouping arm that the test's private MinAreaFreeRect helper and the benchmark's DiagonalGrouping arm implemented identically (test wrapped it in a private DiagonalIndex class, benchmark inlined the same HashMap walk). The test's DiagonalIndex helper moved into the solution class as a private nested type: it is bespoke bookkeeping for this one problem, not a Representation/Operations/content witness, so it earns no tier of its own. No hoisted overload: the benchmark's [GlobalSetup] builds int[][] _points, which IS LeetCode's input shape, so a second overload would have been ambiguous with nothing to gain (same shape as the already-migrated MinimumAreaRectangleBenchmarks). problems.strategies: MinAreaFreeRectByQuadrupleScan, MinAreaFreeRectByDiagonalGrouping

problems.title: K Closest Points to Origin
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Heap.Heap<Element,TOrder> with MaxHeapOrder<(int,int,int)> (KthLargestElementTests/KthLargestBenchmarks size-k-heap precedent) - a size-k max-heap over (SquaredDistance, X, Y), popping the farthest point whenever the heap grows past k. ValueTuple<int,int,int> already implements IComparable<(int,int,int)> lexicographically, so MaxHeapOrder's Element:IComparable<Element> constraint needs no new comparer type.
problems.notes: Two strategies inventoried: the test's private KClosest helper and the benchmark's SizeKMaxHeap arm were the same size-k Heap<(int,int,int), MaxHeapOrder> algorithm written twice (reconciled into KClosestBySizeKMaxHeap); the benchmark's [Benchmark(Baseline = true)] FullSort arm had no test at all and is now the first-class KClosestByFullSort. PROMOTED MEASUREMENT: the benchmark's two arms both returned a long sum of squared distances rather than the points themselves - a weaker question than LeetCode 973 asks. Both methods now return LeetCode's real answer, int[][] of the k nearest points, and the benchmark arms return that; the baseline's internals stay BCL (Array.Sort with a comparer over a (distance, point) array). No hoisted overload: [GlobalSetup] builds the int[][] point cloud, which is already LeetCode's own input shape, so the measured method is handed it directly and no construction is charged to it. No fixture types existed for this pair. Test grew from 2 [Fact]s to 6 examples x 2 strategies = 12 assertions; because LeetCode permits any order (and the heap arm drains farthest-first while the sort arm returns nearest-first) every example is compared as a set, and no example has a distance tie straddling the k boundary. Ledger: one check-responsibility-extraction waiver added for the test harness ('K' prefix shared by the class name and both strategy-named facts), mirroring the existing MergeTwoSortedListsTests entry.
problems.strategies: KClosestPointsToOriginSolution.KClosestByFullSort(int[][] points, int k); KClosestPointsToOriginSolution.KClosestBySizeKMaxHeap(int[][] points, int k)

problems.title: Odd Even Jump
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Sorting.MergeSort.Sort<int,ArrayIndexedSequence<int>> with a custom IComparer<int> (QueueReconstructionByHeightTests/LargestTriangleAreaTests custom-comparer precedent) sorting indices by (value, index) - ascending for odd jumps, descending for even jumps, ties toward the smaller index - plus DataStructures.Stack.Stack<int> as a monotonic stack over that sorted order (DailyTemperaturesTests precedent) to recover each index's next-jump target in one O(n) sweep per direction. A backward odd[]/even[] boolean DP then counts good starting indices.
problems.notes: Two strategies inventoried: the test's private OddEvenJumps helper and the benchmark's MergeSortStackSweep arm were the same MergeSort-plus-monotonic-Stack<int> sweep written twice (reconciled into OddEvenJumpsByMergeSortStackSweep); the benchmark's [Benchmark(Baseline = true)] BruteForceScan arm - the O(n^2) per-index forward scan - had no test and is now the first-class OddEvenJumpsByBruteForceScan, internals all BCL. No signature disagreement between the two originals: both counted good starting indices and returned int, so behaviour is unchanged. The shared backward odd/even reachability DP is one private helper both arms call; the benchmark's CountTrue(odd[]) form was kept over the test's goodStarts=1-then-count form (equivalent on every input, including n=1). No hoisted overload: [GlobalSetup] builds the int[] workload, already LeetCode's input shape. No fixture types existed for this pair. Method order in the solution class follows check-vertical-organization's expected DFS call order. Ledger: one check-responsibility-extraction waiver added for the test harness ('Odd' prefix shared by the class name and both strategy-named facts).
problems.strategies: OddEvenJumpSolution.OddEvenJumpsByBruteForceScan(int[] arr); OddEvenJumpSolution.OddEvenJumpsByMergeSortStackSweep(int[] arr)

problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Sorting.MergeSort.Sort<int,ArrayIndexedSequence<int>> (SortAnArrayTests precedent) sorts side lengths ascending; a single backward scan then checks the triangle inequality on each consecutive triple from the top, returning the first (largest) valid perimeter.

problems.title: Unique Paths III
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Backtracking.Backtrack.Search (choose/explore/unchoose over one shared mutable state, WordSearchTests/SudokuSolverTests precedent) closed over a 4-directional grid walk whose candidate set is every unvisited non-obstacle neighbor - a Hamiltonian-path count. Candidates stops offering moves the instant the walk steps onto the '2' square (matching LeetCode's rule that the walk must end there, not merely pass through it); a walk only counts via IsSolution once every non-obstacle cell has been visited.
problems.notes: Three arms, two strategies: the test's private CountUniquePaths helper and the benchmark's BacktrackEngine arm were the same Backtrack.Search composition (including a verbatim duplicated private sealed class State, identical in both files) - they reconcile onto CountUniquePathsByBacktrackEngine. The benchmark's [Benchmark(Baseline = true)] SpecializedRecursive - a hand-rolled recursion that marks visited cells by overwriting the grid with -1 and restores on unwind - was never asserted; it is now CountUniquePathsBySpecializedRecursion and under test for the first time. Both arms already returned LeetCode's int walk count, so nothing disagreed and nothing was promoted. The baseline keeps its in-place grid mutation (BCL-only internals per 17.5); it restores every cell as the recursion unwinds, so the shared TheoryData grids are left exactly as found and the two theory methods cannot interfere. State stayed a private nested type of the solution class: it is a witness for THIS problem alone (LC 980's covering-walk rule), which section 17.3 / step 5 put in the problem folder, not DataStructures or Domain - the WordSearchSolution precedent does exactly this. No hoisted overload: [GlobalSetup] builds a fixed literal int[][] grid, which is already LeetCode's input shape. Kept all 3 original examples and added [[1,2]] -> 1, the degenerate case where the walk ends on its first step. Benchmark keeps its fixed 3x4 grid workload (no [Params] originally, per the NQueens/SudokuSolver fixed-board convention it cites). No fixture types and no new primitive, so section 18 owes nothing.
problems.strategies: CountUniquePathsBySpecializedRecursion(int[][]), CountUniquePathsByBacktrackEngine(int[][])

problems.title: Time Based Key-Value Store
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<TKey,TValue> keyed by `key`, each holding parallel DataStructures.DynamicArray.DynamicArray<int>/DynamicArray<string> histories (Timestamps/Values) appended in the problem-guaranteed strictly increasing timestamp order Set is called in - the same parallel-array shape OnlineElectionTests already uses. problems.title: Rotting Oranges
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Queue.Queue<(int Row, int Col)> as the multi-source BFS frontier, seeded with every already-rotten orange at minute 0 - same multi-source shape as ZeroOneMatrixTests. Two behaviour-relevant reconciliations, both noted deliberately: (1) the test's private helper mutated the caller's grid in place (writing 2 into rotted cells), which would have made repeated benchmark invocations non-idempotent - the migrated multi-source strategy instead tracks rot state in its own visited map and leaves the input grid untouched, exactly as the benchmark's MultiSourceBfs arm already did; the returned answer is unchanged on every original input. No new DataStructures/ or Algorithms/ types, so no section 18 obligation. Test keeps all three original examples and adds [[0]]->0, [[1]]->-1, [[2]]->0, [[1,2]]->1 and [[2,1,1,1,1]]->4.

problems.title: Minimum Number of K Consecutive Bit Flips
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Queue.Queue<int> holding active flip-start indices; queue.Count % 2 gives O(1) cumulative flip parity per position in a single left-to-right sweep. Benchmark baseline is the textbook in-place k-window flip; Queue-tracked parity measured ~7-20x faster with ~80-98% less allocation (BenchmarkDotNet ShortRun, K=300, Length=3000/30000 - chosen so the O(n*k) vs O(n) gap is actually visible).
problems.notes: No fixture types existed for this pair, so nothing was relocated and no new DataStructures/Algorithms type was created (section 18 not triggered). The test helper and the QueueTrackedParity benchmark arm were already the same algorithm written twice; they agreed on the answer shape (int, -1 for impossible), so reconciliation was mechanical - the shared -1 is now LeetCodeAnswer.None. The baseline was the untested arm: it lived only in the benchmark with K hard-coded at 300, and is now parameterized by k and asserted against the same six examples. One deliberate behaviour tightening: the baseline clones its input before flipping in place, so it no longer destroys the caller's array (the benchmark previously cloned at the call site; the clone simply moved inside). No hoisted overload was needed - the LeetCode shape is (int[], int) and that is exactly what [GlobalSetup] prepares, so nothing beyond the array is constructed inside the measured method. [Params(3_000, 30_000)], K=300 and the seeded random bit workload are preserved verbatim (seed 1). Tests grew from 3 assertions to 12 (6 examples x 2 strategies): LC's three published examples plus all-ones/exact-fit/window-wider-than-array boundaries.
problems.strategies: MinKBitFlipsByInPlaceWindowFlip (baseline, BCL-only O(n*k) window rewrite, promoted from the benchmark's private InPlaceWindowFlip/FlipWindows/AllOnes trio and now under test for the first time); MinKBitFlipsByQueueTrackedParity (DataStructures.Queue.Queue<int> of active flip start indices, Count parity as the effective bit)

problems.title: Number of Squareful Arrays

problems.strategies: NumSquarefulPermsByFullPermutationFilter (baseline, BCL recursion over a used[] flag array generating every distinct permutation and testing squarefulness at the leaves, promoted from the benchmark's private CountViaFullPermutations/Permute/TryPlace/IsSquareful/PermutationState cluster); NumSquarefulPermsByPrunedBacktracking (Algorithms.Backtracking.Backtrack.Search with both the duplicate-value skip and the perfect-square adjacency folded into candidate enumeration)

problems.title: Construct Binary Search Tree from Preorder Traversal
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Graph.Engines.Dags.Trees.BinarySearchTree<int>.Insert, called once per preorder value - inserting values in preorder order rebuilds the exact source BST. Benchmark: repeated BinarySearchTree.Insert on an adversarial ascending preorder (O(n) per insert, O(n^2) total) vs. the classic O(n) upper-bound recursion building BinaryTreeNode<int> directly; Dry-job smoke run at Length=200/2000 showed the bounded recursion 2.9x-16x faster as n grows.
problems.notes: Two strategies: the test's private helper / benchmark baseline arm RepeatedTreeInsert (compose BinarySearchTree<int>.Insert per value) and the benchmark-only BoundedRecursion (upper-bound single-pass build), which was never asserted. Answer shape reconciled onto LeetCode's real answer - the built BinaryTreeNode<int>? root: the test helper already returned it, but BOTH benchmark arms measured something weaker (baseline returned tree.Count, an O(1) read; the other arm ran a separate CountNodes traversal it was then charged for). Both strategies now return the root, and the benchmark takes root?.Value ?? 0 purely as a keep-alive, which costs both arms the same O(1) - a deliberate, symmetric change in what is measured, noted per section 17.8's precedent. No hoisted overload is needed: [GlobalSetup] prepares an int[], which is already LeetCode's own input shape, so adding a second overload would only create ambiguity. LC examples 1 and 2) and ReducedBoardExamples, the same five scenarios at boardSize 500, asserted by BOTH strategies so they are shown to agree cell for cell. No fixtures existed for this problem and no new DataStructures/Algorithms type was needed - it composes existing Algorithms.Traversal.DepthFirst.DepthFirstSearch.Traverse and DataStructures.Set.Set<T>, so section 18 owes nothing here.

problems.title: Print in Order
problems.notes: Genuine primitive gap, not an effort gap. LeetCode 1114 requires synchronizing three concurrently-running threads (first()/second()/third() invoked by separate threads in arbitrary scheduling order) so second() only runs after first() returns and third() only after second() returns - the actual challenge is a thread-synchronization mechanism (semaphore/monitor/condition-variable/event), not a sequential algorithm. This repo (per ARCHITECTURE.md's Representation/Topology/Operations model) is entirely single-threaded: a repo-wide search confirms zero uses of Semaphore, Monitor/lock, AutoResetEvent/ManualResetEvent, Interlocked, Thread, or Task anywhere under DSAExperimentation/DataStructures or DSAExperimentation/Algorithms. Composing a correct solution would require inventing a new concurrency-coordination primitive from scratch, which the task explicitly disallows building ad hoc. A trivial single-threaded stand-in (just calling the three methods in sequence with no real threads) wouldn't actually exercise any repo primitive and wouldn't prove anything about synchronization, so it isn't a legitimate substitute.

problems.title: Print FooBar Alternately
problems.notes: Same root gap as #1114. LeetCode 1115 requires two threads to alternate printing 'foo'/'bar' n times, enforced via real thread synchronization (semaphore/monitor-style signaling) so the interleaving is guaranteed regardless of OS scheduling - not something a sequential data structure or algorithm can express. This repo has no concurrency/synchronization primitive anywhere (confirmed by the same repo-wide search as #1114: no Semaphore, Monitor/lock, ResetEvent, Interlocked, Thread, or Task in production code). Building one would be inventing a new production primitive ad hoc, which is out of scope here; marking blocked rather than faking a single-threaded, non-concurrent stand-in.

Adjacent manifest entries for the same concurrency cluster (#1114 Print in Order, #1115 Print FooBar Alternately, #1195 Fizz Buzz Multithreaded) are all still pending with no prior precedent closing this gap. This is a genuine missing primitive domain, not an effort shortfall, so no ad hoc synchronization primitive was built per the task's constraint.

problems.title: Longest Well-Performing Interval
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/HashMap/HashMap.cs only: a running +1 (tiring day) / -1 (non-tiring day) prefix score turns this into the same 'HashMap first-occurrence-of-a-prefix-value' pattern already established by ContinuousSubarraySumTests.cs/Benchmarks.cs - a well-performing interval has positive total score iff prefixScore[j] > prefixScore[i], so the answer is either the whole prefix (when the running score is already positive) or the span back to the earliest index whose score was exactly one less. Verified: dotnet build (Debug, Tests project) 0 warnings/errors; dotnet test --filter LongestWellPerformingInterval passes all 3 new Facts (LeetCode's own example plus an all-tiring and a never-tiring edge case); dotnet build -c Release (Benchmarks project) 0 warnings/errors; a BenchmarkDotNet --job Dry run confirms both strategies execute and agree, with the expected crossover - BruteForce (O(n^2)) ahead at Length=200 but HashMapPrefixScore (O(n)) ~7x faster at Length=5,000, hours generated as an unweighted 9-vs-6 coin flip so the running score keeps oscillating near zero instead of drifting monotonically.
problems.notes: Two distinct strategies across the pair: the benchmark's [Benchmark(Baseline = true)] BruteForce (O(n^2), previously untested by anything) and the linear HashMap<int,int> first-occurrence-of-a-running-score pass, which the test's private LongestWpi/ScoreTracker helper and the benchmark's HashMapPrefixScore/PrefixScoreState arm implemented twice; both returned the same int, so they reconciled onto one method (the test's ScoreTracker form, kept verbatim as a private nested class). Brute force was restructured into an outer loop plus a private LongestIntervalFrom(hours, start) - equivalent, since within a fixed start the longest positive-score interval is just the last end at which the running score is still positive. No hoisted overload: LeetCode's own input shape here IS the prepared input (int[] hours built in [GlobalSetup]), matching the migrated ContinuousSubarraySum precedent. TiringThreshold = 8 moved into the solution as the problem's semantics; the workload's TiringHour/NotTiringHour/coin-flip generation and [Params(200, 5_000)] stayed in the benchmark. Test kept all 3 original examples and added 4 (single tiring day, single non-tiring day, [6,9,9], and [6,6,9,9,6] whose answer comes only from the map-lookup branch rather than the running-score-already-positive branch). No fixtures existed; no new DataStructures/Algorithms types, so no section 18 obligation.
problems.strategies: LongestWpiByBruteForce(int[] hours), LongestWpiByPrefixScoreMap(int[] hours)

problems.title: Smallest Sufficient Team
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms/DynamicProgramming/Memoizer.cs (bitmask memo state over 'which required skills are still missing', the same shape CanIWinTests.cs/Benchmarks.cs already establish) composed with DataStructures/HashMap/HashMap.cs (skill-name -> bit-index assignment) and DataStructures/Set/Set.cs (coverage verification in test assertions). people.Length <= 60 fits a long bitmask of chosen team members, so the memoized TResult IS the team itself, not just its size; each step branches only on the lowest still-missing skill bit and keeps whichever person's completion yields the fewest team members. Verified: dotnet build (Debug, Tests project) 0 warnings/errors; dotnet test --filter SmallestSufficientTeam passes all 3 new Facts (both of LeetCode's own official examples, verified by minimal team size + full skill coverage rather than exact indices since multiple optimal teams are valid, plus a trivial single-person-covers-everything case); dotnet build -c Release (Benchmarks project) 0 warnings/errors; a BenchmarkDotNet --job Dry run confirms both strategies execute and agree, with the expected crossover at SkillCount=10 (MemoizedRecursion ~2.5x faster than BruteForceRecursion, each of PeoplePerSkill=3 people per skill deliberately routing every branch at a given recursion level to the identical child mask, so brute force pays true O(3^SkillCount) recomputation of only SkillCount+1 actually-distinct states).
problems.notes: ANSWER-SHAPE RECONCILIATION: the test's helper returned the actual team (int[] of person indices) while BOTH benchmark arms returned only PopCount of the team mask - a weaker measurement. Per the section 17.8 precedent both strategies now return LeetCode's real answer, int[], and the benchmark harness takes .Length; the recursion work is unchanged, only the final mask-to-array extraction is now charged to the measured method. The baseline arm (BruteForceRecursion - the unmemoized self-recursion, previously asserted by nothing) is now a first-class method under test. Both strategies share the private BestTeam/BestTeamCoveringBit recursion body exactly as the original benchmark shared ComputeSmallestTeam between its two arms, so the only difference is memoization; the baseline's internals are plain recursion over BCL int[]/long/List, with Memoizer used only by the composed arm. Hoisted overloads take SkillMasks so mask construction is charged to [GlobalSetup]; [Params(6, 10)] SkillCount and PeoplePerSkill = 3 workload preserved. Test kept all 3 original examples (including both published LeetCode examples) with the same Set<string>-based minimal-coverage assertion, now stated once as TheoryData and run once per strategy, plus 3 added cases (single skill, three disjoint specialists, and a 4-skill grid with two valid minimal teams); the original's extra Assert.Equal(0, team[0]) is subsumed by the size-plus-coverage check, which only person 0 can satisfy there. No new DataStructures/Algorithms types, so no section 18 obligation.
problems.strategies: SmallestTeamByBruteForceRecursion(string[] reqSkills, string[][] people) + SmallestTeamByBruteForceRecursion(SkillMasks), SmallestTeamByMemoizedBitmask(string[] reqSkills, string[][] people) + SmallestTeamByMemoizedBitmask(SkillMasks)
problems.relocatedTypes: SkillMasks -> DSAExperimentation.LeetCode/SmallestSufficientTeam/SkillMasks.cs (new, problem-local): the skill-bit indexing and per-person mask building that the test carried as private BuildSkillBitIndex/BuildPersonSkillMasks helpers, plus the FullMask. It fixes LC 1125's own content and is meaningless elsewhere, so per ARCHITECTURE.md section 17.3 it sits beside the solution (the CountWaysToBuildRoomsInAnAntColony precedent), not in Domain/ - and being a sealed class rather than an IEnumerable it also serves as the section 17.4 prepared-input parameter with no overload ambiguity against string[][].

problems.notes: Design problem, so the strategies are CreateBy<Strategy> factories returning a stateful object - the same shape the already-migrated TimeBasedKeyValueStoreSolution uses, which the original test's own comment already pointed at as its sibling. RECONCILIATION: the test and the benchmark disagreed about what they were even answering. The test implemented the full published LC 1146 interface (a private SnapshotArray class with Set/Snap/Get over parallel DynamicArray<int> SnapIds/Values columns plus BinarySearch.UpperBound over a DynamicArraySequence<int>). The benchmark implemented neither Set nor Snap: its two arms were loose methods over raw pre-seeded DynamicArray<int> columns that measured only the floor lookup, so its [Benchmark(Baseline = true)] LinearFloorScan arm was a bare loop nothing asserted. Per 17.5 its internals stay BCL (List<(int SnapId, int Value)>[] and a forward scan), while CreateByBinarySearchFloor keeps the test's exact composition. Both strategies agree that a later Set inside the same snapshot wins and that an index with no history before the queried snapshot reads 0; both are now covered by added examples. problems.title: Longest Chunked Palindrome Decomposition
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.RollingHash.RollingHash for O(1) equality screening of the growing left/right chunk pair in the classic greedy two-pointer walk, with every hash hit confirmed via a real SequenceEqual before being trusted - the same screen-then-verify shape RollingHashSearch.FindAll already uses (RollingHash is an equality screen, not an oracle, per RollingHashValue's own doc comment). Benchmark compares the textbook O(n^2) repeated-string-concatenation solution against the RollingHash-screened O(n) walk, forced through their full worst case with an all-distinct-character input so no chunk match ever short-circuits the window growth.
problems.notes: Two distinct strategies, both the same greedy two-pointer walk, differing only in how the growing left/right chunk pair is compared. LongestDecompositionByRollingHash is the test's and the benchmark's non-baseline arm merged (they were byte-for-byte the same algorithm written twice, the exact 17.1 defect): RollingHash gives an O(1) equality screen over text's own indices, confirmed by a real SequenceEqual per RollingHashSearch.FindAll's screen-then-verify convention. LongestDecompositionByStringConcatenation is the benchmark's previously-unasserted [Benchmark(Baseline = true)] NaiveConcatenation arm, promoted to a first-class method so it is finally under test; per 17.5 its internals stay BCL (repeated string concatenation and ==). No reconciliation of answer shape was needed - unlike LC 1146, both files already returned the same int chunk count - but the two arms wrote their tail condition differently (the concatenation arm's `Left.Length > 0 || I == J` vs the hash arm's `MatchStart <= J`); I verified by hand that they agree on every example, including the degenerate lengths, and added "a" (1), "aa" (2), "ab" (1), "aba" (3), "aaa" (3) and "abab" (2) as cases precisely because those are where the tail condition turns. All three original LeetCode examples are kept. Benchmark preserves [Params(200, 2_000)] and the all-distinct-code-point [GlobalSetup] text; the measured method takes the prepared string, which is already LeetCode's own input shape, so no hoisted overload was needed and RollingHash construction stays inside the measured arm exactly as before. No fixture types existed; the loop-carried state record structs are private implementation details. Build clean; 18 tests pass.
problems.strategies: LongestChunkedPalindromeDecompositionSolution.LongestDecompositionByRollingHash(string text), LongestChunkedPalindromeDecompositionSolution.LongestDecompositionByStringConcatenation(string text)

problems.title: Online Majority Element In Subarray
problems.primitivesUsed: HashMap<int, DynamicArray<int>> position index keyed by value, queried via DynamicArraySequence<int> as the BinarySearch.LowerBound/UpperBound IRandomAccessSequence witness (same idiom as RangeModuleTests/LC715). A seeded-Random bounded-sample query (the problem's official approach, valid since LeetCode guarantees 2*threshold > range whenever an answer exists) counts occurrences in O(log n) instead of an O(range) rescan.
problems.notes: Design problem, so the two strategies are classes behind a shared IMajorityChecker (same shape as the already-migrated StreamOfCharacters LC 1032), not static methods. Three arms reconciled into two strategies: the test's private MajorityChecker and the benchmark's HashMapWithBinarySearchPerQuery were the SAME strategy, but the benchmark arm was weaker - it only ever tried _values[left] as the candidate, which is correct only because its generated queries sat inside a uniform run. It is promoted to LeetCode's real answer (randomized sampling, the problem's own official approach), per the 'weaker measurement may be promoted' rule; on the run-shaped workload the first sample always lands on the answer, so the measurement is unchanged apart from one Random.Next per query. The benchmark's [Benchmark(Baseline = true)] LinearScanPerQuery arm was previously asserted by nothing and is now MajorityCheckerByRangeTally, under test. Construction stays hoisted: both checkers are built in [GlobalSetup] (originally BuildPositionIndex was), so the measured methods only replay the 200 queries; [Params(1_000, 8_000)], RunLength 25, QueryCount 200 and seed 1 all preserved. -1 now comes from LeetCodeAnswer.None. Examples grew from 2 facts to 5 examples x 2 strategies (13 queries each); every query obeys LeetCode's 2*threshold > right-left+1 guarantee, which is what makes both strategies unambiguous. No fixture types existed to relocate and no new DataStructures/Algorithms types were added, so section 18 owes nothing here.
problems.strategies: OnlineMajorityElementInSubarraySolution.IMajorityChecker (shared surface); MajorityCheckerByRangeTally (baseline, BCL Dictionary per-query tally); MajorityCheckerByPositionIndex (HashMap<int, DynamicArray<int>> position index + randomized sampling + BinarySearch.LowerBound/UpperBound over DynamicArraySequence<int>)

problems.title: Remove Zero Sum Consecutive Nodes from Linked List
problems.primitivesUsed: SinglyLinkedListNode<TValue> + HashMap<int, SinglyLinkedListNode<int>> - standard prefix-sum trick: map remembers the last node seen at each running sum (pass 1), then each node is relinked to map[sum].Next (pass 2), splicing out every zero-sum run in O(n).
problems.notes: BEHAVIOUR CHANGE, deliberate, in the baseline arm only. The benchmark's NestedLoopRescan baseline was incorrect and nothing asserted it: its inner walk began at `end = start` rather than `end = start.Next`, so the running sum it tested included start's own value. The effect is that a zero-sum run that begins at a real node (rather than at the dummy head) had only its tail spliced out. On LeetCode's own example 2, [1,2,3,-3,4], the original baseline returned [1,2,3,4] instead of the correct [1,2,4]; it happened to agree with the map strategy on examples 1 and 3 only because the cancelling run there started at the head. LeetCode's real answer wins, so the promoted baseline starts the inner walk at start.Next; it now agrees with RemoveZeroSumSublistsByPrefixSumMap on all six harness examples and, cross-checked, on the 300-node benchmark workload (31 of 300 nodes survive in both). No hoisted overload: both strategies splice nodes out of the list they are handed, so - exactly as the already-migrated RemoveLinkedListElements pair does - [GlobalSetup] hoists only the int[] workload values (seed 1, [Params(300, 3_000)] preserved) and each [Benchmark] rebuilds the list, since a cached list would only be valid for the first measured iteration. Benchmark arms return object? rather than SinglyLinkedListNode<int> because the node type is internal (CS0050); the original's private Count(...) helper was dropped with the counting, which was harness bookkeeping rather than the answer. Test examples grew from 3 Facts to 6 TheoryData rows x 2 strategies = 12 assertions: LeetCode's three published examples plus 'nothing cancels', 'the whole list cancels', and two adjacent cancelling runs. No fixture types existed for this problem and no Fixtures/ folder had to be deleted. No new DataStructures/ or Algorithms/ type was needed, so section 18 owes nothing here.
problems.strategies: RemoveZeroSumSublistsByNestedRescan (was the benchmark's untested [Benchmark(Baseline = true)] NestedLoopRescan private helper), RemoveZeroSumSublistsByPrefixSumMap (was written twice - once as the test's private RemoveZeroSumSublists helper, once again as the benchmark's HashMapPrefixSum helper; both copies were identical, so no reconciliation was needed there)

problems.title: Sort Items by Groups Respecting Dependencies
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms/TopologicalSort.TopologicalSort.TrySort (Kahn's algorithm), applied twice - once over an item-dependency graph, once over a derived group-dependency graph - via IGraphTopology/ListChildren/NaturalChildOrder witnesses, the same composition CourseScheduleII already uses. Local ItemNode/GroupNode/ItemTopology/GroupTopology fixtures under a Fixtures/ subfolder (two distinct node types needed, mirroring CourseSchedule/Fixtures). problems.notes: Two strategies: the benchmark's baseline NaiveRescanTwoLevelSort (O(V^2 + V*E) rescan per level, untested before) and the composed KahnsTwoLevelSort, which was also the test's private SortItems helper. BEHAVIOUR RECONCILED IN LEETCODE'S FAVOUR, as instructed: the test's helper returned [] when either TopologicalSort.TrySort reported a cycle, but BOTH benchmark arms ignored cycle detection entirely - KahnsTwoLevelSort discarded TrySort's bool and used the partial `out` order, and NaiveRescanTwoLevelSort's rescan simply stopped early and Combine sized the result to the partial count. LeetCode's real answer is an empty array on a cycle at either the item or the group level, so both migrated strategies now return []. On the benchmark's own workload (acyclic by construction) this changes nothing measured. The naive arm's internals stay BCL (Dictionary in-degree map + List rescan), per 17.5; only the ItemNode/GroupNode input containers are repo-adjacent, and those are the caller's choice. Hoisted overloads follow the CourseScheduleII precedent: 4-param LeetCode shape vs 2-param prepared-graph shape, unambiguous by arity, and the group count is read off groups.Count rather than the benchmark's GroupCount constant. beforeItems is typed int[][] (matching CourseScheduleII's int[][] prerequisites and xUnit's TheoryData serialization) instead of the old List<int>[]; same values, same behaviour. [Params(50, 1_000)], GroupCount = 5, MaxFanOut = 3 and the full acyclic fan-out [GlobalSetup] workload are preserved. The two relocated node/topology pairs answer LC 1203 alone (ItemNode.GroupId is this problem's two-level semantics), so per ARCHITECTURE.md 17.3/17.6 they belong in the LeetCode problem folder, exactly as CourseScheduleII keeps CourseNode/CourseTopology - not DataStructures/ or Algorithms/, so section 18 owes no new mirrored unit-test file. Tests went from 2 assertions to 5 shared examples x 2 strategies = 10; because a valid ordering is not unique the harness asserts LeetCode's actual properties (permutation of 0..n-1, every beforeItems edge respected, each group contiguous) rather than one arbitrary array. Added a discriminating case the original lacked: an acyclic ITEM graph whose derived GROUP graph is cyclic (n=4, m=2, group=[0,1,1,0], beforeItems=[[],[0],[],[2]]) -> [], which a single item-level sort would answer wrong.

problems.notes: Test and benchmark did not disagree on answer shape here; the defect was that the recursive List-recovery baseline existed only in the benchmark and was never asserted, and that RecoverHooks was written out twice. Both are fixed. The benchmark's private BuildCompleteTree helper was deleted in favour of the existing tier-5 workload builder Benchmarks/Fixtures/BinaryTrees.Balanced(nodeCount), which constructs the identical complete binary tree (its initial values are i rather than -1, which is immaterial: recovery overwrites every node's Value from its position, and in a complete tree the recovered value at index i is exactly i). [Params(200, 2_000)], the 200-target sample, the 2x target range and the Random(1) seed are unchanged; the per-arm 'count how many of the sampled targets are found' loop stays in the harness as a private CountFound(IFindElements) so each [Benchmark] arm is a one-line call into the solution. Test examples grew from 2 facts to a 4-case TheoryData covering LeetCode's three published examples ([-1,null,-1]; [-1,-1,-1,-1,-1]; [-1,null,-1,-1,null,-1] whose recovered values are {0,2,5,11}) plus a root-only case, stated as LeetCode's own level-order int?[] arrays because BinaryTreeNode<int> is internal and cannot appear in a public TheoryData signature (the DiameterOfBinaryTreeTests convention). The pre-migration test's full Find(0..6) sweep is preserved on the five-node case. The spurious 'partial' on the old test class (there was only ever one part) is gone. 8 assertions now, up from 7 in 2 facts; no new DataStructures/ or Algorithms/ types, so section 18 owes nothing extra.

problems.title: Find Winner on a Tic Tac Toe Game
problems.primitivesUsed: None beyond plain fixed-size row/column/diagonal running-count arrays - same 'no stronger reusable repo primitive beyond ordinary array bookkeeping' shape JumpGameTests already documents; this problem is O(1) extra space by nature, and Grid/GridNode model pathfinding adjacency, not score tracking, so they would not be a genuine fit.
problems.notes: THE TWO ARMS DISAGREED ON THE ANSWER AND BOTH BENCHMARK ARMS MEASURED SOMETHING WEAKER THAN LEETCODE'S REAL ANSWER; LeetCode wins, as instructed. (1) The benchmark arms never returned "Draw": they returned a `lastResult` that stayed "Pending" unless some line completed, so a full board with no winner reported "Pending" rather than "Draw". (2) They also kept replaying after a win instead of stopping at the first completed line, overwriting an earlier winner with a later one - not LC 1275's semantics. The migrated methods both return "A"/"B" at the first completed line, "Draw" once moveCount == boardSize*boardSize, and "Pending" otherwise, matching the test's original private helper exactly on 3x3. This does not weaken the measurement: the workload is a random alternating fill of every cell, where a completed line of length n (n = 10 or 60) is vanishingly unlikely, so both arms still walk every move and now both report "Draw". The benchmark's n x n generalization is preserved via the second `boardSize` overload (LeetCode's own overload delegates with the public BoardSize = 3), and the anti-diagonal test generalizes correctly from the test helper's hardcoded `row + col == 2` to `row + col == boardSize - 1`. The benchmark's [GlobalSetup] now shuffles cells into `int[][]` instead of `(int Row, int Col)[]` so the measured methods take LeetCode's own move shape; that is workload construction, still charged to [GlobalSetup], and [Params(10, 60)] Size and the deterministic shuffle are unchanged (seed renamed to MoveSeed = 1275, the problem number, matching the OpenTheLock convention). All four original test examples kept, plus a column win, an anti-diagonal win, and an empty move list - none of which the originals covered. Constants PlayerCount/PendingResult/PlayerAResult/PlayerBResult that lived in the benchmark are now private consts on the solution class alongside Draw. No repo primitive applies to either strategy (Grid/GridNode model pathfinding adjacency, not line occupancy), so nothing was invented and no fixture types existed to relocate; no new DataStructures/ or Algorithms/ type means no section 18 obligation for either problem.
problems.strategies: FindWinnerByBoardRescan(int[][] moves) + FindWinnerByBoardRescan(int[][] moves, int boardSize) (baseline, promoted out of the benchmark's private RebuildAndRescanEveryMove/ScanAllLines/ScanRows/ScanColumns/ScanMainDiagonal/ScanAntiDiagonal/LineWinner helpers - now asserted for the first time); FindWinnerByRunningCounts(int[][] moves) + FindWinnerByRunningCounts(int[][] moves, int boardSize) (the incremental +/-1 row/column/diagonal tallies, previously written once as the test's private FindWinner/TicTacToeBoard and again as the benchmark's IncrementalRunningCounts/LineTallies/ApplyMove)

problems.title: Iterator for Combination
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Backtracking.Backtrack.Search (CombinationSumIII/PalindromePartitioning precedent) enumerates increasing-index combinations, which is already lexicographic order since the input is sorted; CombinationIterator itself is just a List<string> + cursor over that precomputed, already-ordered result (same 'no algorithm primitive beyond a cursor' shape as BinarySearchTreeIteratorTests).
problems.notes: Two strategies. The test carried only one (a private CombinationIterator class wrapping Backtrack.Search); the benchmark carried that same backtracking walk a second time as BacktrackComposed plus an unasserted [Benchmark(Baseline = true)] BitmaskEnumeration (scan all 2^n masks, filter by popcount, sort ordinally). SHAPE RECONCILED: the test's arm produced LeetCode's real answer (a stateful iterator) while both benchmark arms produced only a List<string> of combinations - the precomputation step. LeetCode's real answer wins, so both strategies now return a CombinationIterator; the baseline is promoted from 'build the list' to 'build the iterator', which is the same generation work plus a cursor wrapper, and is what finally gets it under test. The private SearchState (List<char> Chosen, Stack<int> Starts, int Start) existed identically in both files and is now one nested type in the solution; DataStructures.Stack is deliberately not imported, so Stack<int> binds to the BCL type exactly as before. BENCHMARK MEASUREMENT NOTE: CombinationIterator is internal, so a public [Benchmark] cannot return one (CS0050); each arm therefore drains the iterator to an int, following the BinarySearchTreeIteratorBenchmarks precedent. That charges an extra O(combination count) cursor walk that the old arms did not pay - negligible against 2^n mask scanning, and it keeps the result from being elided. Original [Params(10, 16)] and the [GlobalSetup] alphabet/half-length workload are preserved; no prepared-input overload is needed since the inputs are a string and an int. Test keeps both original examples and adds three (abc/1, abcd/3, ab/2). No fixture types existed to relocate; no new DataStructures/ or Algorithms/ types, so section 18 is not triggered.
problems.strategies: CreateByBitmaskEnumeration, CreateByBacktrackEngine (each returning the nested IteratorForCombinationSolution.CombinationIterator, LeetCode's own next()/hasNext() answer shape)

On the benchmark's oversized 200/5000-bit workloads both arms still agree with each other, because the shift fold and the weight fold both compute the value modulo 2^32. No fixture types existed for this problem; list construction stays in each harness (MiddleOfTheLinkedList precedent). problems.title: Find the City With the Smallest Number of Neighbors at a Threshold Distance

problems.notes: The two arms did NOT disagree on answer shape here - the test's private FindCity helper and the benchmark's FloydWarshallAllPairs arm were the same Floyd-Warshall strategy written twice; the defect was that the benchmark's [Benchmark(Baseline = true)] DijkstraPerSource arm was never asserted by anything. It is now a first-class method and agrees with the Floyd arm on all 5 examples. ONE DELIBERATE DEVIATION FROM SECTION 17.5: this baseline's internals are NOT rewritten to BCL. The pair's whole point (stated in the original benchmark's own doc comment) is 'this repo's single-source primitive, run once per city, vs. this repo's all-pairs primitive run once' - the mirror image of ShortestPathAlgorithmBenchmarks' wrong-tool point. AllPairsShortestPathsTests/BellmanFordTests) and the old benchmark used its own Benchmarks/Fixtures' WeightedGraphNode/WeightedGraphTopology copy (still used by ~9 other benchmarks) - both stay put. problems.title: Jump Game V
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.TopologicalSort.TopologicalSort.TrySort (Kahn's algorithm) over an implicit graph where edge i->j exists only when arr[i] strictly exceeds every value strictly between i and j and arr[j] itself, guaranteeing a DAG; the returned topological order then drives one linear longest-path relaxation pass (plain Dictionary, glue logic in the test/benchmark, not a new production primitive).
problems.notes: Three copies of the reachability DAG collapsed to one: the test fixture pair, the benchmark's own private nested copy, and the two separately-inlined BuildReachabilityDag/ConnectReachableEdges + ComputeLongestPaths walks. The benchmark's [Benchmark(Baseline = true)] MemoizedDfsPerStart (BCL Dictionary memo, per-start recursion) was never asserted; it is now a first-class method whose internals stay BCL per section 17.5, and it agrees with the topological arm on every example. problems.title: Product of the Last K Numbers
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.DynamicArray.DynamicArray<long> as a running prefix-product array - TimeBasedKeyValueStoreTests' 'parallel/running DynamicArray history' shape. Add(0) resets to a fresh [1] prefix instead of dividing by zero; GetProduct(k) is one division of two prefix entries.
problems.notes: Design problem, so it follows the CreateBy<Strategy> factory shape TimeBasedKeyValueStoreSolution/AllOneDataStructureSolution established rather than a pure function: the stateful object itself is the strategy, so no separate hoisted overload is needed - [GlobalSetup] seeds each returned store and the measured arm is one GetProduct call. The test's private ProductOfNumbers (running DynamicArray<long> prefix products, Add(0) resetting to [1]) became CreateByPrefixProductDivision; the benchmark's ReplayLastKFromRawStream baseline became CreateByRawStreamReplay and was promoted from 'multiply the whole raw array' to LeetCode's actual GetProduct(k) over a BCL List<int>, which is what makes it assertable - it was previously never asserted by anything. Baseline internals stay BCL per 17.5. Test keeps all three original examples and adds a one-number stream and a stream opening with a zero; 10 assertions where there were 3 test methods. Benchmark keeps [Params(200, 5_000)], MaxFactorValueExclusive 10 and the original Random(1) seed (now named FactorSeed), seeds both stores in [GlobalSetup] and answers GetProduct(Length) so the replay arm is forced through its full O(Length) worst case - the divisor of the prefix arm is always prefix[0] = 1, so the wrapped long products at Length=5000 cannot divide by zero, same as before. Nomos gate: one check-vertical-organization finding fixed (call-order of CreateResetPrefix); the only remaining finding is check-single-letter-name on the parameter k, which is LeetCode's own published signature and is shared by 106 already-migrated solution files, so it was left to match the tier's convention.
problems.strategies: CreateByPrefixProductDivision() and CreateByRawStreamReplay(), both returning the nested IProductOfNumbers (Add/GetProduct)

problems.title: Apply Discount Every n Orders
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<int,int> mapping product id to price - TwoSumTests' 'one HashMap, O(1) lookup per line item' shape, built once in the constructor. GetBill sums looked-up-price * amount per line item and applies the discount whenever the running customer count is a multiple of n.
problems.notes: Design problem, so the CreateBy<Strategy> factory shape (TimeBasedKeyValueStoreSolution precedent) rather than pure functions; the factory IS the hoisted construction, so [GlobalSetup] builds both cashiers and each [Benchmark] is a single GetBill call - no separate prepared-input overload was needed. BEHAVIOUR CHANGE, deliberate and promoted to LeetCode's real answer: the benchmark's [Benchmark(Baseline = true)] LinearScanLookup arm measured something WEAKER than the problem - it summed price*amount by linear catalogue scan but never applied the discount cadence at all, and had no n/discount at all. It is now the full LC 1357 answer (linear-scan price lookup PLUS the every-n-th-customer discount), which is what the test's private Cashier helper computed. The test's helper and the benchmark's HashMapLookup arm agreed on the lookup half and are unchanged in behaviour. The benchmark now fixes DiscountEvery=3/DiscountPercent=50 so the cadence branch is exercised; [Params(200, 5_000)] ProductCount, the catalogue construction and the reverse-order bill are preserved verbatim. Nomos: check-nested-call and check-parameter-count findings introduced by the first draft of the harness were fixed (named locals; constructor args bundled into one tuple parameter); the remaining check-vertical-organization/check-test-coverage findings on the benchmark file are the pre-existing repo-wide BenchmarkDotNet pattern and fire identically on the already-migrated UniqueBinarySearchTrees/TimeBasedKeyValueStore benchmarks.
problems.strategies: ApplyDiscountEveryNOrdersSolution.CreateByHashMapLookup(int n, int discount, int[] products, int[] prices); ApplyDiscountEveryNOrdersSolution.CreateByLinearCatalogScan(int n, int discount, int[] products, int[] prices); both return the nested public ApplyDiscountEveryNOrdersSolution.ICashier with GetBill(int[] product, int[] amount). Private implementations: HashMapLookupCashier (repo HashMap<int,int>, one O(1) probe per line item), LinearCatalogScanCashier (BCL arrays, O(catalogue) scan per line item - the baseline, internals BCL only), sharing a private DiscountCadence struct for the every-n-th-customer discount.

problems.title: Count All Valid Pickup and Delivery Options

problems.title: Minimum Cost to Make at Least One Valid Path in a Grid
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Heap.Heap<Element,TOrder> ordered by DataStructures.Graph.ShortestPaths.ByPriorityOrder<TNode,TWeight> - the same Dijkstra-shaped grid frontier SwimInRisingWaterTests already proves, here summing 0/1 edge costs (0 to follow a cell's own arrow, 1 to override it) with settle-once bookkeeping mirroring ShortestPath.cs's own Explore loop (additive costs need settle-at-pop, unlike SwimInRisingWater's minimax settle-at-push shortcut).

problems.title: Maximum Sum BST in Binary Tree
problems.primitivesUsed: BinaryTreeNode<TValue> (DataStructures/Graph/Engines/Dags/Trees) via direct hand-rolled post-order recursion, not TreeFold/BinaryTreeChildren (which compact away missing-child positional identity that a BST check needs) - same shape as existing ValidateBinarySearchTreeTests/BinaryTreeMaximumPathSumTests precedent.

LC 1373's third published example ([-4,-2,-5] -> 0) settles that the empty subtree is a valid BST with sum 0, which is the floor on the answer; both strategies now start from EmptySubtreeSum = 0. Nothing either harness actually asserted or measured changes: all three original test examples (21, 6, 7) and the skewed benchmark workload have positive answers. Test now states LC's own three examples (20, 2, 0) alongside the three originals, encoded in LeetCode's level-order int?[] shape with a private BuildTree, following the migrated BinaryTreeMaximumPathSumTests precedent (BinaryTreeNode<int> is internal and cannot appear in a public TheoryData signature). Benchmark keeps [Params(200, 2_000)] and Fixtures.BinaryTrees.Skewed, which stays in Benchmarks/Fixtures as workload sizing per section 17.7 (it is shared and size-parameterized, not domain code). No new DataStructures/Algorithms types, so no section-18 obligations.
problems.strategies: MaxSumBSTByRevalidatingEachNode (baseline, BCL recursion revalidating and re-summing each node's whole subtree, O(n^2) - was the benchmark's untested RevalidatePerNode arm plus its IsValidBst/Sum helpers), MaxSumBSTByBottomUpScan (one post-order pass combining child Summary(IsBst,Min,Max,Sum) records - was the test's private MaxSumBST helper and the benchmark's OnePassBottomUpScan arm, duplicated verbatim including a second copy of the Summary record struct)

problems.title: Design a Stack With Increment Operation

The benchmark's [Benchmark(Baseline=true)] ArrayBackedIndexedIncrement was NOT a CustomStack at all - a bare increment loop over a List<int> copy, with no maxSize cap, no Push and no Pop - so it was promoted to LeetCode's full CustomStack surface (capped Push, Pop returning -1 on empty, Increment over the bottom min(k,size)) and is now asserted for the first time; its measured work is unchanged apart from now pushing values one at a time (with the cap check) instead of copying the array, which is exactly what the repo-Stack arm already did. No hoisted overload needed: [GlobalSetup] prepares the call workload, not a strategy argument. No fixture types existed.
