Implementations: StackDrainCustomStack (two repo Stack<int> instances, drain-and-rebuild) and IndexedListCustomStack (BCL List<int>, direct indexed increment; BCL-only internals per section 17.5).

problems.title: Balance a Binary Search Tree
problems.primitivesUsed: InOrderTraversal.Walk/IInOrderHooks + DynamicArray<int> to collect sorted values, then BinaryTreeNode<int> midpoint-split rebuild (same helper ConvertSortedArrayToBinarySearchTreeTests already uses).
problems.notes: The test's private Balance helper (repo InOrderTraversal/IInOrderHooks collecting into DynamicArray<int>, then midpoint-split rebuild, with the CollectHooks struct and AsyncLocal state) became BalanceByInOrderTraversal; the benchmark's [Benchmark(Baseline=true)] RepeatedKthSmallestScan (O(n) in-order walk per rank k=1..n, O(n^2), BCL-only internals) became BalanceByRepeatedKthSmallest and is now asserted for the first time - it needed a node count the benchmark previously got from its [Params], so a BCL CountNodes recursion was added. Both benchmark arms previously returned Height(rebuilt), a proxy; both now return LeetCode's real answer (the rebuilt root) and the harness walks it for a height so the rebuild is not dead code - a deliberate change in the section 17.8 sense. Benchmark workload preserved exactly: [Params(200, 2_000)] NodeCount over Fixtures.BinaryTrees.Skewed, built in [GlobalSetup] (workload sizing stays tier 5). No hoisted overload needed - the prepared input is already the LeetCode-shaped BinaryTreeNode<int> parameter. Test examples grew from 3 to 5, stated as LeetCode's level-order int?[] arrays (BinaryTreeNode<int> is internal so it cannot appear in public TheoryData) and checked against the two properties LeetCode actually accepts: in-order values preserved, and height-balanced. No fixture types existed and no new DataStructures/ or Algorithms/ type was created, so no section 18 obligation arose.
problems.strategies: BalanceABinarySearchTreeSolution.BalanceByInOrderTraversal(BinaryTreeNode<int>?) and BalanceByRepeatedKthSmallest(BinaryTreeNode<int>?), both returning BinaryTreeNode<int>? (the rebuilt root).

problems.title: Sort Integers by The Power Value
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Sorting.MergeSort.Sort over DataStructures.Sequence.ArrayIndexedSequence<(int Power,int Value)>, relying on ValueTuple's lexicographic IComparable (Power then Value) so no custom comparer is needed - same composition SortAnArrayTests/HeightCheckerTests already use.
problems.notes: Two distinct strategies: the test's private GetKth (repo MergeSort over ArrayIndexedSequence) and the benchmark's [Benchmark(Baseline = true)] InsertionSort arm, which was the only place the textbook O(n^2) sort lived and was never asserted; it is now a first-class method under test. Its internals stay BCL (plain array + Comparer<(int,int)>.Default), per 17.5. Shared private BuildPowerPairs/PowerOf carry the Collatz walk once instead of in both harnesses; the benchmark's CollatzDivisor/CollatzMultiplier constants moved onto the solution. Signature reconciliation: the benchmark arms returned pairs[^1].Value over the range [1, RangeLength], which is exactly GetKth(lo: 1, hi: RangeLength, k: RangeLength) — LeetCode's real answer shape — so the arms are now one-line calls with k = RangeLength and measure the same work. [Params(200, 5_000)] preserved; the original [GlobalSetup] only assigned _lo = 1 and carried no workload, so it became a private const Lo = 1 (behaviour identical, nothing hoisted out of the measured methods, so no prepared-input overload was warranted). Test grew from 2 InlineData cases to 5 TheoryData examples (both LeetCode examples kept, plus lo==hi, a historical example 10/20/5 -> 13, and 1/4/4 -> 3 which exercises the value tie-break); 26 tests pass across this problem and LC 1390. No fixtures existed to relocate; no new DataStructures/Algorithms types, so section 18 owes nothing.
problems.strategies: SortIntegersByThePowerValueSolution.GetKthByMergeSort(int lo, int hi, int k); SortIntegersByThePowerValueSolution.GetKthByInsertionSort(int lo, int hi, int k)

problems.title: Four Divisors
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound over a test-local IRandomAccessSequence<int> witness (SquareExceedsSequence) to anchor floor(sqrt(num)) in O(log num) - the exact ClosestDivisorsTests (LC 1362) precedent already in this repo - then a downward trial-division walk from that anchor, bailing out as soon as a fifth divisor is found.
problems.notes: Two distinct strategies: the test's anchored walk (BinarySearch.LowerBound over SquareExceedsSequence to floor(sqrt(num)), then a downward walk bailing out at a fifth divisor) and the benchmark's [Benchmark(Baseline = true)] FullRangeScan arm, the textbook 1..num trial division, which was never asserted and is now a first-class method under test with BCL-only internals. The benchmark's anchored arm and the test's helper agreed on the answer shape (int sum) — the only divergence was bookkeeping style (a tuple-returning AccumulateDivisorPair vs DivisorTally); the tally form from the proven test was kept. The benchmark hoists its random int[] into [GlobalSetup], but that prepared input IS LeetCode's own shape (int[] nums), so the arms pass _nums straight into the single overload — no second overload needed and no ambiguity risk. [Params(200, 2_000)], seed 1390 and MaxGeneratedNumber 20_000 preserved; the benchmark's TargetDivisorCount/DistinctDivisorPairCount/MaxSafeDivisorBound moved to the solution, the last renamed SqrtAnchorCeiling to match the identical constant ClosestDivisorsSolution already declares (I did not touch that migrated file to share it). Test grew from 2 InlineData cases to 8 TheoryData examples (both LeetCode examples kept, plus 1, 2, 3 and 5-divisor numbers that must contribute nothing, and 8 -> 15). No new DataStructures/Algorithms types, so section 18 owes nothing.
problems.strategies: FourDivisorsSolution.SumFourDivisorsByBinarySearchAnchor(int[] nums); FourDivisorsSolution.SumFourDivisorsByFullRangeScan(int[] nums)
problems.relocatedTypes: None moved. The pair carried two copies of a private SquareExceedsSequence struct (one in the test, one in the benchmark); both were deleted in favour of the existing tier-4 witness DSAExperimentation.LeetCode/SqrtX/SquareExceedsSequence.cs, which ClosestDivisorsSolution already reuses from SqrtX for the same sqrt-anchoring technique. The test's private DivisorTally is an internal detail of the anchored walk, not a fixture, so it stays as a private nested type in the solution class.

problems.title: Check if There is a Valid Path in a Grid
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Traversal.DepthFirst.DepthFirstSearch.Traverse(start, successors) over a bespoke street-opening successor function - the generic 'arbitrary successor relation' shape (ARCHITECTURE.md 12), the same pattern PacificAtlanticWaterFlowTests uses - checking whether the bottom-right corner is in the reachable set from (0,0). The repo's existing Grid/GridTopology primitives were not usable here since they model a boolean passable/impassable check, not per-cell directional street-opening compatibility (the same reason MinimumCostToMakeAtLeastOneValidPathInAGridTests also hand-rolls its grid adjacency instead of reusing GridTopology).
problems.notes: Test arm and benchmark arm agreed on shape (both bool), so no answer-shape reconciliation was needed. The Openings table (street piece -> its two open directions) was duplicated verbatim in the test and the benchmark; it is LC 1391's own content and meaningless elsewhere, so per section 17.3 it lives as a private static in the solution class beside the strategies - the same placement PacificAtlanticWaterFlowSolution uses for its Directions table. No new DataStructures/ or Algorithms/ type was created, so section 18.4 owes nothing. The baseline was generalized from the benchmark's square Size x Size assumption to grid.Length x grid[0].Length so it answers the non-square test examples; behaviour on square inputs is unchanged. Both strategies share one private BCL-only helper, OpensBackToward (bounds check + Array.IndexOf), rather than re-writing the street-compatibility rule twice - only the input container rule of section 17.5 constrains a baseline, and this helper is plain array indexing. Test kept all 4 original assertions and added LeetCode's official example 1 ([[2,4,3],[6,5,2]] -> true) and a 1x1 grid; benchmark keeps [Params(10, 30)], seed 1391 and the same [GlobalSetup] random-grid workload. No fixture types existed for this problem (no Fixtures/ subfolder, no Benchmarks/Fixtures entry), and the grid is LeetCode's own input shape, so no hoisted overload was warranted.
problems.strategies: HasValidPathByRecursiveDfs (was the benchmark's untested [Benchmark(Baseline = true)] RecursiveDfs arm - hand-rolled recursion over a bool[,] visited array, internals stay BCL per section 17.5), HasValidPathByDepthFirstTraverse (was written twice: the test's private HasValidPath helper and the benchmark's DepthFirstSearchTraverse arm, both over Algorithms.Traversal.DepthFirst.DepthFirstSearch.Traverse)

problems.title: Longest Happy Prefix
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.StringMatching.PrefixFunctionSearch.ComputeFailureFunction (KMP prefix/failure function) - the longest happy prefix is exactly its last entry's length
problems.notes: THE TWO ARMS DISAGREED ON ANSWER SHAPE, exactly the LC 1-style drift this migration exists to remove: the test solved for the prefix STRING while both benchmark arms returned only its LENGTH (an int). LeetCode 1392's real answer is the string, so both strategies now return the string and the benchmark arms return string. That is a deliberate promotion of the benchmark's measurement in the section 17.8 sense - it now charges a substring slice - but on this benchmark's chosen workload it charges neither arm anything: an (n-1)-run of 'a' followed by one 'b' has an empty happy prefix, so both arms return string.Empty with no allocation, and the O(n^2)-vs-O(n) comparison the workload was chosen to isolate is unchanged. The baseline's early-return length semantics are preserved exactly (same descending candidate scan, same first match). No new DataStructures/ or Algorithms/ type was created, so section 18.4 owes nothing; no fixture types existed for this problem, and the input is a plain string (LeetCode's own shape) so no hoisted overload was warranted. Test kept all 3 original assertions and added LeetCode's "ababab" -> "abab" overlapping-repeat example and a single-character case pinning the PROPER-prefix requirement; benchmark keeps [Params(200, 5_000)] and the same [GlobalSetup] workload.
problems.strategies: LongestPrefixByShrinkAndCompare (was the benchmark's untested [Benchmark(Baseline = true)] ShrinkAndCompare arm - O(n^2) span comparison, BCL only), LongestPrefixByPrefixFunction (was written twice: the test's private LongestPrefix helper and the benchmark's PrefixFunctionLookup arm, both over Algorithms.StringMatching.PrefixFunctionSearch.ComputeFailureFunction)

problems.title: Count Number of Teams
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.FenwickTree.FenwickTree<int,SumOperation<int>> + Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound/UpperBound + DataStructures.Sequence.ArraySequence - rank-then-Fenwick-sweep run once left-to-right and once right-to-left (same shape as the existing CountOfSmallerNumbersAfterSelf coverage), teams[j] = leftLess[j]*rightGreater[j] + leftGreater[j]*rightLess[j]
problems.notes: Test and benchmark agreed on the answer shape (int team count), so nothing had to be reconciled; the only defect was the twice-written algorithm plus the unasserted baseline. No hoisted overload: [GlobalSetup] only builds the int[] rating, which IS LeetCode's input shape, so the LeetCode-shaped method already takes the prepared input (unlike OpenTheLock, where a graph was constructed). No fixture types existed for this pair and none were created; the workload (seeded random ratings, [Params(80, 200)], seed 1395) stays inline in [GlobalSetup] as before. Examples kept all three the old test asserted ([2,5,3,4,1]=3, [2,1,3]=0, [1,2,3,4]=4) and added four hand-checkable ones ([1,2,3]=1, [3,2,1]=1, [1,1,1]=0 for the strict-inequality/equal-ratings case, [1,2]=0 for the too-few-soldiers guard). Two named constants replace the magic 3 / 2 that were previously split across the two files. No new DataStructures/ or Algorithms/ types, so section 18 owes nothing here.
problems.strategies: CountTeamsByTripleLoop (the benchmark's former [Benchmark(Baseline = true)] TripleLoopScan, now a first-class method and under test for the first time; internals stay BCL int[] loops), CountTeamsByFenwickSweeps (the test helper and the benchmark's FenwickTreeSweeps arm, which were already identical: coordinate compression via BinarySearch.LowerBound/UpperBound over ArraySequence<int> plus two directional FenwickTree<int, SumOperation<int>> sweeps)

problems.title: Find All Good Strings
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.StringMatching.PrefixFunctionSearch.ComputeFailureFunction (KMP automaton over evil; the fallback transition walk is rebuilt from the public failure array since PrefixFunctionSearch keeps its own Advance private) + Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer (memoized digit DP over (position, automaton-state, isTightToS1, isTightToS2))
problems.notes: BEHAVIOUR NOTE - the baseline arm was weaker than the real answer and was promoted, as allowed. The old EnumerationScan hard-coded the benchmark's own workload: it iterated exactly 26^Length strings starting at s1, which only counts the range [s1, s2] when s1 is all 'a' and s2 is all 'z', and it never applied the modulus. The migrated CountGoodStringsByEnumeration walks from s1 to s2 inclusive (string.CompareOrdinal bound, so the all-'z' odometer wrap can't run away) and reduces mod 1e9+7. On the benchmark's own inputs ('aaa'..'zzz') it visits the identical candidate set and the count never exceeds 26^4, so the measured work and the returned value are unchanged there; the generalization is what lets the baseline be asserted against LeetCode's published examples (it now returns 51 / 0 / 2 alongside the DP). The DP arm's answer shape was already LeetCode's and is unchanged. The duplicated private const Modulus = 1_000_000_007 (one copy in each file) is now Domain.Modular.ModularArithmetic.Modulo, the declared home for LeetCode's reporting modulus per ARCHITECTURE 17.6/17.9, matching CountAnagrams and CountKReducibleNumbersLessThanN. No hoisted overload: [GlobalSetup] only builds the s1/s2/evil strings, which are LeetCode's input shape, and the failure function was charged to the measured method in the original, which is preserved. The GoodStringBounds/GoodStringWalk record structs are bespoke to this problem and stay private inside the solution class (17.3's CountWaysToBuildRoomsInAnAntColony precedent); nothing was moved to another tier. Examples kept all three the old test asserted and added 1/'a'/'z'/'a'=25 and 2/'aa'/'zz'/'zz'=675. No new DataStructures/ or Algorithms/ types, so section 18 owes nothing here.
problems.strategies: CountGoodStringsByEnumeration (the benchmark's former baseline EnumerationScan, promoted to LeetCode's real signature - see notes; internals stay BCL: char[] odometer + string.IndexOf/CompareOrdinal), CountGoodStringsByAutomatonDigitDp (the test helper and the benchmark's AutomatonDigitDp arm, two independent copies of the same KMP-failure-function automaton wired through Memoizer's memoized digit DP, now one method; the test's more decomposed GoodStringBounds/GoodStringWalk version was kept and the benchmark's DigitDpContext copy dropped)

problems.title: Circle and Rectangle Overlapping
problems.primitivesUsed: None in the coverage test itself (O(1) clamp-and-distance scalar arithmetic - same 'lighter repo-primitive fit' case as RectangleOverlapTests LC 836 / RectangleAreaTests LC 223). Benchmark's brute-force baseline composes DataStructures.DynamicArray.DynamicArray<bool> as a lattice-point coverage scan, mirroring RectangleOverlapBenchmarks.
problems.notes: Two strategies inventoried: the test's private CheckOverlap helper (= the benchmark's ClosedFormClampAndDistance arm) and the benchmark's untested LatticePointScan baseline. Signature reconciled onto LeetCode's real shape (7 ints -> bool); the test's private `Rectangle` record struct was a harness-local convenience and was dropped rather than relocated, since LeetCode's own signature passes the four bounds directly. Per ARCHITECTURE 17.5 the baseline's internals were switched from DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.DynamicArray<bool> to a BCL List<bool> - a baseline represents "what you would write without this repo", and no input container is handed to it; the scan still builds the complete membership buffer before checking it, so the worst-case work the benchmark was designed to force is unchanged. Return values unchanged on every original input. The lattice scan only samples integer coordinates, so it answers the continuous question only where the two agree; that is documented on the method and all five asserted examples are ones where they agree (verified by hand and by the passing run). [GlobalSetup] only assigns ints, so no hoisted overload was needed. Examples kept all four the original test asserted plus LeetCode's published example 3 (radius 1, centre (0,0), rect (-1,0,0,1) -> true); 10 assertions now, both arms covered. No new DataStructures/ or Algorithms/ types, so section 18 owes nothing here.
problems.strategies: CircleAndRectangleOverlappingSolution.CheckOverlapByClampedDistance(int radius, int xCenter, int yCenter, int x1, int y1, int x2, int y2); CircleAndRectangleOverlappingSolution.CheckOverlapByLatticePointScan(same signature, the promoted [Benchmark(Baseline = true)] arm)

problems.title: Number of Steps to Reduce a Number in Binary Representation to One
problems.primitivesUsed: None in the coverage test itself (O(n) single-pass carry-propagation scan over the binary string, two plain ints - same 'lighter repo-primitive fit' case as RectangleOverlapTests). Benchmark's brute-force baseline composes DataStructures.Stack.Stack<char> via the exact LSB-first binary-add technique AddBinaryTests/AddBinaryBenchmarks already use for LC 67, doing a full stack-based '+1' rebuild on every odd step.
problems.notes: Two strategies inventoried: the test's private NumSteps helper (= the benchmark's CarryPropagationScan arm, identical code) and the benchmark's untested StackAddSimulation baseline with its StackAddOne helper. Both already returned an int step count on a string, so no signature reconciliation was needed. Per ARCHITECTURE 17.5 the baseline's bit buffer was switched from DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.Stack.Stack<char> to the BCL System.Collections.Generic.Stack<char> (aliased explicitly as BitStack to avoid any ambiguity with the repo's Stack namespace); the Push/TryPop usage is identical, so the algorithm and its results are unchanged. Return values unchanged on every original input (hand-checked 1101->6, 10->1, 1->0, 111->4 against both arms). Input is a plain string built in [GlobalSetup], which is also LeetCode's own shape, so no hoisted overload was needed and the benchmark's [Params(100, 1000)] alternating-"10" workload is preserved verbatim. Examples kept all four the original test asserted and added "1000"->3, "1011"->6 and "1010"->6 (the benchmark's own bit pattern); 14 assertions now, both arms covered. No new DataStructures/ or Algorithms/ types, so section 18 owes nothing here.
problems.strategies: NumberOfStepsToReduceANumberInBinaryRepresentationToOneSolution.NumStepsByCarryPropagationScan(string s); NumberOfStepsToReduceANumberInBinaryRepresentationToOneSolution.NumStepsByStackAddSimulation(string s) (the promoted [Benchmark(Baseline = true)] arm)

problems.title: Stone Game III
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer<TState,TResult> - same minimax score-difference recurrence shape as StoneGameTests (LC 877)/StoneGameIITests (LC 1140), keyed on a single int index with a 3-way inner loop over taking 1, 2, or 3 stones.
problems.notes: Two arms disagreed on answer shape: the test's private Winner helper returned LeetCode's actual answer ("Alice"/"Bob"/"Tie") while BOTH benchmark arms returned the raw score difference int. LeetCode's real answer wins, so both strategies now return the winner's name; the sign test is one switch on top of the same recurrence and is identical in both arms, so the benchmark still isolates memoization alone. The benchmark's [Benchmark(Baseline = true)] UnmemoizedRecursion arm was previously never asserted; it is now WinnerByUnmemoizedRecursion and carries the same examples as the memoized arm. No hoisted overload: [GlobalSetup] builds the int[] stoneValue array, which IS LeetCode's own input shape (same as the already-migrated StoneGameII pair), so a second overload would be redundant and ambiguous. Composes the existing Algorithms/DynamicProgramming/Memoizer; no new DataStructures/ or Algorithms/ types, so §18 owes nothing. Examples kept all 4 originals and added [2,2]->Alice and [-1,-2,-3]->Tie. [Params(20,24)], seed 1406 and the stone-value bounds preserved.
problems.strategies: StoneGameIIISolution.WinnerByUnmemoizedRecursion(int[]), StoneGameIIISolution.WinnerByMemoizedRecursion(int[])

problems.title: String Matching in an Array
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.StringMatching.PrefixFunctionSearch (KMP) - FindAll(text, pattern) used as the substring-containment check for each word against every other word.
problems.notes: Both benchmark arms measured something weaker than the real answer - they COUNTED contained words rather than building LeetCode's List<string>. Promoted both to the real answer (the §17.8 WordLadderII precedent); the benchmark harness takes .Count, so the extra work is one List add per contained word, identical in both arms. The benchmark's baseline NaiveNestedLoop (raw char-index double loop, previously untested scaffolding) is now the first-class FindContainedWordsByNaiveScan with BCL-only internals - no string.Contains, no repo primitive - and is asserted against the same examples as the KMP arm. The two strategies deliberately keep their own copy of the all-pairs sweep rather than sharing it through a Func predicate, so the naive arm's per-pair delegate-free tightness (the thing the benchmark comment is about) is not distorted. Composes the existing Algorithms/StringMatching/PrefixFunctionSearch; no new primitives, so §18 owes nothing. Examples kept all 3 originals (including LeetCode example 3) and added ["ab","abc","abcd"]->["ab","abc"] and ["a","a","a"]->["a","a","a"]. [Params(60,150)] and the adversarial a^n-b word generator preserved in [GlobalSetup]; it builds string[], LeetCode's own input shape, so no hoisted overload was needed.
problems.strategies: StringMatchingInAnArraySolution.FindContainedWordsByNaiveScan(string[]), StringMatchingInAnArraySolution.FindContainedWordsByPrefixFunctionSearch(string[])

problems.title: Queries on a Permutation With Key
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.DynamicArray.DynamicArray<int> - Get/RemoveAt/Insert(0,...) used to simulate the permutation P as a move-to-front sequence (same DynamicArray-as-shrinking/growing-sequence idiom as the existing PermutationSequence coverage).
problems.notes: Drift reconciled: the test's private ProcessQueries returned the full List<int> of queried indices (LeetCode's real answer), while BOTH benchmark arms (ListMoveToFront baseline and DynamicArrayMoveToFront) returned only the LAST index as an int - a weaker measurement. Per the §17.8 precedent I promoted both arms to LeetCode's real answer: they now build and return the full index list, so the benchmark measures exactly what the test proves. The list allocation this adds is the answer itself, not scaffolding. The baseline (ListMoveToFront) is now a first-class method under test for the first time; its internals stay pure BCL (List<int>.IndexOf/RemoveAt/Insert) per §17.5, while the other strategy drives the identical simulation over DataStructures/DynamicArray<int>. The private IndexOf scan helper (duplicated verbatim in the test and the benchmark) now exists once, in the solution, and returns LeetCodeAnswer.None rather than a bare -1. No hoisted overload was needed: the benchmark's [GlobalSetup] builds the int[] query stream, which IS the LeetCode-shaped parameter, so there is no second input shape to hoist. [Params(200, 1_000)] and the fixed Seed = 1 random query draw are preserved in the benchmark as workload sizing/seeding (§17.7). No fixture types existed for this problem. Test kept both original LeetCode examples and added three cases the original lacked (single query; repeated query that must report 0 once the value is already at the front; a descending query stream that forces a full-length scan every time).
problems.strategies: ProcessQueriesByListMoveToFront(int[] queries, int m), ProcessQueriesByDynamicArrayMoveToFront(int[] queries, int m)

problems.title: Number of Ways to Paint N Ã— 3 Grid
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer<TState,TResult> - Memoize<int,(long Same,long Different)> expresses the coupled row-pattern-count recurrence (NthTribonacciNumber/FibonacciNumber precedent), TResult itself being the (Same,Different) pair.
problems.notes: Three copies of the recurrence collapsed to one pair of strategies: the test's private NumOfWays/Ways (Memoizer-driven) and the benchmark's Tabulation baseline plus its own second copy of Ways. Arms agreed on the answer shape here, so no reconciliation was needed - the defect was pure duplication plus an untested baseline. Tabulation is now a first-class method under test; its internals stay BCL (two long locals and a for loop) per §17.5, while NumOfWaysByMemoizedRecurrence composes Algorithms/DynamicProgramming/Memoizer over the (Same, Different) pair. Reused the existing Domain/Modular/ModularArithmetic.Modulo instead of the local `private const long Modulus = 1_000_000_007` that the test and the benchmark each declared - exactly the duplication §17.6 puts that type in Domain/ to remove. The benchmark's four magic-weight constants (Row1PatternCount/SamePatternWeight/DifferentPatternWeight/FirstDpRowIndex) moved into the solution as FirstRowPatternCount/SameFollowerWeight/DifferentFollowerWeight/SecondRow so both strategies share one set. No [GlobalSetup] input to hoist (the only input is the scalar n, which is the [Params] value), so no second overload. [Params(1_000, 5_000)] preserved. No fixture types existed. Test kept all four original assertions (n = 1, 2, 3, 300 including the modular large case) restated once as TheoryData and added n = 4 -> 1122 to pin a second iteration of the recurrence before the modulus starts biting. No new DataStructures/ or Algorithms/ types were created, so §18 owes nothing here.
problems.strategies: NumOfWaysByTabulation(int n), NumOfWaysByMemoizedRecurrence(int n)

problems.title: Display Table of Food Orders in a Restaurant
problems.primitivesUsed: HashMap<TKey,TValue> (nested table->food->count grouping, plus a HashMap<string,bool> for food-name dedup) + MergeSort.Sort over ArrayIndexedSequence<T> (Algorithms/Sorting, DataStructures/Sequence) to sort table numbers and food names, matching AccountsMergeTests.cs's grouping/sorting composition.
problems.notes: The pair disagreed on the answer shape: the test's private DisplayTable helper built LeetCode's real table (List<List<string>>), while BOTH benchmark arms only summed cell counts and returned an int. Promoted both arms to LeetCode's real answer -- the baseline now materializes the same header/rows the grouped arm does, so the [Benchmark(Baseline = true)] arm is finally asserted. That is a deliberate change in what is measured (§17.8's precedent), not an oversight; the rescan arm still pays O(orders) per cell because tables/foods come from small fixed pools. Both strategies keep the two sort orders LeetCode fixes: StringComparer.Ordinal for foods, integer order for table numbers. No fixture types existed to relocate; the benchmark's [GlobalSetup] is pure workload sizing/seeding (RandomSeed 1418, TableCount 30, FoodCount 15) and stayed inline, and [Params(200, 2_000)] is unchanged. No hoisted overload is needed -- the prepared input IS LeetCode's own string[][] shape. The test class lost a stray `partial` (there was no second part) and grew from 2 ad-hoc facts to 4 shared examples x 2 strategies = 8 assertions, adding LeetCode's published examples 1 and 3. No new DataStructures/Algorithms types, so no §18 obligation. Nomos gate on the folder is clean apart from one ADVISORY check-transposable-parameters on CountOrdersForCell(orders, tableText, food) -- the same accepted class §17.9 records -- and check-dependency-isolation reporting 'LOOKED AT NOTHING', an artifact of scoping the run to one folder.
problems.strategies: DisplayTableByRescanPerCell (baseline; BCL LINQ Distinct/OrderBy + per-cell rescan of every raw order), DisplayTableByGroupedHashMap (one grouped pass into nested HashMap<int, HashMap<string,int>> + HashMap<string,bool> food set, both axes sorted with MergeSort over ArrayIndexedSequence)

problems.title: Constrained Subsequence Sum
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Deque.Deque<int> used as a monotonic deque of dp-value-ordered indices, the same window-maximum technique SlidingWindowMaximumTests.cs already proves, applied to a dp array computed on the fly instead of a fixed input array.
problems.notes: No behaviour change: the test's SlidingWindowState helper and the benchmark's MonotonicDequeDp arm were the same algorithm written twice and are now one method; the benchmark's RescanWindowEachPosition baseline was the only place the O(n*k) arm existed and is now a first-class, tested method. Both return LeetCode's real answer (the max over the dp array). The private window class was renamed DpWindow -> BestSumWindow and dp/_dp -> bestSums/_bestSums to clear check-abbreviations, and ComputeDpValue was split into DropExpiredFront/WindowMaximum/DropDominatedBack to clear check-function-size. No fixture types existed to relocate; [Params(2_000, 20_000)], the K=50 window, RandomSeed 1425 and ValueRange 1_000 are unchanged and stayed inline in the benchmark as workload sizing/seeding. No hoisted overload needed -- the prepared input is LeetCode's own int[]. Test grew from 2 facts to 4 shared examples x 2 strategies = 8 assertions (LeetCode examples 1-3 plus a single-element case). No new DataStructures/Algorithms types, so no §18 obligation. The only remaining gate finding is check-single-letter-name on the public `int k` parameters, which deliberately mirror LeetCode's own signature and match the existing migrated tier (SlidingWindowMaximumSolution, BestTimeToBuyAndSellStockIVSolution etc. all take `int k`); I left them rather than diverging from the convention.
problems.strategies: MaxSumByWindowRescan (baseline; BCL int[] only, rescans the trailing k-window at every position, O(n*k) -- previously existed ONLY as the benchmark's unasserted baseline arm), MaxSumByMonotonicDeque (repo Deque<int> holding indices in decreasing best-sum order, O(n))

problems.title: Number of Ways to Wear Different Hats to Each Other

problems.title: Maximum Number of Darts Inside of a Circular Dartboard

The underlying O(n^2) pairwise-candidate-center technique is the established correct algorithm for this problem (a correct 'brute force' alternative doesn't exist below it - checking only the darts themselves as centers is provably wrong, since the optimal circle need not be centered on any input dart), so the benchmark instead contrasts the candidate buffer's container: plain BCL List<T> vs. this repo's DynamicArray<T>.
problems.notes: The pairwise candidate-center geometry existed three times: the test's private MaxDarts/BuildCandidateCenters/AddBoundaryCandidates (DynamicArray), and both benchmark arms (PairwiseCandidateCentersWithList, the never-asserted baseline, and PairwiseCandidateCentersWithDynamicArray). problems.title: Design Browser History
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.DynamicArray.DynamicArray<string> as the history backing store: Visit truncates everything past the cursor via RemoveAt then Add, Back/Forward clamp the cursor and Get the entry - the same 'sequence + access constraint' composition Stack<T> already makes over DynamicArray<T> (ARCHITECTURE.md §4.1).
problems.notes: Design-shaped problem, so it follows the established DesignCircularQueueSolution shape (two classes over a shared internal interface) rather than static <Operation>By<Strategy> methods. Behaviour change of note, flagged per instructions: the benchmark's baseline arm (ListBrowserHistory) had NO Forward method at all - it implemented only Visit/Back, i.e. a strictly weaker object than LeetCode asks for, and nothing asserted it. It is promoted here to the real LeetCode API (Forward added, clamped to _history.Count-1 exactly as the DynamicArray arm does) so both strategies now answer the full problem and both are asserted by the test harness. Visit/Back/Forward semantics on the shared inputs are otherwise byte-identical to the originals. The two original benchmark arms and the original test helper are algorithmically the same object; only the truncation mechanism differs (RemoveRange vs. repeated RemoveAt), which is the comparison the benchmark exists to make. Benchmark: original [Params(200, 5_000)] OperationCount, BackSteps=2 and the Visit/Back/Visit churn cycle are preserved verbatim; the only change is that the url strings are now materialized in a new [GlobalSetup] (the original had none and formatted $"url{i}.com" inside the measured loop), so string construction is charged to setup per ARCHITECTURE.md 17.4 instead of to both measured arms. Test harness gains a BrowserHistoryOp call-script record struct modelled on the existing CircularQueueOp, Apply returning null for Visit to match LeetCode's judge output; both original test cases are kept verbatim and a third (single-page history, Back/Forward both clamp to the homepage) was added. No fixture types existed to relocate and no new DataStructures/Algorithms primitive was introduced, so no section 18 obligation. 14 tests pass; Architecture/LayeringTests pass; Benchmarks project builds clean.
problems.strategies: DesignBrowserHistorySolution.IBrowserHistory (shared surface: Visit/Back/Forward); BrowserHistoryByListBacked (BCL List<string> + cursor + RemoveRange baseline, promoted from the benchmark's private ListBrowserHistory); BrowserHistoryByDynamicArrayBacked (repo DynamicArray<string> truncate-then-append, promoted from the test's private BrowserHistory helper)

problems.notes: Test arm and benchmark arm did not disagree on the answer (both returned the kth ancestor id / -1); the test's arm returned a TreeAncestorNode.Id and the benchmark's stored raw ints, so the solution settles on LeetCode's actual shape - an int node id, with -1 as LeetCodeAnswer.None. The BuildAncestorChains precompute deliberately stays INSIDE the measured [Benchmark] arm rather than moving to [GlobalSetup]: the whole point of that comparison is whether one O(n log n) pass pays for itself across a 1,000,000-query batch, and hoisting it would have measured only the O(1) index. Examples grew from 2 [Fact]s (4 assertions) to 14 cases x 3 theory methods = 42 assertions, adding a straight chain (deepest node reaching the root at k = depth and running out one step later) and a single-node tree.

problems.title: Best Position for a Service Centre
problems.skipReason: missing primitive: continuous multivariate numerical optimization
problems.notes: Best Position for a Service Centre requires continuous multivariate numerical optimization (minimizing sum of Euclidean distances to a point set has no closed form - needs Weiszfeld's algorithm for the geometric median, or 2D ternary search / gradient descent / simulated annealing over real-valued (x,y), to converge within LeetCode's 1e-5 tolerance). Repo-wide search for Weiszfeld/GeometricMedian/SimulatedAnnealing/GradientDescent/TernarySearch/GoldenSection found nothing. The only existing search primitive, Algorithms/Searching/BinarySearch.cs, is index-based over a sorted IRandomAccessSequence<Element> with integer-arithmetic midpoints and a discrete found/not-found predicate - it has no notion of a continuous domain or a convex objective to descend, so it cannot be composed into this without writing new continuous-optimization logic (a new production primitive), which this pass is not supposed to do ad hoc. Genuine primitive gap, not an effort issue.

problems.title: Minimum One Bit Operations to Make Integers Zero

Benchmark contrasts this against the closed-form O(log n) inverse-Gray-code loop (result ^= n; n >>= 1), which needs no container.

No signature disagreement existed - both returned int. Behaviour preserved exactly, including the exhausted-frontier fallback, now expressed as LeetCodeAnswer.None (== the original literal -1). Deliberate judgment call on section 17.5: the BFS arm keeps this repo's Queue<int>/HashMap<int,int> rather than being rewritten onto BCL Queue/HashSet. It is the [Benchmark(Baseline=true)] arm, but it is not a 'what you would write without this repo' baseline - it is the repo-composed arm the closed form is measured against, and the original test's comment justifies those primitives explicitly. Converting it would have changed what the benchmark measures. Test grew from 3 Facts (n=0,3,6) to a 6-case Examples table x 2 strategies = 12 assertions, adding n=1 (single flip), n=4 (7) and n=9 (14) - points far enough along the Gray-code path that the search and the closed form would visibly disagree if either drifted. The baseline's internals stay BCL (List<int>, RemoveRange, InsertRange) per section 17.5; only the input/output container is the repo's SinglyLinkedListNode<int>. No hoisted overload: following the already-migrated RotateList (LC 61) precedent, [GlobalSetup] hoists the int[] workload values but both benchmark arms rebuild their chains inside the measured method, because the splice strategy rewires the nodes it is handed and a cached chain would only be valid for the first measured iteration. Original [Params(200, 5_000)] and the SecondListLength/SecondListValueOffset/SpliceStartDivisor sizing are preserved; WindowBoundaryOffset moved into the solution where the walk now lives. No fixtures existed in either file, so nothing was relocated and no new DataStructures/ or Algorithms/ type was created (no section 18 obligation). Test keeps both original [Fact] examples, restated once as TheoryData<int[], int, int, int[], int[]>, and adds the two boundary windows the constraints allow: a == b (single node removed) and the widest window (everything but the first and last node). problems.title: Design Front Middle Back Queue
problems.primitivesUsed: Two Deque<int> instances (front half + back half, DesignCircularDeque precedent) kept within one element of each other in size; push/pop at front, middle, or back is O(1) via PushFront/PushBack/TryPopFront/TryPopBack plus a single-element rebalance move.
problems.notes: No fixtures existed for this problem (no test Fixtures/ folder, no Benchmarks/Fixtures entry), so nothing was relocated and no section 18 obligation was created. TWO deliberate changes, both flagged as required by the task rules: (1) The benchmark's [Benchmark(Baseline = true)] ArrayListInsertAtPosition arm only performed pushes and returned list.Count - it measured something weaker than the real answer and was never asserted. It is promoted to FrontMiddleBackQueueByListInsert, a full six-operation implementation whose index arithmetic is LeetCode's own wording (push at n/2, pop at (n-1)/2), and it is now under test. (2) The two-deque strategy carried a latent correctness bug, exposed the moment the baseline became assertable. The old Rebalance only moved an element when the halves differed by MORE than one, so the FRONT half could legally run one longer than the back (e.g. after PushFront into an empty queue: front=[1], back=[]). In that state PushMiddle inserted at index front.Count instead of n/2, and PopMiddle took the back half's first element instead of index (n-1)/2 - both the wrong element. LeetCode's real answer wins, so Rebalance now restores the standard invariant that the BACK half carries the extra element (front.Count is back.Count or back.Count-1, never more). Behaviour is unchanged on both of the original test's inputs (LC's published example sequence and the four-PushBack/two-PopMiddle case) - they pass identically - and the three added examples (PushFront+PushMiddle on a one-element queue, a front-loaded script, a PushMiddle into an empty queue) are the cases that separate the old code from LeetCode's answer; both strategies now agree on all six. The interface carries a Count member that is not one of LeetCode's six operations: it exists so the benchmark can return a non-dead value, which is exactly what both original benchmark arms returned (list.Count / queue.Count). Benchmark preserves the original [Params(5_000, 50_000)] Calls and the push front/middle/back cycle, and keeps the original arm names.
problems.strategies: DesignFrontMiddleBackQueueSolution.IFrontMiddleBackQueue (shared surface: Count, PushFront, PushMiddle, PushBack, PopFront, PopMiddle, PopBack); FrontMiddleBackQueueByListInsert (baseline, BCL List<int> internals); FrontMiddleBackQueueByTwoDeques (composed over DataStructures.Deque.Deque<int>). Design-problem shape, following the DesignCircularDequeSolution precedent (two classes over one interface) rather than <Operation>By<Strategy> static methods.

problems.title: Find the Most Competitive Subsequence
problems.primitivesUsed: Stack<int> monotonic-stack greedy (RemoveKDigits precedent): pop any still-poppable strictly-greater top while enough elements remain to still reach length k, then push only while there is room left for k.
problems.notes: No fixtures existed for this problem, so nothing was relocated and no section 18 obligation was created. No hoisted overload was needed: the benchmark's [GlobalSetup] only generates the workload (seeded random int[] and k = Length/3), which IS LeetCode's own input shape - there is no domain object to pre-build, so adding a second overload would have had nothing to take. Workload sizing/seeding stays inline in [GlobalSetup] per section 17.7; nothing was added to the shared Benchmarks/Fixtures folder. ONE deliberate change: both benchmark arms previously returned only a COUNT (current.Count / stack.Count) rather than the subsequence, so the baseline's arm was measuring something weaker than the real answer and nothing asserted it. Both are promoted to return int[], LeetCode's actual answer - the same section 17.8 move WordLadderII took. The baseline's greedy (remove the first element a strictly smaller one follows, else the last) is the same rule the monotonic stack applies in one pass, so the two agree on every case; the test verifies that directly. Both original InlineData examples are kept ([3,5,2,6] k=2 and [2,4,3,3,5,4,9,6] k=4) and seven boundary cases were added (k equal to the array length on both increasing and decreasing input, k=1, a run of equal elements, an already non-decreasing array, and a single-element array), since the original test was thin at two rows.
problems.strategies: MostCompetitiveByRepeatedRemoval(int[] nums, int k) (baseline, BCL List<int> internals, (n-k) first-descent scans); MostCompetitiveByMonotonicStack(int[] nums, int k) (composed over DataStructures.Stack.Stack<int>, single sweep)

problems.title: Minimize Deviation in Array
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Heap.Heap<int,MaxHeapOrder<int>> - normalize every odd value to its doubled (even) form, then repeatedly pop the max, halve it while tracking a running min, and push the half back until the max is odd. Same 'repeatedly reduce the current max via a max-heap' shape LastStoneWeightTests/LastStoneWeightBenchmarks already use for a different reduction rule.
problems.notes: Two distinct strategies across the pair. The test's private MinimumDeviation helper (+ its DeviationReducer class) and the benchmark's MaxHeapReduce arm were the SAME strategy written twice (Heap<int,MaxHeapOrder<int>>) - reconciled onto one MinimumDeviationByMaxHeap. The benchmark's [Benchmark(Baseline = true)] LinearRescanEachStep arm (+ its IndexOfMax helper) was never asserted by anything; it is now the first-class, BCL-internals method MinimumDeviationByLinearRescan and is covered by the harness. Both return LeetCode's real answer (int deviation), so no answer-shape disagreement had to be resolved. MEASUREMENT CHANGE, deliberate: the old [GlobalSetup] hoisted the 'double it if odd' normalization into _transformed. That normalization is problem semantics (the core insight of LC 1675), not input construction, so leaving it in the harness would have kept algorithm code in tier 5 - it moved into the solution's shared private EvenForm, and both measured arms now pay the same extra O(n) pass. No hoisted overload was warranted: what remains in [GlobalSetup] is only seeded random generation (workload sizing, tier 5), and the extra pass is <1% against the heap arm's O(n log n log max) and negligible against the baseline's O(n^2 log max). [Params(200, 2_000)], seed 1675 and the 1..1_000_000 value range are unchanged. Test kept all three original assertions ([1,2,3,4]=1, [2,10,8]=3, [5]=0) and added LeetCode's remaining published example [4,1,5,20,3]=3 plus [3,5]=1 (halving drives the running minimum below every value the array started with). No fixture types existed to relocate; no new DataStructures/ or Algorithms/ primitive was introduced, so no section-18 obligation arose.
problems.strategies: MinimumDeviationByLinearRescan, MinimumDeviationByMaxHeap

problems.title: Minimum Incompatibility
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer<TState,TResult> (bitmask DP where TState is the 'elements still needing a group' mask, the same memoized-recurrence shape StoneGameVTests/StoneGameIIITests already use for a different state type) composed with DataStructures.Set.Set<int> (catches 'two equal values in the same candidate subset' - the problem's own feasibility rule - while a group is built). Subset enumeration itself is plain bit arithmetic (submask trick), not a separate primitive.
problems.notes: Two distinct strategies. The test's private MinimumIncompatibility helper (Memoizer + Set<int>, with its GroupingContext record) and the benchmark's MemoizedRecursion arm were the same strategy written twice; the benchmark's untested [Benchmark(Baseline = true)] UnmemoizedRecursion arm is now first-class and under test. ANSWER-SHAPE DISAGREEMENT RESOLVED IN FAVOUR OF LEETCODE: the test solved the real problem - signature (nums, k), infeasible mapped to -1 - while the benchmark's arms hard-coded a private const GroupSize = 2 (never taking k) and returned the raw int.MaxValue/2 sentinel instead of -1, i.e. they measured something weaker than the real answer. Both strategies now take (int[] nums, int k) and return LeetCodeAnswer.None (-1) when no valid grouping exists; the benchmark passes k = Length / 2, which reproduces the old GroupSize = 2 workload exactly, and since the workload is a permutation of 1..Length it is always feasible so the measured value is unchanged. Per section 17.5 the baseline's internals are now pure BCL: its duplicate-value check uses a BCL HashSet<int> where the old benchmark baseline reached for this repo's Set<int>; behaviour is identical (both reject a repeated value in a candidate group), and the composed arm keeps Set<int>. The two recurrences are written as parallel chains rather than sharing one body, matching the StoneGameVSolution precedent for a memoize-or-not pairing; only the neutral PopCount bit trick is shared. [Params(10, 14)] and seed 1681 preserved; the trivially derived _fullMask dropped from [GlobalSetup] since it is O(1) inside the method. Test kept all three original assertions ([1,2,1,4] k=2 = 4, [6,3,8,1,3,1,2,2] k=4 = 6, [5,3,3,6,3,3] k=3 = -1) and added k=1 ([1,2,3,4] = 3, the whole array as one group) and k=n ([1,1] k=2 = 0, singleton groups so repeats are harmless). No fixture types existed to relocate; no new DataStructures/ or Algorithms/ primitive was introduced, so no section-18 obligation arose.
problems.strategies: MinimumIncompatibilityByUnmemoizedRecursion, MinimumIncompatibilityByMemoizedRecursion

problems.title: Stone Game VI
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Sorting.MergeSort.Sort<Element,TSequence> over DataStructures.Sequence.ArrayIndexedSequence<(int Alice, int Bob)> with a descending-by-(aliceValue+bobValue) comparer - the standard greedy proof for this problem (sort by 'swing' value, alternate picks), identical shape to TwoCitySchedulingTests/TwoCitySchedulingBenchmarks, not the game-theory minimax DP the title might suggest.

Two smaller harness-side changes: the descending-swing comparer is now one static readonly IComparer shared by both arms instead of being re-created per call by the MergeSort arm only, and [GlobalSetup] now seeds the two int[] value arrays (same seed 1686, same interleaved draw order, same [Params] 200/4_000) which the LeetCode-shaped method pairs up, replacing the pre-paired tuple array that each measured arm used to Clone - an equivalent O(n) cost inside the measured region, so no hoisted overload was needed. problems.title: Number Of Ways To Reconstruct A Tree
problems.primitivesUsed: HashMap<TKey,TValue> (map-of-set adjacency, same shape as AccountsMergeTests) + Algorithms/Sorting/MergeSort over ArrayIndexedSequence for degree ordering. Candidate-parent tree-reconstruction algorithm composed on top: build symmetric adjacency from pairs, sort nodes by degree, for every node but one arbitrary root find its minimal-qualifying-degree neighbor as parent, verify adjacency[node]\{parent} subset-of adjacency[parent], flag ambiguity on a degree tie. Verified against LeetCode's 3 official examples plus a hand-derived two-max-degree-node ambiguity case (all via dotnet test), and cross-checked the benchmark's two independent implementations (BCL Dictionary/LINQ baseline vs. repo HashMap/MergeSort) against each other at both Params sizes via a throwaway smoke harness -- results matched exactly.
problems.notes: The test arm and the benchmark's repo arm were the same algorithm decomposed differently: the test's EvaluateCandidateParent returned bool? (null / true=ambiguous / false) via a two-pass FindMinQualifyingDegree + CountNeighborsAtDegree, while the benchmark's EvaluateNode returned int? (null / 2 / 1) via a single ConsiderNeighbor fold. They are provably equivalent - the first neighbour in iteration order at the final minimum qualifying degree is exactly the one that last lowered the running minimum - so I kept the benchmark's fold shape and LeetCode's own answer codes (0/1/2), which is the real answer shape. ConsiderNeighbor is shared by both strategies because it reads degrees, not containers; everything container-specific is duplicated per arm so the baseline's internals stay BCL. [Params(50, 2_000)] and the star-of-chains workload are preserved verbatim. Kept all four original assertions (LeetCode examples 1-3 plus the two-max-degree-nodes case) and added three: the smallest ambiguous input [[1,2]] -> 2, a forced three-level tree -> 1, and a case that returns 0 through the neighbour-subset check rather than through the initial degree check, which no original assertion covered.

problems.title: Cat and Mouse II
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer over a (MouseRow, MouseCol, CatRow, CatCol, Turn) state tuple - the same turn-based optimal-play minimax shape CanIWinTests/PredictTheWinnerTests already use for bitmask/interval DP, here keyed on a 2D grid position tuple instead, with Turn capped at rows*cols*2 (the well-known pigeonhole bound for this problem) standing in for the official 1000-turn rule while keeping the memoized state space finite.

problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer.Memoize<int,BigInteger> driving the recurrence maxProduct(remaining)=max(remaining, 2*maxProduct(remaining-2), 3*maxProduct(remaining-3)) - a 'nice divisor' count is the product of the chosen exponents summing to primeFactors (same maximize-product-of-parts shape as Integer Break/LC343), and many different peel-2/peel-3 orders converge on the same remaining budget, which is exactly Memoizer's overlapping-subproblem use case (same idiom as the existing CountAllPossibleRoutes/FibonacciNumber coverage).
problems.notes: 5 xUnit cases pass; all 5 expected values (including 5->6 and 8->18) were derived and cross-checked by hand-tracing the recurrence itself, not solely from memory of LeetCode's official examples. No modular-exponentiation primitive exists in this repo (searched DataStructures/Algorithms - none), so the benchmark deliberately stays within a range (PrimeFactors 40/50, mirroring FibonacciNumberBenchmarks' scale) where a naive un-memoized BigInteger recursion vs. the Memoizer-backed one is a fair, real complexity comparison, rather than reaching for LeetCode's full 1e9 bound (which would need O(log n) modular exponentiation this repo doesn't have - not needed here since the exercise is proving Memoizer suffices, not matching LeetCode's judge limits). Full test suite: 2382 passed, 1 pre-existing skip, 0 failed.

Remainder-0 groups are always served first (free); the recurrence searches every serving order of the rest, with many orders converging on the same state.

Full Tests-project build is currently blocked by an unrelated pre-existing compile error in FindTheShortestSuperstringTests.cs (being actively edited by a different concurrent session, not part of this cluster and not touched); the DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks project - which shares the identical algorithm code and the production DSAExperimentation project - built clean with 0 errors.

problems.title: Maximum Compatibility Score Sum
