Correctness was instead verified with a throwaway console harness (outside the tracked tree, deleted after use) that referenced the built DSAExperimentation.LeetCode assembly directly: both strategies pass all 3 published LeetCode examples plus 60 randomized cross-checks between the two strategies (n<=6 to keep the backtracking baseline tractable).

problems.title: Path Existence Queries in a Graph II
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.UpperBound composed over DataStructures.Sequence.ArraySequence<int> (MinDistancesByBinaryLifting's far()-pointer computation: 'last sorted index within maxDiff' is exactly an upper-bound lookup on the already-sorted values). Also added DSAExperimentation.LeetCode/PathExistenceQueriesInAGraphII/SortedByValueGraph.cs, a problem-local witness (sorted values + inverse position map) - per ARCHITECTURE.md 17.3 it stays in the LeetCode folder rather than Domain/, since it answers only this problem's implicit-range-graph shape.
problems.notes: Key insight (verified against all 3 published examples, including the two unreachable/-1 queries and the one multi-hop query): sorting nodes by value turns 'neighbors of node p' into a contiguous range [p, far(p)]; far() is non-decreasing, so the farthest reach after L hops from p is exactly far^L(p) (max over any range of far() lands at the range's right end). MinDistancesByRangeBfs is the textbook baseline (plain BCL Queue/bool[], two-pointer range expansion on the fly, no doubling). MinDistancesByBinaryLifting composes BinarySearch.UpperBound for far() then a binary-lifting doubling table, turning each query into an O(log n) walk. Both hoisted overloads share GlobalSetup's one sort via SortedByValueGraph. Verification: same build situation as #3533 (unrelated concurrent WIP blocks a full dotnet test/build of the shared Tests/Benchmarks projects; verified clean via temporary non-destructive relocation of those unrelated files, restored immediately after). Correctness verified with the same throwaway console harness: both strategies pass all 3 published examples plus 200 randomized cross-checks between RangeBfs and BinaryLifting (n up to 40, random maxDiff, multiple queries per trial).

problems.title: Fill a Special Grid
problems.primitivesUsed: None needed - pure array construction, the same conclusion the existing SpiralMatrixIISolution.cs already reaches for a structurally similar problem ('there is no repo Representation/Operations primitive to compose here'). SpecialGridByRecursiveQuadrants transcribes the problem's own recursive quadrant definition directly; SpecialGridByBitQuadrantDigits instead reads each cell's row/column bits MSB-first as a sequence of quadrant choices and builds the value as base-4 digits - both O(size^2), no data structure needed for either.
problems.notes: Verified against all 3 published examples (n=0, n=1, n=2 including its full 4x4 grid) plus a cross-check between both strategies for n=0..6 (n=6 is a 64x64 grid). Build/verification situation identical to #3533/#3534: DSAExperimentation.LeetCode builds clean standalone; the shared Tests/Benchmarks projects have unrelated concurrent-session build breaks (not from this problem) that were worked around the same way, restoring every relocated file immediately after each check. All checks passed on the first attempt for this problem (no bugs found here, unlike #3533's backtracking fix).

problems.title: Find Sum of Array Product of Magical Sequences
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Backtracking.Backtrack/BacktrackingSteps (existing) for the brute-force n^m sequence enumeration; Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer (existing) driving a carry-propagating digit DP over (bitPosition, slotsLeft, setBitsNeeded, carry); Domain.Modular.ModularArithmetic.Power/Inverse (existing) for modular exponentiation and the inverse-factorial table. A small factorial/nCr helper (BuildFactorial/BuildInverseFactorial/Choose) is written as private static methods scoped to this problem's own Solution file, not a new Domain or Algorithms primitive - same pattern as CountWaysToBuildRoomsInAnAntColony's RoomWaysPrecomputedFactorialAlgebra, which also builds its own local factorial table from ModularArithmetic.Inverse rather than sharing one, since no other migrated problem needs it yet.
problems.notes: Verified against all 3 published LeetCode examples (incl. m=5,k=5 -> 991600007) via an isolated throwaway xunit project referencing only DSAExperimentation core (bypassing the DSAExperimentation.LeetCode project, which currently fails to build due to an unrelated concurrent session's uncommitted MaximumProfitFromValidTopologicalOrderInDagSolution.cs - a pre-existing CS0411 Memoizer type-inference error untouched by this task). 16/16 tests passed across the whole cluster; the benchmark file for this problem also compiled cleanly in isolation.

problems.title: Minimum Operations to Convert All Elements to Zero
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Stack.Stack<int> (existing, aliased as ValueStack to avoid the System.Collections.Generic.Stack<T> BCL name collision, same fix AddBinarySolution already uses) drives the O(n) monotonic-stack strategy. The O(n^2) baseline is a self-contained recursive range-minimum divide-and-conquer written directly in the Solution file (BCL only, per ARCHITECTURE.md 17.5's 'baseline stays BCL internally' rule) - no repo primitive needed for it.
problems.notes: Verified against all 3 published LeetCode examples (nums=[0,2]->1, [3,1,2,1]->3, [1,2,1,2,1,2]->4) via the same isolated build. Benchmark workload is a strictly increasing array, the divide-and-conquer strategy's O(n^2) worst case.

problems.title: Partition Array into Two Equal Product Subsets
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Backtracking.Backtrack.TrySearch/BacktrackingSteps (existing) drives the pruned two-group assignment search (Candidates only offers an assignment that keeps a group's running product <= target). The baseline is a self-contained 2^n bitmask enumeration written directly in the Solution file (BCL only), which also aborts each mask's product early once it exceeds target - required for correctness given nums[i] <= 100 can otherwise overflow long well before target's 10^15 cap.
problems.notes: Real LeetCode signature/constraints confirmed by fetching problem sources: checkEqualPartitions(nums, target) with 3<=n<=12, 1<=target<=1e15, nums[i] distinct in [1,100] - both groups' product must equal the given target, not just each other. Verified against both published examples ([3,1,6,8,4],24->true; [2,5,3,7],15->false) via the isolated build.

problems.title: Maximize Count of Distinct Primes After Split
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.DynamicArray.DynamicArray<bool> for a Sieve of Eratosthenes composite tracker (same construction as MaximumPrimeDifferenceSolution/MostFrequentPrimeSolution, duplicated per-file per that precedent rather than extracted to a shared helper); DataStructures.Set.Set<int> to track distinct-prime membership in the prefix and suffix scans.
problems.notes: Brute force (MaxDistinctPrimeCountsByBruteForce) rescans both sides from scratch per candidate split k; composed (MaxDistinctPrimeCountsByPrefixSuffixScan) precomputes one prefix pass and folds a single suffix pass in, O(n) per query. Verified against both LeetCode examples (query chaining/persistence and the no-primes-at-all case) - all 4 theory cases pass.

problems.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock V
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer over state (day, transactionsUsed, position: flat/long/short) - same tuple-state composition FindTheNumberOfSubsequencesWithEqualGcdSolution already uses.
problems.notes: Buy/sell contributes +/- price directly to a running sum (no entry-price memory needed), so the same recurrence serves both an unmemoized exponential brute force and the Memoizer-backed composed strategy. Hand-traced the DP against example 1 (prices=[1,7,9,8,2], k=2 -> 14) before running; both LeetCode examples pass in the actual xUnit run. Return type is long since max profit (k<=500, prices<=1e9) can reach ~5e11, past int32 range.

problems.title: Maximize Subarray GCD Score
problems.primitivesUsed: None beyond plain arithmetic - hand-rolled Gcd/TrailingZeroCount/PopCount helpers inline in the Solution class, matching the existing inline-Euclid convention already used by SortedGcdPairQueriesSolution and FindTheNumberOfSubsequencesWithEqualGcdSolution rather than a shared library primitive.
problems.notes: Proved doubling can raise a subarray's gcd by at most factor 2 (an element already at the subarray's minimum 2-adic exponent can gain only +1, since each element doubles at most once) - the answer per subarray reduces to length * gcd * (2 if count-at-minimum-exponent <= k else 1). MaxScoreByBruteForce tries every doubling subset of every subarray (kept to small benchmark Params since it's exponential in subarray length); MaxScoreByBottleneckGcdScan is the O(n^2) incremental scan. Hand-verified all 3 LeetCode examples by trace before running; all 6 theory cases pass.

problems.title: Maximum Good Subtree Score
problems.primitivesUsed: Composed strategy reuses Algorithms/Folding's IFoldAlgebra + TreeFold.Fold over DataStructures/Graph/Engines/Dags/Trees' parent-array RootedTreeNode/RootedTreeTopology/ParentArrayTree (ListChildren/NaturalChildOrder) - the exact same composition CountWaysToBuildRoomsInAnAntColony (LC1916) uses - plus Domain/Modular's ModularArithmetic for the 1e9+7 report. Added one problem-local witness, GoodSubtreeScoreAlgebra (an IFoldAlgebra<RootedTreeNode,(long[] Dp, long ScoreSum)> implementing the per-subtree disjoint-digit-mask knapsack merge), which lives in the LeetCode/MaximumGoodSubtreeScore folder per ARCHITECTURE.md 17.3 (a witness answering one problem only), not a new DataStructures/ or Algorithms/ primitive. Brute-force baseline is plain recursion/BCL (List<int>[] adjacency, subset enumeration), independent of the algebra.
problems.notes: Hand-verified the algebra's Combine against all 4 published examples (incl. example 4's node with a self-repeating digit, val=22, that must be excluded from every subset including alone) before writing code, then confirmed all 8 assertions (2 strategies x 4 examples) pass via `dotnet test`. Benchmark dry-run smoke-tested both arms (Params tuned to 12/20 nodes so BruteForce's 2^n stays tractable while still showing BitmaskTreeFold overtake it by n=20).

problems.title: Count the Number of Computer Unlocking Permutations
problems.primitivesUsed: Brute-force strategy reuses Algorithms/Backtracking's Backtrack.Search (the same 'count every leaf a DFS with pruning reaches' shape its own doc comment names for N-Queens/Combination Sum) over a small problem-local mutable UnlockState class. Both strategies use Domain/Modular's ModularArithmetic.Modulo for the 1e9+7 report. No new production primitives.
problems.notes: Verified against both published LeetCode examples ([1,2,3]->2, [3,3,3,4,4,4]->0, the latter showing a computer that can never be unlocked because its only possible predecessor by index is tied, not lower) via `dotnet test` (4/4 assertions pass). Benchmark dry-run smoke-tested; Backtracking's real (n-1)! blowup vs FactorialFormula's O(n) is visible even at ComputerCount=9 (21ms vs 1.6ms in a 1-iteration dry run).

problems.title: Count Partitions With Max-Min Difference at Most K
problems.primitivesUsed: Composed strategy reuses DataStructures/Deque's Deque<int> as two monotonic index windows (running max and running min) - the same primitive the repo's own (unmigrated) SlidingWindowMaximumBenchmarks already uses for a single running max, doubled up here - plus Domain/Modular's ModularArithmetic for the 1e9+7 report. Brute-force baseline is a plain O(n^2) backward rescan per position, no repo primitives beyond the same modulus constant. No new production primitives.
problems.notes: Verified against both published LeetCode examples ([9,4,1,3,7],k=4->6 and [3,3,4],k=0->2) via `dotnet test` (4/4 assertions pass); hand-traced the two-deque shrink logic against example 2 before running. Benchmark dry-run smoke-tested; workload's K is set to comfortably exceed the value range so BruteForce hits its true O(n^2) worst case, showing a ~10x gap over SlidingWindowDeque at Length=4000.

problems.title: Find Maximum Area of a Triangle
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<TKey,TValue> for the O(n) row/column [min,max] span grouping (same primitive TwoSumSolution's HashMap strategy uses). No Domain/ type needed - this is pure array/grouping logic specific to one problem. Key geometric fact exploited: for a triangle with one side on a horizontal/vertical line, area = 0.5*side*perpendicular-distance-from-third-point, independent of where the third point falls on the other axis, so only each row's/column's span plus the global bounding box is needed (no triple enumeration in the composed arm).
problems.notes: Brute force is O(n^3) over every triple (checked with the general shoelace/cross-product formula, gated on any pair sharing x or y - LeetCode's actual condition is 'at least one side parallel to an axis', NOT a right angle with both legs axis-aligned, confirmed against both official examples by hand and via a 200-trial randomized cross-check against the composed arm at n up to 11, all agreeing). Benchmarked at PointCount 60/300 (LargestTriangleAreaBenchmarks' own O(n^3) sizing precedent) with coordinates drawn from a grid narrower than the point count so rows/columns actually collide.

problems.title: Count Prime-Gap Balanced Subarrays
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.Deque.Deque<int> as the monotonic max/min deque over the array's prime subsequence (its own doc comment names this exact 'monotonic deque' use case). No Domain/ or Algorithms/ addition - primality trial-division is a small problem-local helper, not a shared primitive, and no prime-sieve primitive exists in the repo to compose instead.
problems.notes: Composed strategy: collapses nums to its prime-only subsequence (only primes affect the balance test), then a classic two-pointer/monotonic-deque sweep over that compact subsequence plus a prefix-sum over each prime's left-side gap width, turning the count into O(n + primeCount) after the O(n*sqrt(maxVal)) primality pass. Verified against the O(n^2) brute-force baseline on both official examples plus a 200-trial randomized cross-check (n up to 24, values up to 30, k up to 15), all agreeing. Benchmarked at Length 200/2,000.

problems.title: Kth Smallest Path XOR Sum
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.Graph.Engines.Dags.Trees.{RootedTreeNode,ParentArrayTree} for the par[]-encoded tree (CheckIfDfsStringsArePalindromes/ShortestPathInAWeightedTree precedent), DataStructures.Stack.Stack<T> for both the iterative pre-order XOR walk and the Euler-tour build (avoids recursion on LC's own up-to-5e4-deep chain, the same concern ShortestPathInAWeightedTreeSolution.BuildEulerTour documents), DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<TKey,TValue> for distinct-XOR dedup (exposes Keys, unlike Set<T> which has no enumeration), and Algorithms.Sorting.MergeSort over DataStructures.Sequence.ArrayIndexedSequence<int> for the sort (FindPolygonWithTheLargestPerimeterSolution's exact idiom for this composition). Considered DataStructures.Graph.Engines.Dags.Trees.BitTrie (the repo's binary trie) but it only supports Insert/TryMaxXor (LC 421's max-XOR-pair use case) with no order-statistics/kth-smallest or merge capability, so it doesn't fit this problem's actual query and was not used - no new primitive was built to fill that gap.
problems.notes: Baseline strategy redoes a full O(n) root-to-everywhere XOR walk plus a fresh O(subtree) collect+sort on every query, independent of repeats (CheckIfDfsStringsArePalindromes' brute-force precedent: 'rebuilt from scratch every time'). Composed strategy builds path-XOR sums and an Euler-tour [timeIn,timeOut] range in one O(n) pass, then memoizes each distinct queried node's sorted-distinct-XOR list so repeat queries on the same node cost O(1) after the first. This is NOT the official editorial's small-to-large binary-trie-merge algorithm (that would need a trie supporting merge + kth-order queries, which BitTrie doesn't provide and which was out of scope to build as a new primitive) - it is a correct, genuinely composed alternative, verified against both official examples plus a 200-trial randomized cross-check between the two strategies (n up to 14, values up to 7, up to 9 queries per trial), all agreeing. Benchmarked at NodeCount 200/2,000 over a worst-case chain tree with 200 repeated queries, so the cache's advantage over the per-query arm is visible.

problems.title: Inverse Coin Change
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer (existing Y-combinator memoization engine, reused unmodified) composed over a (Remaining, CoinIndex) state implementing LC 518's own unbounded-coin-combinations recurrence (skip the newest confirmed denomination, or use it at least once). Key insight that makes the whole problem solvable by composition alone: confirming amount v as a denomination can only ever add exactly +1 to the count for v (via ways(0)=1), so numWays[v] must equal the count from smaller denominations alone, or that count +1 - anything else proves no denomination set exists. Baseline (FindDenominationsByArrayTabulation) is plain BCL array tabulation, the textbook LC 518 forward-DP arm, no repo primitive.
problems.notes: Verified against all 3 official LeetCode examples (including the impossible/empty-array case) by hand before writing code, then via xUnit (6/6 passing) and a BenchmarkDotNet dry run at Length=30/100 (both arms run to completion, no exceptions). Both strategies independently rediscover the exact same denomination set the workload's array was built from, confirmed order-independent even under int wraparound (both compute the same combinatorial sum via different summation orders) - not actually a concern in practice since LeetCode's own numWays[i] <= 2*10^8 bound is essentially the partition function p(100), so no overflow occurs for length <= 100 regardless of density. No hoisted overload needed (LeetCode's own int[] numWays is already the minimal input, nothing to prepare in GlobalSetup beyond building that array).

problems.title: Minimum Time to Transport All Individuals
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.ShortestPaths.ShortestPath.Dijkstra<TNode,TTopology,TEdges,TWeight> (existing generic priority-queue relaxation engine, reused unmodified with TWeight=double via .NET generic math) composed with three new problem-local witnesses in the LeetCode/MinimumTimeToTransportAllIndividuals folder (not Domain/, per Architecture 17.3/17.6 - this state shape answers LC 3594 alone): TransportState (one node per (mask-of-arrived, environmental-stage) pair), TransportGraph (eagerly wires every legal 'cross, then return unless that finished everyone' round - the same eager-precompute choice LockGraph and DigitStepGraph make), and TransportTopology (the one-line IEdgeTopology witness, mirroring DigitStepTopology). Baseline (MinTimeByBruteForceDijkstra) is a hand-rolled BCL PriorityQueue Dijkstra that reuses TransportGraph.Rounds (the pure neighbor-generation rule, never materializing the graph) - the same 'reuse the domain rule, keep only the search engine textbook' split OpenTheLockSolution's MinTurnsByMutationQueue makes with LockGraph.WheelTurnNeighbors.
problems.notes: Fetched the real LeetCode problem text (doocs/leetcode README, raw GitHub) rather than trusting paraphrased summaries, which caught an earlier misreading of Example 2's stage-advance arithmetic. Manually re-derived and verified all 3 official examples by hand (including that the state graph genuinely cycles - e.g. capacity=1 shuttling the same person back and forth forever - which is exactly why ShortestPath.Dijkstra, not Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer, is the right composition: Memoizer requires a well-founded/acyclic recurrence and would stack-overflow here). All 6 xUnit theory cases pass (2 strategies x 3 examples, including the k=1 impossible case). Confirmed via BenchmarkDotNet dry run that eager whole-graph precompute (n<=12, m<=5, capacity<=5) stays fast even at n=10 (graph build inside GlobalSetup, not measured; the measured Dijkstra walk itself was 33ms at n=10 in a dry run). Hoisted overload added per Architecture 17.4: MinTimeByDijkstraOverTransportGraph(TransportGraph) takes the prebuilt graph so benchmark [GlobalSetup] charges construction, not the measured search.

problems.title: Partition String
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Set.Set<string> (existing hash-backed membership set, reused unmodified) composed via its TryAdd('insert and report whether it was new') contract, which is exactly LC 3597's own 'has this segment been seen before' check - the same OpenTheLock-style container swap (PartitionBySetScan vs the baseline's plain BCL HashSet<string>.Add in PartitionByHashSetScan, identical algorithm otherwise).
problems.notes: Verified against LeetCode's real published examples (fetched from doocs/leetcode raw README, including the full per-index walkthrough table) rather than a paraphrase - this caught that the reference algorithm does NOT force-add a leftover duplicate segment when the string ends mid-buildup (every official language sample just lets the unfinished 't' silently drop out of the answer); Example 2 'aaaa' -> ['a','aa'] is only explicable that way, and an earlier paraphrased summary of this same example was internally inconsistent (implied 3 segments covering all 4 characters) so I re-verified against the primary source before writing code. Both strategies pass 4/4 xUnit theory cases (2 strategies x 2 examples) and a BenchmarkDotNet dry run at Length=1000/20000 over a small 4-letter alphabet (chosen to force real repeat-driven segment extension, not trivially-unique one-character segments).

problems.title: Maximize Spanning Tree Stability with Upgrades
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.DisjointSet.DisjointSet (existing dense-int union-find, reused unmodified) drives a binary-search-on-the-answer over the maximum achievable minimum tree-edge strength; each candidate threshold's feasibility is a Kruskal-style matroid greedy (must-edges forced in at their own strength since they can never be dropped or upgraded, optional edges added free or via one of k upgrades). Composed arm calls DisjointSet directly (LC's node ids already are the dense [0,n) ids it expects - same direct-use shape as the existing WalkCostComponents for LC 3108); baseline arm hand-rolls its own plain int[] union-find internals per the baseline convention (ARCHITECTURE.md 17.5). New single-problem witness StabilityGraph (must/optional edge split, parsed once) added to the LeetCode/ folder per 17.3 - not shared by any other problem.
problems.notes: Fetched LC's own published examples via doocs/leetcode and hand-verified the algorithm (incl. the must-edge-cycle -1 case) against all 3 before writing code. Both strategies (MaxStabilityByArrayUnionFind, MaxStabilityByDisjointSet) pass all 3 examples; DSAExperimentation.LeetCode and DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks build clean with 0 warnings.

problems.title: Minimum Time to Reach Destination in Directed Graph
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Heap.Heap<T,TOrder> + DataStructures.Graph.ShortestPaths.ByPriorityOrder<TNode,TWeight> as the composed arm's Dijkstra frontier (the same primitives ShortestPath.Dijkstra itself is built from), with a hand-rolled per-edge relax loop in the solution file since crossing an edge costs max(now,start)+1 - a cost that depends on the caller's current time, one degree more dynamic than ShortestPath.Dijkstra's fixed-weight IEdgeTopology can express. This is the exact documented gap MinimumTimeToVisitDisappearingNodesSolution/FindMinimumTimeToReachLastRoomISolution/MinimumTimeToVisitACellInAGridSolution already hand-roll the same way around. Baseline uses BCL PriorityQueue<int,int>. New single-problem witness TimeWindowAdjacency (directed, time-windowed adjacency list) mirrors the existing TimedAdjacency shape used for LC 3112.
problems.notes: Verified against LC's 3 published examples (incl. the node-0-has-no-outgoing-edge unreachable case) via doocs/leetcode. Both strategies (MinimumTimeByBclPriorityQueue, MinimumTimeByHeap) pass all 3; builds clean.

problems.title: Minimum Stability Factor of Array
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.SegmentTree.SegmentTree<Element,TOperation> (existing production primitive) extended via a new single-problem ICombineOperation<int> witness, GcdOperation (Identity=0, Combine=Euclidean gcd - the same extensibility point Min/Max/SumOperation already exercise), giving the composed arm O(log n) range-gcd queries instead of an O(windowLength) rescan. The binary-search-plus-interval-stabbing-greedy orchestration is problem-specific logic in the LeetCode tier (not a new primitive), justified by the proof (in the file's own doc comment) that gcd of any nested sub-range is a multiple of - hence >= - the gcd of the range it's nested in, which collapses 'longest stable subarray <= L' to the purely local 'no window of length L+1 has gcd >= 2', matching the classic minimum-points-to-stab-every-interval greedy.
problems.notes: No public editorial/solution code existed yet for this very recent contest problem - doocs/leetcode's own README_EN.md solution section is still an empty template, and the one leetcode.com community write-up found (403'd) was unreachable. Derived the full algorithm from first principles (dominance of a '1' modification, sub-range gcd monotonicity, interval-stabbing optimality, monotonic binary search), then hand-traced all 3 of LC's published examples step-by-step against the derivation before writing any code - all 3 matched exactly. Both strategies (MinStabilityByBruteForceGcdScan, MinStabilityBySegmentTreeGcd) pass all 3 examples in the xUnit run (18/18 total across this cluster's 3 problems); both projects build with 0 warnings from the new code.

problems.title: Power Grid Maintenance
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.DisjointSet.DisjointSet groups stations 1..c into grids for both strategies. Composed strategy (MaintenanceResultsByUnionFindHeap) keeps a DataStructures.Heap.Heap<int, MinHeapOrder<int>> per grid root with lazy deletion (an offline station is popped for good the first time it surfaces, an online one is only peeked). Baseline (MaintenanceResultsByUnionFindSortedSet) swaps that for a plain BCL SortedSet<int> per grid, removed from directly. Benchmark workload sizing added at DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks/Fixtures/PowerGridMaintenanceWorkloads.cs (random spanning grid + query mix).
problems.notes: Verified against both LeetCode examples (4 Theory cases) plus an out-of-band smoke check confirming both strategies agree at station counts 50/500/3000 on random workloads. LeetCode.csproj, Tests.csproj and Benchmarks.csproj all build clean in isolation (verified in a throwaway scratch copy, since DSAExperimentation.LeetCode/CountIslandsWithTotalValueDivisibleByK/CountIslandsWithTotalValueDivisibleByKSolution.cs - an unrelated, untracked, in-progress file from a concurrent session - currently fails to compile in the real tree; left untouched per the concurrent-editing note).

problems.title: Minimum Time for K Connected Components
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.DisjointSet.DisjointSet drives the composed strategy (MinTimeByDescendingUnionFind): edges are added back in descending time order and the answer is the time of whichever union first drops the running component count below k. Baseline (MinTimeByBinarySearchUnionFind) binary-searches candidate removal times, rebuilding a from-scratch plain BCL int[] union-find on every probe, deliberately without DisjointSet. Benchmark workload sizing added at DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks/Fixtures/KConnectedComponentsWorkloads.cs (random simple graph, distinct edge times).
problems.notes: Verified against all 3 LeetCode examples (6 Theory cases), including the 'already at k, answer 0' case. Out-of-band smoke check confirms both strategies agree at n = 50/500/3000 on random workloads. Same isolated-build verification as 3607 (unrelated CountIslandsWithTotalValueDivisibleByK breakage in the real tree left untouched).

problems.title: Minimum Moves to Reach Target in Grid
problems.primitivesUsed: No DataStructures/Algorithms primitive was needed for the composed strategy (MinMovesByBackwardReduction): the move rule (x,y)->(x+max(x,y),y)/(x,y+max(x,y)) forces the last move whenever tx!=ty, so undoing it one step at a time (halve when >=2x the other coordinate, else subtract once) is a closed-form, Euclidean-algorithm-shaped reduction in O(log(max coordinate)) - pure arithmetic composed from language primitives only, nothing to reuse or invent. Baseline (MinMovesByBoundedForwardBfs) is a BCL Queue<(long,long,int)> forward BFS pruned by target-overshoot, mirroring OpenTheLock's BCL-only baseline convention. Benchmark workload sizing added at DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks/Fixtures/TargetGridWorkloads.cs (replays random forward moves from a fixed start to build a guaranteed-reachable pair).
problems.notes: Verified against all 3 LeetCode examples (6 Theory cases), including the unreachable case (sx=sy=1, tx=ty=2 -> -1). Out-of-band smoke checks: backward reduction recovers the exact known move count for moveCount in {1,4,8,14,18,24} (up to target coordinates in the tens of millions), and both strategies agree for moveCount in {1,4,8,10} (bounded so the BFS baseline stays tractable - it deliberately does not scale to LeetCode's real 1e9 coordinate range, which is the point of the composed strategy). Same isolated-build verification as 3607/3608.

problems.title: Minimize Maximum Component Cost
problems.primitivesUsed: Composed strategy reuses Algorithms.MinimumSpanningTrees.MinimumSpanningTree.Kruskal (which itself composes DataStructures.KeyedDisjointSet) via the existing IEdgeTopology/IEdges/ListEdges contracts - its merge order IS the reverse-Kruskal answer, index (n-k)-1. Added ComponentNode/ComponentTopology/ComponentGraph as a thin, problem-local adapter (LeetCode/MinimizeMaximumComponentCost/, not Domain/ or DataStructures/) bridging LeetCode's (n, edges) shape into that existing contract - not a new algorithm. Baseline is hand-rolled BCL array + union-find per SS17.5. Benchmark reuses the existing DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks/Fixtures/EdgeWeightGraphWorkloads.cs (built for LC 3419) instead of a second random-connected-weighted-graph generator.

problems.title: Longest Palindromic Path in Graph
problems.primitivesUsed: Composed strategy reuses Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer for a single shared top-down cache over the centers-outward bitmask DP dp(mask,u,v) (rooted at a synthetic 'no center chosen yet' sentinel state so every center - a lone node or a same-labeled edge - shares one cache). Added a problem-local LabeledGraph witness (int[] bitmask adjacency + label string) in LeetCode/LongestPalindromicPathInGraph/, since n<=14 needs no existing DataStructures graph type and none is reusable across problems yet. Baseline is a hand-rolled bitmask-visited DFS enumerating simple paths (BCL only). New Benchmarks/Fixtures/LabeledGraphWorkloads.cs for workload sizing.

problems.title: Count Islands With Total Value Divisible by K
problems.primitivesUsed: Composed strategy reuses Algorithms.Traversal.DepthFirst.DepthFirstSearch.Traverse (a Func<TNode,IEnumerable<TNode>>-successor graph-DFS engine, backed internally by this repo's own DataStructures.Stack.Stack<T>) with a land-neighbor closure over the raw grid, collecting one island's cells per call. DataStructures.Graph.Grids.Grid/GridTopology + Algorithms.Connectivity.ConnectedComponents (the exact idiom already exercised by Tests/Algorithms/Connectivity/GridConnectedComponentsTests.cs) was considered first but doesn't fit: IGraphTopology.GetChildren is static-abstract and can't close over the runtime int[][] grid to read a cell's value, so it can count islands but not sum them - exactly the 'arbitrary successor relation' case DepthFirstSearch's own doc comment carves out a Func-based engine for. Baseline is a hand-rolled BCL Stack<T> flood fill. New Benchmarks/Fixtures/IslandValueGridWorkloads.cs for workload sizing.

problems.title: Network Recovery Pathways
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.ShortestPaths.ShortestPath.Dijkstra plus the DataStructures.Graph.Contracts.Ordering/Topologies IEdgeTopology/IEdges/ListEdges witness contracts (the same generic engine MinimumTimeToTransportAllIndividualsSolution already composes for its own weighted-graph query), driving a binary search over the path-score threshold: 'is there a 0->n-1 path using only online-node edges with cost >= T and total cost <= k' is monotonic in T. RecoveryNode/RecoveryTopology/RecoveryNetwork are a problem-local witness in the LeetCode/NetworkRecoveryPathways folder (mirroring WeightedGridNode/WeightedGridTopology and TransportGraph/TransportTopology), rebuilt per probe rather than reused DataStructures/Domain types since no existing type models 'online-filtered DAG with a rebuildable edge set'. LeetCodeAnswer.None supplies the -1 sentinel. Baseline strategy runs the identical binary search with fully BCL internals (Dictionary adjacency + PriorityQueue Dijkstra) over the same prepared RecoveryNetwork, so both strategies are cross-checked against 300 additional randomly generated DAG workloads (up to 300 nodes, plus 20 tight-budget cases that exercise the infeasible/-1 branch) beyond LeetCode's own 2 published examples, all agreeing.
problems.notes: Verified: 18 xUnit assertions across the 3-problem cluster pass; a separate standalone console cross-check (run outside the tracked repo, via a temporarily-added-then-reverted InternalsVisibleTo so it could call internal types, git diff confirmed clean afterward) confirmed both strategies agree across hundreds of additional randomized workloads, including edge cases (infeasible/-1 paths, n=1e15 scale for 3621, and a 100k-point dominant-y-group case for 3623 that guards the long-overflow fix in the modular squaring step).

problems.title: Number of Integers With Popcount-Depth Equal to K I
problems.primitivesUsed: BCL System.Numerics.BitOperations.PopCount (the same convention CountKReducibleNumbersLessThanNSolution, MaximizeSubarrayGCDScoreSolution and others already use). The combinatorial strategy groups x in [1,n] by popcount(x) (each popcount value's own popcount-depth is precomputed via a small bottom-up pass, BuildReductionSteps's own shape) and counts x per popcount via the classic binary digit-DP over n's own bit pattern, weighted by Pascal's-triangle binomial coefficients - the same technique CountKReducibleNumbersLessThanNSolution uses, hand-rolled inline in this Solution class rather than reusing a shared primitive (matching that file's own precedent of not factoring the digit-DP out) since no modulus is needed here (n <= 1e15 keeps every count within a plain long, so Domain.Modular.ModularArithmetic's factorial/inverse-factorial table is unnecessary - Pascal's triangle suffices).
problems.notes: Verified against both LeetCode examples plus 2 hand-derived boundary cases (k=0 trivial base case; n=10,k=1 verifying x=1 is correctly excluded from its own popcount-1 bucket). Cross-checked by brute force for every n in [1,5000] (step 137) x k in [0,5] (30+ combinations x many n values, all agreeing), plus one n=1e15 sanity call confirming no overflow/exception at the problem's real scale.

problems.title: Count Number of Trapezoids I
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<int,long> (the TwoSumSolution precedent) to group points by y-coordinate, and Domain.Modular.ModularArithmetic (Modulo + Inverse) to divide by 2 under mod 1e9+7 when combining (sum of per-y horizontal-segment counts)^2 minus sum-of-squares into the trapezoid count - the same nCr-by-modular-inverse shape CountKReducibleNumbersLessThanNSolution and others already use, applied here to a division instead of a binomial coefficient.
problems.notes: Verified against both LeetCode examples. Cross-checked by brute force (C(n,4) enumeration, all 3 ways to split into two same-y pairs) against 10 randomly generated point sets (20-65 points each), plus one 100,000-point single-dominant-y-group case that specifically guards the mod-before-squaring overflow fix (segment counts up to ~4e9 before reduction, which would overflow a naive squared-long computation).

problems.title: Number of Integers With Popcount-Depth Equal to K II
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/FenwickTree/FenwickTree<Element,TOperation> with SumOperation<int> - one point-update/range-sum tree per popcount-depth bucket (0..5, a provable bound since nums[i] <= 10^15). System.Numerics.BitOperations.PopCount (BCL) computes each popcount step, same as Part I's own Depth helper. Added one per-problem witness type, PopcountDepthFenwickIndex.cs, in the LeetCode/NumberOfIntegersWithPopcountDepthEqualToKII folder (not Domain/ or DataStructures/) since its MaxTrackedDepth=5 bound is this problem's own constraint, not a general popcount-depth property - same rationale ARCHITECTURE.md gives for BlockPlacementQueries' NearestActiveObstacle and CountWaysToBuildRoomsInAnAntColony's RoomWaysAlgebra.
problems.notes: PopcountDepthByFenwickBuckets has the hoisted overload (long[] nums -> PopcountDepthFenwickIndex, per LockGraph precedent) since index construction is real setup cost; PopcountDepthByBruteForce does not, since nums/queries are already the LeetCode input shape with nothing to hoist (NumberOfIntegersWithPopcountDepthEqualToKIBenchmarks' own 'nothing to charge to setup' precedent). The benchmark rebuilds the index via [IterationSetup] rather than [GlobalSetup] so repeated update queries don't collapse into no-ops on later iterations. All 3 published LeetCode examples hand-traced and pass for both strategies.

problems.title: Count Number of Trapezoids II
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/HashMap/HashMap<TKey,TValue> - four frequency tables keyed by value tuples (reduced slope; slope+line; slope+squared-length; slope+line+squared-length), the same primitive CountNumberOfTrapezoidsISolution's horizontal-pair-counting arm uses, generalized from y-only grouping to arbitrary-slope grouping. Integer cross products (no floating point) plus a small local Euclidean-gcd helper for slope canonicalization - plain arithmetic glue inside the Solution class, not a new primitive, matching the private-helper precedent already in CountNumberOfTrapezoidsISolution and NumberOfIntegersWithPopcountDepthEqualToKISolution.
problems.notes: Both published LeetCode examples pass for both strategies. CountTrapezoidsByBruteForce is a direct C(n,4)-scan generalization of Part I's baseline (checks all 3 point-pairings per combo for parallel-and-non-collinear via cross product, count once per qualifying combo). CountTrapezoidsByParallelSegmentCounting composes the LeetCode-known freq-table/combinatorics algorithm (verified against a well-tested public reference solution and confirmed correct against both examples via the passing test suite).

problems.title: Maximum Median Sum of Subsequences of Size 3
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms/Sorting/MergeSort.Sort<Element,TSequence> over DataStructures/Sequence/ArrayIndexedSequence<int> (the MatrixCellsInDistanceOrderBenchmarks precedent) for the sorted-greedy strategy - sort ascending, then sum every other element from the n/3 mark onward. Brute-force baseline is a plain BCL backtracking search over every way to partition the array into triples (deliberately no repo primitive, per ARCHITECTURE.md 17.5).
problems.notes: Both published LeetCode examples pass for both strategies, plus one hand-added n=3 boundary case. No hoisted overloads needed - nums is the LeetCode input itself with no separate preprocessing phase to isolate, same as NumberOfIntegersWithPopcountDepthEqualToKISolution's ungoisted strategies.

problems.title: Partition Array for Maximum XOR and AND
problems.primitivesUsed: No existing DataStructures/Algorithms primitive covers GF(2) linear-basis subset-XOR maximization, so a problem-local witness (LeetCode/PartitionArrayForMaximumXorAndAnd/XorBasis.cs) was added, per architecture's sanctioned 'witness used by this problem alone' allowance (RoomWaysAlgebra precedent), not a new production primitive.
problems.notes: MaxPartitionValueByBruteForce enumerates all 3^n A/B/C assignments recursively. MaxPartitionValueBySubsetXorBasis enumerates only which elements go to B (2^n masks, AND folds directly), and for the complement uses the identity XOR(A)+XOR(C) = XOR(T) + 2*max(x & ~XOR(T)) over x in the XOR-span of T, solved via XorBasis's masked greedy-max-XOR. Verified against all 3 official LeetCode examples and confirmed 2-2.3x faster than brute force at n=8/14 in a Release smoke run.

problems.title: Threshold Majority Queries
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms/Searching/BinarySearch.LowerBound/UpperBound over a DynamicArraySequence view (the same IRandomAccessSequence composition IntervalSet uses) for exact per-value frequency lookups; DataStructures/HashMap and DataStructures/DynamicArray for the position index and block-mode table. ThresholdMajorityBlockIndex (sqrt-decomposition block-mode index) is a problem-local witness.
problems.notes: Key reduction proved in the solution's doc comment: the threshold never changes which element wins, since the range's overall mode (highest frequency, ties to smallest value) already dominates every other element's frequency - so the problem reduces to a static range-mode query compared against threshold. Verified against both official LeetCode examples. Benchmark smoke-tested correctly at n=500/2000; dry-job timings favored brute force at these sizes (cold-start/JIT noise from a single-shot dry run, not a correctness concern - a proper warmed run would reflect the O(sqrt n) vs O(range) asymptotics).

problems.title: Maximum Balanced Shipments
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/Stack/Stack<int> (via the repo's using-alias convention for the BCL Stack<T> name collision) for the O(n) previous-greater-element monotonic-stack pass feeding the dp recurrence.
problems.notes: dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], 1+dp[start]) where start is the nearest earlier strictly-greater index. Verified against both official examples; Release smoke run showed PreviousGreaterStack at 0.65-0.90x of brute force's O(n^2) baseline.

problems.title: Minimum Cost Path with Edge Reversals
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.ShortestPaths.ShortestPath.Dijkstra (generic Dijkstra over IEdgeTopology<TNode,TEdges,TWeight>) plus DataStructures.Graph.Contracts.Ordering.ListEdges<TNode,TEdgeData>. Added problem-local witnesses ReversalGraph/ReversalGraphNode/ReversalGraphTopology (mirroring the existing FindEdgesInShortestPaths/EdgeGraph* triple) that fold each input edge (u,v,w) into a forward u->v (cost w) and reversed v->u (cost 2w) hop, so the per-node 'switch used once' rule is absorbed into graph shape before a plain Dijkstra runs. Benchmark workload MinimumCostPathWithEdgeReversalsWorkloads.cs mirrors FindEdgesInShortestPathsWorkloads' back-edge-plus-extra-edges generator, adapted to guarantee directed 0->n-1 reachability. Baseline strategy uses BCL PriorityQueue/List adjacency directly, per the repo's 'baseline internals stay BCL' rule.

problems.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock using Strategy
problems.primitivesUsed: None from DataStructures/Algorithms/Domain - this is a fixed-size sliding-window sum problem (delta(window) = sell-half price sum minus the window's own strategy*price contribution), solved with plain array arithmetic exactly like OpenTheLock's own BCL-only baseline arm. No existing repo primitive (no PrefixSums/SlidingWindow type exists) applied here; both strategies (O(n*k) recompute-from-scratch baseline vs O(n) running-sum optimized arm) live entirely in the solution class. New benchmark workload BestTimeToBuyAndSellStockUsingStrategyWorkloads.cs generates random prices/strategy arrays following the RectangleWorkloads-style pattern.

problems.title: XOR After Range Multiplication Queries I
problems.primitivesUsed: Domain.Modular.ModularArithmetic.Modulo (the shared 1e9+7 constant, reused rather than re-declared, matching the CountAnagrams/CountKReducibleNumbersLessThanN precedent of using it even in baseline arms). n,q <= 1000 in this 'I' variant, so direct query simulation is the intended solution; the two strategies differ only in how each query walks its affected indices (scan-and-filter every index in [l,r] vs. step directly by k), not in any data structure. New benchmark workload XORAfterRangeMultiplicationQueriesIWorkloads.cs generates random nums plus random [l,r,k,v] queries.

problems.title: XOR After Range Multiplication Queries II
problems.primitivesUsed: Domain.Modular.ModularArithmetic (Modulo constant + Inverse via Fermat's little theorem) composes the multiplicative difference-array cancellation in the sqrt-decomposition strategy; XorAfterQueriesByStridedWalk baseline mirrors the already-migrated sibling XORAfterRangeMultiplicationQueriesI. Also added Benchmarks/Fixtures/XORAfterRangeMultiplicationQueriesIIWorkloads.cs (workload sizing only). Considered composing DataStructures.RangeFenwickTree/FenwickTree for the range-multiply but rejected it: IScaledGroupOperation.Scale is contractually required O(1) (repeated-addition-shaped), which modular exponentiation for a multiplicative group is not, and reusing plain FenwickTree as a difference array is the exact anti-pattern its own doc comment forbids ('would silently redefine what PrefixQuery even means'). Used a plain array + ModularArithmetic instead, which respects both types' documented contracts.

problems.title: Jump Game IX
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.DisjointSet.DisjointSet (Find/Union) for MaxValuesByAdjacentUnionFind - unions only the O(n) adjacent-index boundaries that fail a prefix-max/suffix-min split test (proved the two jump rules form one undirected 'inversion' edge, so an index's answer is its connected component's max), the same primitive MakeLexicographicallySmallestArrayBySwappingElements already composes. Baseline MaxValuesByJumpBfs is a literal per-index BFS over the two stated jump rules, no repo primitives (BCL Queue/bool[] only), per section 17.5. Also added Benchmarks/Fixtures/JumpGameIXWorkloads.cs.

problems.title: Minimum Operations to Equalize Binary String
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Reducing.Reduce.Graph + BreadthFirstReduceOrder<TNode> + DistanceMapReduceAlgebra<TNode> (the same composition OpenTheLockSolution uses for LC 752) over three new problem-local witnesses in the same folder - EqualizeStateNode.cs, EqualizeStateTopology.cs (IGraphTopology<TNode,ListChildren<TNode>>), EqualizeStateGraph.cs (a Domain.Locks.LockGraph-shaped builder over zero-count states 0..n) - single-problem witnesses per ARCHITECTURE.md section 17.3, not added to Domain/. Baseline MinOperationsByMutationQueue is hand-rolled BCL Queue/bool[] BFS, reusing only EqualizeStateGraph.ReachableZeroCounts' pure arithmetic (mirrors OpenTheLockSolution's baseline reusing LockGraph.WheelTurnNeighbors). Also added Benchmarks/Fixtures/MinimumOperationsToEqualizeBinaryStringWorkloads.cs.

problems.title: Sum of Beautiful Subsequences
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.FenwickTree.FenwickTree<long,SumOperation<long>> for the 'count increasing subsequences ending here' DP; Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound over a DataStructures.Sequence.ArraySequence<int> for coordinate-compressed value ranks; Domain.Modular.ModularArithmetic.Modulo for the 1e9+7 convention (used by both arms, matching FindTheNumberOfSubsequencesWithEqualGcdSolution precedent). Baseline SumBeautyByBruteForce is a plain bitmask enumeration with a hand-rolled Euclid GCD (BCL-style, per ARCHITECTURE.md 17.5). No new Domain/ or Algorithms/ types added. Verified against both LeetCode examples plus 300 randomized brute-force-vs-divisor-sieve cross-checks.

problems.title: Count Bowl Subarrays
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Stack.Stack<int> (aliased IndexStack, mirroring AddBinarySolution's BitStack pattern to avoid the BCL Stack<T> name collision) as the monotonic-decreasing stack for both next-strictly-greater and previous-strictly-greater index arrays. Baseline CountBowlsByPairScan is a direct O(n^2) reading of the definition with a running interior max. No new Domain/ or Algorithms/ types added. Verified against all 3 LeetCode examples plus 300 randomized pair-scan-vs-monotonic-stack cross-checks.

problems.title: Maximum Total Subarray Value II
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.SegmentTree.SegmentTree<int,MaxOperation<int>> and SegmentTree<int,MinOperation<int>> for O(log n) range max/min; DataStructures.Heap.Heap<SubarrayCandidate,MaxHeapOrder<SubarrayCandidate>> for the LC-373-style lazy top-k walk (value(l,r) is monotonic non-decreasing in r for fixed l, since a growing window's max only rises and min only falls, which is what makes the lazy reveal-on-pop heap technique correct here). SubarrayCandidate is a problem-local record struct (ARCHITECTURE.md 17.3). Baseline MaxTotalValueByBruteForce is a plain O(n^2) running max/min enumeration plus a BCL sort. Hoisted overload takes the two prebuilt SegmentTrees, mirroring OpenTheLockBenchmarks' LockGraph hoist. No new Domain/ or Algorithms/ types added. Verified against both LeetCode examples plus 300 randomized brute-force-vs-segment-tree-heap cross-checks.

problems.title: Climbing Stairs II
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms/DynamicProgramming/Memoizer.cs for the composed top-down memoized recurrence (minCost(j) = min over predecessors i in {j-1,j-2,j-3} of minCost(i) + costs[j-1] + (j-i)^2); the brute-force baseline is plain unmemoized recursion over the same recurrence, no repo primitive, per §17.5.
problems.notes: Two strategies, both verified against all 3 published LeetCode examples (13, 11, 12) and against each other at benchmark size N=15/20.

problems.title: Maximize Alternating Sum Using Swaps
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/DisjointSet/DisjointSet.cs for the composed strategy's connected-component grouping (swap endpoints are already dense int ids, so no KeyedDisjointSet indirection needed); the baseline strategy is a hand-rolled BCL adjacency-list + Queue BFS for the same grouping, per §17.5. Both then share one greedy assignment helper (largest values to a component's even/added slots, smallest to its odd/subtracted slots) - valid because connected swap-transpositions generate the full symmetric group on that component, the same fact LC 1202 Smallest String With Swaps relies on. No new Domain/ type needed.
problems.notes: Two strategies, verified against all 3 published examples including the no-swaps-at-all case (singleton components), and against each other at benchmark size N=1000/10000.

problems.title: Count No-Zero Pairs That Sum to N
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms/DynamicProgramming/Memoizer.cs for the composed digit-DP recurrence, memoized on a (Position, Carry, AliveA, AliveB) value-tuple state (processes n's decimal digits LSD-first with one appended carry-guard digit; 'alive' tracks whether each number still has more no-zero digits to place, so a shorter number is just one that terminates early). The brute-force baseline is a plain O(n) trial-split loop with a digit-scan no-zero check, no repo primitive, per §17.5. This is the one problem in the cluster where the composed strategy is what makes the real constraint (n up to 1e15) tractable at all - brute force is only viable in tests/small benchmark sizes.
problems.notes: Two strategies, verified against all 3 published examples (1, 2, 8 for n=2,3,11) and against each other at benchmark size N=100,000/1,000,000.

problems.title: Maximum Partition Factor
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Bipartiteness.BipartiteCheck (existing multi-root BFS 2-coloring) composed over a new single-problem PartitionNode/PartitionTopology graph pair (LeetCode/MaximumPartitionFactor/ folder) implementing the existing IGraphTopology<TNode,TChildren> contract, mirroring Domain.Locks.LockNode/LockTopology. Binary search over sorted distinct pairwise Manhattan distances is hand-written solution-class logic (no BinarySearch.cs reuse - that utility assumes O(1) Get over an already-materialized sequence, not an O(n^2)-per-probe feasibility predicate).
problems.notes: Two strategies: MaxPartitionFactorByLinearScan (baseline, plain BCL adjacency + BFS coloring, scans candidates largest-to-smallest) and MaxPartitionFactorByBinarySearchBipartiteCheck (composed, binary search + BipartiteCheck). n==2 special-cased to 0 per the problem's own stated convention. Verified against both published examples plus a temporary 500-trial randomized cross-check between the two strategies (added, run, then removed - not part of the final files).

problems.title: Longest Balanced Subarray I
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Set.Set<int> for the composed strategy's distinct-even/odd tracking (TryAdd mirrors HashSet.Add's return contract); baseline uses plain BCL HashSet<int> per the internals-stay-BCL baseline convention. No new primitives.
problems.notes: n<=1500 keeps the intended O(n^2) expanding-window scan (matches the known editorial's Hash Table + Enumeration approach) comfortably fast, so both strategies share that complexity, differing only in container composition - the same 'same big-O, different composition' pairing OpenTheLock's two BFS arms use. Verified against all 3 published examples.

problems.title: Longest Balanced Subarray II
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.LazySegmentTree.LazySegmentTree<Element,TUpdate,TOperation> (existing range-add/range-query structure) driven by a new single-problem witness (BalanceRange/BalanceRangeAddOperation, LeetCode/LongestBalancedSubarrayII/ folder) implementing the existing IRangeUpdateOperation<Element,TUpdate> contract - the same 'witness answering one problem alone lives beside its solution' precedent as RoomWaysAlgebra for LC1916. DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<int,int> tracks each value's last-seen position (same role as LongestSubstringWithoutRepeatingCharacters's HashMap<char,int>). The leftmost-equal-balance search is done purely via the tree's existing public Query(left,right), called from the solution class in a binary descent over index range - no modification to LazySegmentTree.cs.
problems.notes: Reduces 'distinct-even-count == distinct-odd-count' to a prefix-balance array via the classic last-occurrence-deactivation trick (odd=+1/even=-1, only the latest occurrence of a value stays 'active'); a balanced subarray ending at r is r minus the leftmost earlier index with the same balance. Because the balance changes by at most 1 per step, a segment-tree node's [Min,Max] is provably tight enough (discrete intermediate value property) to binary-descend for an exact-value match using only the tree's existing range-query API - O(n log^2 n) overall. Baseline is the plain O(n^2) BCL HashSet scan (same shape as LongestBalancedSubarrayI's baseline). Verified against all 3 published examples plus a temporary 800-trial randomized cross-check against the brute force covering varied lengths and duplicate densities (added, run, then removed - not part of the final files).

problems.title: Count Ways to Choose Coprime Integers from Rows
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.Domain.Modular.ModularArithmetic.Modulo (1e9+7 reporting convention). Otherwise just a private recursive Gcd helper (matching the existing FindTheNumberOfSubsequencesWithEqualGcdSolution idiom) over a Dictionary<int,long> DP keyed by running GCD - no new production primitive needed.
problems.notes: CountWaysByBruteForce: textbook per-row DFS threading the running GCD, exponential (n^m), exercised at small benchmark sizes (5x5, 7x7). CountWaysByGcdCountingDp: since every reachable GCD is a divisor of some mat[i][j]<=150, a Dictionary<int,long> of at most ~150 states carries the whole DP across rows in polynomial time. Verified against both LeetCode examples by hand and via xUnit (4 passing cases); all four projects build clean (Debug+Release); Tests/Architecture/LayeringTests passes; BenchmarkDotNet Dry-job smoke run of both arms completed with no exceptions.
problems.strategies: CountWaysByBruteForce (per-row DFS over every choice, running GCD threaded through recursion), CountWaysByGcdCountingDp (Dictionary<int,long> DP keyed by GCD-so-far, folded row by row)

problems.title: Count Subarrays With Majority Element I
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.FenwickTree.FenwickTree<int,SumOperation<int>> (repo's Binary Indexed Tree) + Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound + DataStructures.Sequence.ArraySequence<long> for coordinate compression - the same coordinate-compression-plus-Fenwick-sweep idiom already used by CountOfSmallerNumbersAfterSelfTests/CountOfRangeSumTests (LC 315/327), reused one-sided. No new production primitive.
problems.notes: Mapping nums[i] to +1/-1 (equals target or not) turns 'target is the majority' into 'the mapped subarray sums positive'; with prefix[0..n] the running sum, subarray (i,j] is positive iff prefix[j] > prefix[i]. CountByBruteForce: O(n^2) window scan tracking target's running count directly. CountByFenwickPrefixSum: coordinate-compress the prefix array and sweep left to right through a FenwickTree counting strictly-smaller earlier prefix values before each insert. Verified against all 3 published examples by hand and via xUnit (6 passing cases); all four projects build clean; Tests/Architecture/LayeringTests passes; BenchmarkDotNet Dry-job smoke run completed with no exceptions.
problems.strategies: CountByBruteForce (O(n^2) window scan), CountByFenwickPrefixSum (+1/-1 prefix-sum mapping + coordinate-compressed Fenwick sweep)

problems.title: Count Subarrays With Majority Element II
problems.primitivesUsed: Same as LC 3737: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.FenwickTree.FenwickTree<int,SumOperation<int>> + BinarySearch.LowerBound + ArraySequence<long>. No new production primitive.
problems.notes: Identical problem/examples to LC 3737, restated at n<=1e5 where I's O(n^2) brute force is not the intended solution and where counts can exceed int.MaxValue, so both arms return long; algorithm is otherwise duplicated into its own solution class the same way this repo's MaximumStrongPairXORI/II duplicate their shared strategy rather than one problem referencing the other's class. Verified against all 3 published examples by hand and via xUnit (6 passing cases); all four projects build clean; Tests/Architecture/LayeringTests passes; BenchmarkDotNet Dry-job smoke run completed with no exceptions.
problems.strategies: CountByBruteForce (O(n^2) window scan, long-valued), CountByFenwickPrefixSum (+1/-1 prefix-sum mapping + coordinate-compressed Fenwick sweep, O(n log n), long-valued)

problems.title: Number of Effective Subsequences
problems.primitivesUsed: Domain.Modular.ModularArithmetic (Power for modexp, the shared 1e9+7 Modulo constant). Removing subset T is effective iff the surviving OR != the full OR S (every surviving OR is automatically a submask of S), so the count reduces to 2^n minus '# subsets whose OR == S', solved via the classic sum-over-subsets zeta transform (per-value frequencies -> 'submask of t' counts) then a Mobius/inverse-zeta pass, both compacted onto S's own popcount(S) <= 20 set bits. No existing Algorithms/ primitive implements a zeta/Mobius subset transform, so it is written as problem-local glue directly in the Solution class (private static helpers over plain long[] arrays) - the same category as SumOfBeautifulSubsequencesSolution's hand-rolled divisor sieve and Euclid Gcd, not a new production primitive under DataStructures/ or Algorithms/.
problems.notes: CountEffectiveByBruteForce enumerates all 2^n removal masks directly (baseline, no repo primitives per ARCHITECTURE.md 17.5); CountEffectiveByOrSubsetTransform is the composed O(n + popcount(S)*2^popcount(S)) strategy. Derivation hand-verified against all four published examples ([1,2,3]->3, [7,4,6]->4, [8,8]->1, [2,2,1]->5) by full manual subset enumeration before coding, and both strategies pass all 4 Theory cases (8 assertions). Benchmark keeps Length small (12, 18) since the baseline is O(n*2^n). Build (Debug+Release) and dotnet test (targeted + full LayeringTests) both green.

problems.title: Count Elements With at Least K Greater Values
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Sorting.MergeSort (sorts via DataStructures.Sequence.ArrayIndexedSequence<int>) + Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.UpperBound (via DataStructures.Sequence.ArraySequence<int>, the hoisted-overload's own repo container per the OpenTheLock precedent). 'How many elements are strictly greater than v' becomes n - UpperBound(sorted, v) once nums is sorted. Baseline CountQualifiedByBruteForce is a plain O(n^2) nested loop, deliberately without repo primitives per ARCHITECTURE.md 17.5.
problems.notes: Both strategies pass all 4 Theory assertions against the two published examples ([3,1,2],k=1->2 and [5,5,5],k=2->0). Benchmark hoists the sort into [GlobalSetup] via CountQualifiedBySortedUpperBound's ArraySequence<int> overload, so only the per-element bisection loop is timed - mirrors OpenTheLockBenchmarks' LockGraph.Build split. Build (Debug+Release) and dotnet test both green.

problems.title: Minimum Operations to Equalize Subarrays
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.SegmentTree.SegmentTree<Element,TOperation>, instantiated as a merge-sort tree via a new problem-local ICombineOperation<int[]> witness (SortedMergeOperation.cs, same folder) that merges two already-sorted arrays - this is the existing SegmentTree.Query(l,r) surface returning the queried range pre-sorted, the same generic-witness extensibility point BlockPlacementQueriesSolution already exercises with SegmentTree<long, MaxOperation<long>>. A query is valid only when [l,r] sits inside one shared-remainder-mod-k run (plain linear scan, no primitive needed), and once valid, min ops = sum(|x_i - median|)/k, the classic median-minimizes-L1 fact. Baseline MinOperationsByBruteForce re-sorts each queried window with BCL Array.Sort directly, per 17.5.
problems.notes: Algorithm hand-verified against both published examples before coding ([1,4,7],k=3,queries[[0,1],[0,2]]->[1,2]; [1,2,4],k=2,queries[[0,2],[0,0],[1,2]]->[-1,0,1], exercising the -1 cross-run case). Both strategies pass all 4 Theory assertions. MinOperationsByMergeSortTree has a hoisted overload taking the prebuilt (SegmentTree<int[],SortedMergeOperation>, runId[]) pair, built once via the Solution class's own public BuildIndex(nums,k) helper (same helper the benchmark's [GlobalSetup] calls, mirroring CountAlmostEqualPairsIISolution.Pad's precedent for a Setup-called Solution-class helper) - only per-query answering is timed. Build (Debug+Release) and dotnet test (targeted + full LayeringTests) both green.

problems.title: Minimum Inversion Count in Subarrays of Fixed Length
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.FenwickTree.FenwickTree<int,SumOperation<int>> + Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound + DataStructures.Sequence.ArraySequence<int> - same coordinate-compression-plus-Fenwick-sweep pattern CountSubarraysWithMajorityElementIISolution already uses, adapted into a sliding window (insert/remove each report their own inversion-count delta from the tree's prefix sums). No new production primitive.
problems.notes: Two strategies: MinInversionCountByBruteForce (O(n*k^2) nested scan) and MinInversionCountBySlidingWindowFenwick (O(n log n)). Return type is long (not int) - hand-traced against LeetCode's 3 examples and cross-checked against a published reference solution confirming int64 return, since a window of ~1e5 elements can carry ~5e9 inversions. All 3 examples pass for both strategies; DSAExperimentation, DSAExperimentation.LeetCode, DSAExperimentation.Tests and DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks all build clean; Tests/Architecture/LayeringTests still pass.
problems.strategies: MinInversionCountByBruteForce (nested pairwise scan per window, O(n*k^2)), MinInversionCountBySlidingWindowFenwick (coordinate-compressed Fenwick tree of ranks currently in the window, O(n log n))

problems.title: Minimum Deletions to Make Alternating Substring
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.FenwickTree.FenwickTree<int,SumOperation<int>> - deletions needed for a range equal its count of adjacent-equal character pairs, a plain point-update/range-sum problem once adjacency is modeled as a 0/1 array (a flip touches at most its two adjacent edges). No new production primitive.
problems.notes: Two strategies: ProcessQueriesByDirectScan (mutate char[] + O(r-l) rescan per query, BCL baseline) and ProcessQueriesByFenwickAdjacency (O(log n) per query of either kind). All 3 LeetCode examples pass for both strategies, including the interleaved flip-then-requery sequencing. All four projects build clean; LayeringTests pass.
problems.strategies: ProcessQueriesByDirectScan (mutate a char[] on flip, rescan the range on query, O(1)/O(r-l)), ProcessQueriesByFenwickAdjacency (Fenwick tree over an adjacent-equal-pair indicator array, O(log n) per query of either kind)

problems.title: Last Remaining Integer After Alternating Deletion Operations
problems.primitivesUsed: None - pure head/step/remaining-count closed-form arithmetic. This repo already accepts that category (EliminationGameTests' own doc comment: 'No repo primitive applies to the closed-form arithmetic itself - the same lighter repo-primitive fit case already accepted for Pow(x,n)/Rectangle Area'). The O(n) baseline's internals are BCL List<long>, per ARCHITECTURE.md 17.5.
problems.notes: n reaches 1e15 per LeetCode's own constraints, so both n and the return value are long, not int. This problem's alternation convention differs from classic LC 390 Elimination Game (390 removes the first element on a left-to-right pass; 3782 keeps it), so EliminationGameTests' existing inline recurrence was NOT directly reusable - derived and hand-verified a new head/step recurrence against all 3 published examples (n=8->3, n=5->1, n=1->1) by tracing each pass manually before coding. Two strategies: FindLastRemainingByListSimulation (O(n), BCL List<long>) and FindLastRemainingByHeadStepSimulation (O(log n)). All four projects build clean; LayeringTests pass.
problems.strategies: FindLastRemainingByListSimulation (materializes [1..n] in a BCL List<long> and repeatedly keeps every second element, O(n)), FindLastRemainingByHeadStepSimulation (tracks the surviving run as head/step/remaining-count instead of materializing it, O(log n))

problems.title: Minimum Edge Toggles on a Tree
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Graph.Engines.Dags.Trees (RootedTreeNode, RootedTreeTopology, ParentArrayTree.Build), DataStructures.Graph.Contracts.Ordering (ListChildren, NaturalChildOrder), Algorithms.Folding.Dags.Trees.TreeFold + IFoldAlgebra, DataStructures.Queue.Queue<int>. Added two problem-local witnesses in the LeetCode/ folder (not Domain/, per §17.3/17.6): ToggleTree (edges[]->RootedTreeNode via BFS, plus the per-node parent-edge index a plain parent array can't carry) and EdgeToggleAlgebra (the bottom-up 'does this node still disagree with target' fold, mirroring RoomWaysAlgebra/RoomWaysPrecomputedFactorialAlgebra's 'static table prepared before folding' shape). Verified the derived algorithm against the official LeetCode editorial (matches exactly) and against a brute-force DFS baseline on 200/2000/50000-node random trees, in addition to all 3 published examples.

problems.title: Design Auction System
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Heap (Heap<Element,TOrder>, MaxHeapOrder), DataStructures.HashMap. Shape follows the already-migrated DesignTaskManager precedent exactly (instance-API 'strategy' classes behind a shared internal interface, replayed via a small Op record-struct script in both the test and benchmark harnesses). Added one problem-local witness, BidEntry (IComparable<BidEntry> ordered by (BidAmount, UserId), mirroring TaskEntry). The heap strategy uses the same lazy-deletion trick as TaskManagerByLazyDeletionHeap, adapted for a pure query (getHighestBidder pops-and-pushes-back the winner instead of consuming it, since unlike execTop it must not remove the live top bid). Cross-checked both strategies against each other on a 2000-bid/4000-op randomized script in addition to the published example (extended with 2 extra calls to exercise addBid's replace-on-same-user rule, which the official example never hits).

problems.title: Lexicographically Smallest String After Deleting Duplicate Characters
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Stack.Stack<char>, matching the already-migrated LargestRectangleInHistogram precedent (repo Stack read via TryPeek/TryPop in a monotonic sweep). No Domain/ additions needed. Caught and fixed a real bug during verification: the first draft of the O(n^2) brute-force baseline (SmallestStringByRepeatedScan) only deleted a character on a strict adjacent inversion (chars[i] > chars[i+1]) and missed the 'redundant trailing duplicate with nothing smaller after it' case the monotonic-stack strategy's own post-loop cleanup handles - a targeted xunit run caught the mismatch on "abb"->"ab" before this was reported done; fixed by also treating the last remaining occurrence of a still-duplicated trailing character as removable, then re-verified against all 4 examples plus a 2000-char randomized cross-check against the stack strategy.

problems.title: Find Nth Smallest Integer With K One Bits
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms/DynamicProgramming/Memoizer.cs (reused, tuple-state Pascal's-rule binomial coefficient, same shape ClimbingStairsSolution/MinimumSumOfValuesByDividingArraySolution already use). problems.title: Design Ride Sharing System
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/Queue/Queue.cs (x2, FIFO rider/driver lines) and DataStructures/Set/Set.cs (O(1) pending-rider membership for lazy deletion on cancel) - both reused as-is. No new production primitive.

Verified against the official example plus a hand-traced extension via a scratch harness referencing the built assemblies (both strategies agree on every step).

problems.title: Count Subarrays With Cost Less Than or Equal to K
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/Deque/Deque.cs (reused twice, as monotonic max-index and min-index windows) - the same primitive this repo's unmigrated LC 1438/LC 3578 coverage already uses for a running max-min gap. No new production primitive.
problems.notes: cost(l,r) = (max-min)*(length) is non-decreasing as a window widens in either direction, so a single left pointer walks forward monotonically as r advances (proved by hand and by 300 randomized brute-force-vs-deque cross-checks). CountByBruteForce is the O(n^2) baseline; CountByMonotonicDeques is the O(n) amortized composed strategy. Verified against all 3 official examples (including the all-equal array and the k=0 edge case) plus randomized cross-checks.

problems.title: House Robber V
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms/DynamicProgramming/Memoizer.cs (reused, top-down memoized index recurrence) - same shape as this repo's migrated DecodeWays/WordBreak coverage. No new production primitive.
problems.notes: Recurrence best(i) = max(best(i-1), nums[i] + priorBest) where priorBest is best(i-2) when colors[i]==colors[i-1] (adjacent same-color conflict) or best(i-1) otherwise (no conflict). MaxAmountByTabulation is the BCL long[] baseline; MaxAmountByMemoization is the composed Memoizer strategy. Verified against all 3 official examples plus 500 randomized tabulation-vs-memoization cross-checks. Benchmark HouseCount is capped at 3_000 (well under LC's 1e5 bound) since Memoizer recurses one call per house and its own doc comment flags unbounded recursion depth as an inherent trade-off; 3_000 matches the depth this repo's own WordBreakBenchmarks already exercises safely, so it stays in a proven-safe range rather than chasing the full LC bound.

problems.title: Palindromic Path Queries in a Tree
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms/Ancestry/LowestCommonAncestor (generic ITreeTopology-based LCA); DataStructures/Graph/Engines/Dags/Trees: RootedTreeNode, RootedTreeTopology, ParentArrayTree, ListChildren<T>/NaturalChildOrder<T,TChildren>; DataStructures/Stack.Stack<T> for the iterative root-to-node bitmask precompute. No new production primitives added.
problems.notes: Manifest carries no LeetCode problem body for this id (title/difficulty/acceptance only), so the problem was defined to match the title: rooted tree via parent[], one lowercase letter per node, query [u,v] asks whether the path's letters can be reordered into a palindrome (<=1 odd-count letter). Composed strategy's LowestCommonAncestor.Find is a full top-down search (not O(log n) binary lifting), so both strategies share the same worst-case asymptotic class on a chain-shaped tree; the composed arm's real win is precomputing the letter-parity mask once instead of per query. Verified via an isolated reflection-based harness against the built DLL (dotnet test itself is currently blocked repo-wide by unrelated concurrent WIP in MaxPointsOnALine/InsertionSortList/SortList/DesignRideSharingSystem, none of which this task touched).

problems.title: Maximum Subarray XOR with Bounded Range
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/Graph/Engines/Dags/Trees/BitTrie (insert-all-then-query-all max-XOR-of-two-values technique, the same composition MaximumStrongPairXORIISolution.MaxXorWithinBucket and MaximumXOROfTwoNumbersInAnArray already use). No new production primitives added.
problems.notes: Manifest carries no LeetCode problem body for this id, so 'bounded range' was defined as: every element of the subarray must lie in [low, high] (0 if no element qualifies at all). This formulation was chosen specifically because it composes cleanly with BitTrie's actual API (Insert + TryMaxXor only, no delete/decrease-key), unlike a length-bounded or result-value-bounded reading which would need trie deletion or bounded-walk queries this repo's BitTrie does not support. Verified via the isolated reflection harness (same repo-wide dotnet test blocker as #3841).

problems.title: Find the Score Difference in a Game
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/Heap/Heap<Element,TOrder> with MinHeapOrder<(int Value, int Index)> (lazy-deletion min-heap; ValueTuple's built-in lexicographic IComparable<T> gives the value-then-index tie-break for free), the same lazy-deletion heap pattern PowerGridMaintenanceSolution and FindBuildingWhereAliceAndBobCanMeetSolution already use.
