Deliberately gave the MinHeap strategy no hoisted prepared-input overload: Heap<T> is drained by TryPop, so a shared instance could not safely be reused across repeated benchmark iterations the way a read-only prepared input (e.g. OpenTheLock's LockGraph) can. Verified via the isolated reflection harness (same repo-wide dotnet test blocker as #3841).

problems.title: Count Sequences to K
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms/DynamicProgramming/Memoizer.cs (composed strategy memoizes (index, e2, e3, e5) prime-exponent state - nums[i] in [1,6] only ever factors into 2/3/5, so val never needs to be represented as a fraction). Baseline is a plain BCL 3-way DFS over unreduced numerator/denominator longs. No hoisted overload: inputs are already primitive (int[] nums, long k), matching the FindNthSmallestIntegerWithKOneBits precedent.

problems.title: Sum of K-Digit Numbers in a Range
problems.primitivesUsed: Domain/Modular/ModularArithmetic.cs - Power for the 10^k and c^(k-1) modular exponentiations, Inverse for the modular division by 9 in the repunit formula (10^k-1)/9. Closed-form composed strategy is O(log k), correct up to LeetCode's k<=1e9; baseline is digit-by-digit brute enumeration of all c^k combinations, only used at small k. No hoisted overload needed (l, r, k are already scalars).

problems.title: Minimum Cost to Partition a Binary String
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/FenwickTree/FenwickTree.cs + SumOperation<int> - composed strategy answers each recursive segment's sensitive-element count via O(log n) Fenwick range Query instead of an O(length) scan. Followed the hoisted-overload convention (LeetCode-shaped MinCostByFenwickRangeSum(string,...) builds the FenwickTree once and delegates to a prepared-input MinCostByFenwickRangeSum(FenwickTree<int,SumOperation<int>>,...) overload a benchmark's [GlobalSetup] can build ahead of time, mirroring OpenTheLockSolution's LockGraph overload). Baseline recursion recounts sensitive characters with a raw linear scan each call. The split-only-in-half rule makes both recursions non-overlapping (segment-tree-shaped), so no memoization was needed.

problems.title: Maximum Points Activated with One Addition
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.KeyedDisjointSet<TKey> (composing DisjointSet/DisjointSetForest) reused as-is - same 'composition over redesign' precedent as OpenTheLock. The problem reduces to: points partition into connected components of a bipartite multigraph (x-values vs y-values, one edge per point); the answer is the two largest component sizes plus one (always achievable by picking an existing x from the largest component and an existing y from the second-largest, which can never collide with an existing point since they're in different components). A private AxisKey(bool IsX, int Value) record struct distinguishes the x=5 node from the y=5 node - problem-local, lives in the LeetCode folder per §17.3. Baseline arm is a hand-rolled BCL-Dictionary union-find (§17.5's 'baseline stays BCL' rule).
problems.notes: Two strategies (MaxActivatedByBruteForceUnionFind, MaxActivatedByKeyedDisjointSet), both verified against all 3 published examples (4, 3, 4) plus hand-traced single-point and merge-vs-single-component edge cases. All three projects (LeetCode/Tests/Benchmarks) build with 0 errors/0 warnings; xUnit run: 6/6 passed for this problem.

problems.title: Count Good Subarrays
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.DynamicArray<T> and DataStructures.HashMap<TKey,TValue> reused as the run-length-encoded OR-segment list and the last-seen-index map (TwoSum precedent for preferring the repo's own containers over BCL List/Dictionary in the non-baseline arm). No new Domain/Algorithms primitive needed - the algorithm is a direct, well-known technique (per-right-end distinct running-OR compression, O(n log(max value)) via the bit-superset-chain property) composed from existing generic containers.
problems.notes: Key insight proven and used: OR(l,r) >= max(nums[l..r]) always (bit superset), so a subarray is good iff OR(l,r) == max(nums[l..r]) - this simplifies the O(n^2) baseline to a plain running-OR/running-max scan. Two strategies (CountGoodSubarraysByBruteForce, CountGoodSubarraysByRunningOrGroups), verified against both published examples (4, 6) plus two additional hand-traced cases (all-zeros array, and a mixed-bitmask array with a non-good middle subarray) to confirm the segment-merge/last-seen-clipping logic. All three projects build with 0 errors/0 warnings; xUnit run: 4/4 passed for this problem.

problems.title: Direction Assignments with Exactly K Visible People
problems.primitivesUsed: Domain.Modular.ModularArithmetic (Fermat's-little-theorem Inverse/Power) reused exactly per the RoomWaysPrecomputedFactorialAlgebra / CountNumberOfBalancedPermutationsSolution precedent for building a factorial + inverse-factorial table. No new primitive needed.
problems.notes: The problem reduces to counting ways to split k visible votes between a left segment (size pos) and right segment (size n-1-pos), doubled for the person at pos's own free choice: 2 * sum_a C(pos,a)*C(n-1-pos,k-a). By Vandermonde's identity this collapses to 2*C(n-1,k). Baseline arm (CountAssignmentsByPascalConvolution) builds each segment's binomial row via Pascal's-triangle addition only (no modular inverse) and convolves directly - a genuinely independent derivation from the closed-form arm, not an algebraic restatement of it. Both strategies verified against all 3 published examples (2, 4, 2). All three projects build with 0 errors/0 warnings; xUnit run: 6/6 passed for this problem.

problems.title: Design Event Manager
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Heap.Heap<Element,MaxHeapOrder<Element>> + DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<TKey,TValue> composed as a lazy-deletion max-heap (EventManagerByLazyDeletionHeap), exactly the shape DesignTaskManagerSolution's TaskManagerByLazyDeletionHeap already established for LC 3408. A per-problem witness EventEntry.cs (IComparable<EventEntry>, priority then reversed-eventId for the smallest-id-wins tie-break) lives in the problem folder per §17.3, mirroring TaskEntry.cs. Baseline EventManagerByLinearScan is plain BCL Dictionary + linear scan. No new production primitive needed.
problems.notes: Instance-API design problem (constructor + updatePriority + pollHighest), so both strategies are classes implementing a shared internal IEventManagerStrategy, constructed directly (no CreateBy... factory) - matching DesignTaskManagerSolution's more recent precedent over MinStack/LRUCache's factory-method shape. Verified against both published examples via a replayed call script (EventManagerOp), the same shape DesignTaskManagerTests/LRUCacheTests/MinStackTests use. All three projects (DSAExperimentation.LeetCode, .Tests, .Benchmarks) build 0 errors/0 warnings; xUnit run for this problem: 4/4 passed (2 examples x 2 strategies).

problems.title: Incremental Even-Weighted Cycle Queries
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.DisjointSet.DisjointSet, used purely for its intended O(a(n)) connectivity query/union (Find/Union/IsConnected), not extended or reimplemented. No new production primitive.
problems.notes: The textbook-optimal solution for this problem is a parity/XOR-augmented union-find (path compression tracking XOR-distance-to-root per node) - a capability this repo's DisjointSet deliberately does not expose (no hook for auxiliary per-node state during compression), and KeyedDisjointSet's own doc comment explicitly warns against composing DisjointSetForest directly to fake one, since that re-derives path compression by hand instead of reusing it. Rather than build that ad hoc, both strategies here track the actual accepted-edges adjacency and answer 'what is the parity of some u-v path' via a real BFS (well-defined once same-component, since the invariant guarantees every u-v path in the accepted graph agrees on parity). CountAddedEdgesByBruteForceBfs (baseline, pure BCL) always BFS-checks; CountAddedEdgesByDisjointSetPrunedBfs (composed) uses DisjointSet to skip the BFS entirely whenever the endpoints are in different components (provably safe, since two different components can never already hold a cycle) and only falls back to BFS for same-component pairs - a genuine, correctness-preserving use of the existing primitive, just not the asymptotically optimal O(a(n))-per-query solution a bespoke weighted-DSU primitive would give (that primitive doesn't exist in DataStructures/ and wasn't invented here per the task's ad-hoc-build prohibition). Verified against both published examples (n=3 with a rejected odd-cycle edge -> 2, and the all-accepted even-cycle variant -> 3); traced by hand in addition to the automated run. All three projects build 0 errors/0 warnings; xUnit run for this problem: 4/4 passed (2 examples x 2 strategies).

problems.title: Traffic Signal Color
problems.primitivesUsed: None - a pure three-way range classification over LC's own fixed thresholds (timer==0 -> Green, timer==30 -> Orange, 30<timer<=90 -> Red, else Invalid). No DataStructures/Algorithms primitive applies to a single O(1) range check, the same 'only one strategy here' precedent BalancedBinaryTreeSolution documents for its own single-strategy problem.
problems.notes: Single strategy (ColorByRangeCheck), matching the repo's own precedent for problems with no genuine second approach (BalancedBinaryTree, ClimbingStairs, BinaryTreeMaximumPathSum all ship with exactly one public method). Tests cover both published examples (timer=60 -> Red, timer=5 -> Invalid) plus every boundary the range check has to get right (0, 30, 90 inclusive; 91 and 1000 excluded). All three projects build 0 errors/0 warnings; xUnit run for this problem: 7/7 passed.

problems.title: Angles of a Triangle
problems.primitivesUsed: No repo DataStructures/Algorithms primitive applies (fixed 3-side input, O(1) formula) - pure BCL Math (Acos). Two strategies: InternalAnglesByLawOfCosines (3 Acos calls) vs InternalAnglesByAngleSum (2 Acos calls + 180-derivation), both sharing a triangle-inequality validity check.

problems.title: Good Subsequence Queries
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/SegmentTree/SegmentTree<Element,TOperation> instantiated twice (gcd range query via a local GcdOperation witness mirroring MinimumStabilityFactorOfArray's LC-3605-scoped witness exactly, per ARCHITECTURE.md 17.3; multiple-count via the existing generic SumOperation<int>). problems.title: Count Connected Subgraphs with Even Node Sum

Baseline strategy uses plain BCL Queue<int>/HashSet<int> BFS over adjacency lists for the same connectivity check, matching ARCHITECTURE.md 17.5's 'baseline stays BCL internally' rule.

problems.title: Maximum Sum of Alternating Subsequence With Distance at Least K
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/SegmentTree/SegmentTree<long,MaxOperation<long>> (existing MaxOperation witness), DataStructures/Sequence/ArraySequence, Algorithms/Searching/BinarySearch.LowerBound for value-rank compression. Two ranked segment trees (peak-by-valley-rank, valley-by-peak-rank) with delayed insertion (index j only written once the sweep reaches i=j+k) enforce the distance-at-least-k constraint. No new production primitives added. Verified by hand-tracing all 3 LeetCode examples plus a passing test/benchmark run.

problems.title: Minimum Cost to Buy Apples II
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms/ShortestPaths/ShortestPath.Dijkstra (existing generic Dijkstra over IEdgeTopology), DataStructures/Graph/Contracts/Ordering/ListEdges. New problem-local witnesses (this problem only, per ARCHITECTURE.md 17.3): AppleNode, AppleForwardTopology, AppleReturnTopology (two IEdgeTopology witnesses over the same node - plain cost vs cost*tax edges), AppleNetwork (builder, mirrors NetworkRecoveryPathways' RecoveryNetwork). Runs Dijkstra twice per source (forward-cost graph, return cost*tax graph) since tax varies per road so LC 2473's single-multiplier trick doesn't apply. Also added Benchmarks/Fixtures/ApplesWorkloads.cs for workload sizing. Verified by hand-tracing all 3 LeetCode examples plus a passing test/benchmark run.

problems.title: Smallest Unique Subarray
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/HashMap/HashMap (int->char coordinate compression, the same idiom the unmigrated LongestCommonSubpath coverage already uses since RollingHash only operates over ReadOnlySpan<char>; also used as the window-hash occurrence counter), DataStructures/RollingHash/RollingHash + RollingHashValue for O(1) window hashing. Binary search over candidate length (monotonicity proven in the file's own doc comment) with a RollingHash sweep per probe. Considered but rejected DataStructures/SuffixArray, SuffixAutomaton and SuffixTree for the composed strategy: all three are hard-typed to ReadOnlySpan<char> (16-bit alphabet), which cannot losslessly represent this problem's stated worst case (up to 1e5 distinct values) without a collision-introducing truncation - RollingHash has the same char-domain limit but the repo's own established compression idiom (HashMap<int,char>) is already the accepted way around it elsewhere, so followed that precedent instead of blocking. Found and fixed a real bug in my own brute-force baseline during verification: string.Join(',', nums, start, length) has no (char,int[],int,int) overload, so it silently bound to the params object[] overload instead of slicing - fixed via nums.Skip(start).Take(length). All 6 tests (2 strategies x 3 examples) pass after the fix; benchmark runs clean.

problems.title: Number of Pairs After Increment
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.RangeFenwickTree.RangeFenwickTree<long, ScaledSumOperation<long>> (the two-Fenwick-tree range-add/point-query pair) composed for the smart strategy's per-index current-value lookups; baseline uses a plain long[] with direct range mutation. New problem-local witness DSAExperimentation.LeetCode/NumberOfPairsAfterIncrement/PairQuery.cs is the hoisted-overload input (ARCHITECTURE.md 17.4) both strategies share, plus DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks/Fixtures/NumberOfPairsAfterIncrementWorkloads.cs for sizing. Note: this repo has no value-frequency-under-range-shift structure (the textbook-optimal answer needs a sqrt/block decomposition with per-block histograms, which none of FenwickTree/RangeFenwickTree/SegmentTree/LazySegmentTree provide - they all aggregate by index, not by value) - both arms materialize per-index values on every count query, so the composed arm is correct but not asymptotically optimal versus the true contest-optimal solution; this is documented in the solution file's own comment as a genuine primitive gap, not an effort shortcut.

problems.title: Lexicographically Maximum MEX Array
problems.primitivesUsed: No existing DataStructures/Algorithms primitive fits an in-place MEX/frequency-pointer sweep, so both strategies are self-contained arrays + pointers (private helpers inline in the solution class) - matching this repo's established convention for elementary array/greedy techniques (e.g. MaximizeSubarrayGCDScoreSolution's bottleneck-scan arm), which doesn't route through a shared DataStructures type either. No Domain/ or new production primitive needed.

problems.title: Maximum Score with Co-Prime Element
problems.primitivesUsed: No existing DataStructures/Algorithms primitive needed - gcd and the smallest-prime-factor/divisor-multiple sieve are elementary number theory, written as private helpers inline per this repo's established gcd-problem convention (CountWaysToChooseCoprimeIntegersFromRowsSolution, MaximizeSubarrayGCDScoreSolution, MinimumStabilityFactorOfArraySolution's GcdOperation all keep gcd local rather than as a shared primitive). No Domain/ or new production primitive needed.

problems.title: Maximum Sum of M Non-Overlapping Subarrays I
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/Deque/Deque<T> as the monotonic sliding-window-maximum deque driving the per-j-layer DP transition (same shape CountPartitionsWithMaxMinDifferenceAtMostKSolution already uses). No Domain/ type or new production primitive needed.
problems.notes: Two strategies: MaximumSumByDynamicProgramming (O(n*m*(r-l+1)) baseline) and MaximumSumBySlidingWindowMaximum (O(n*m), Deque-optimized). Tracks EXACT subarray counts (not 'at most j') so example 4's all-negative case can't be won by silently picking zero subarrays.

problems.title: Maximum Sum of M Non-Overlapping Subarrays II
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/Deque/Deque<T> again, inside a Lagrangian-relaxation (aliens-trick) binary search over a per-subarray penalty lambda; the fixed-lambda inner DP is Part I's sliding-window-maximum recurrence collapsed to one unconstrained layer. No Domain/ type or new production primitive needed.
problems.notes: MaximumSumByDynamicProgramming (Part I's O(n*m*(r-l+1)) DP, kept as the baseline arm - self-contained per problem folder, not shared across LC ids) vs MaximumSumByLagrangianRelaxation (O(n*log(PenaltyBound))). Concavity + tie-break design was stress-tested in Python (8000 random trials, 0 mismatches) before porting, then the actual C# was cross-checked against Part I's DP on 4000 more random trials plus all 4 published examples - 0 mismatches.

problems.title: Maximum Subarray Sum After at Most K Swaps
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/FenwickTree/FenwickTree<long,SumOperation<long>> (four instances: inside/outside count+sum) plus Algorithms/Searching/BinarySearch.LowerBound over a private IRandomAccessSequence witness (FenwickPrefixCountSequence) - the same order-statistics composition DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks/ProblemSolutions/FindingMKAverageBenchmarks.cs already uses (there value-indexed; here rank-indexed, so no same-value remainder bookkeeping is needed). No Domain/ type or new production primitive added.
problems.notes: MaxSumByBruteForce (O(n^3 log n), per-window Array.Sort) vs MaxSumByOrderStatisticsFenwick (per window length, slides two Fenwick-backed rank ledgers across start positions; per window, ternary-searches the concave 's swaps' function). Verified against brute force on ~1500+ random trials plus all 3 published examples via a standalone cross-check runner - 0 mismatches.

problems.title: Shortest Path With At Most K Consecutive Identical Characters
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.ShortestPaths.ShortestPath.Dijkstra composed over a this-problem-only IEdgeTopology witness (ConsecutiveRunNode/ConsecutiveRunTopology, mirroring NetworkRecoveryPathways' RecoveryNode/RecoveryTopology) on the expanded (node, runLength) state graph ConsecutiveRunGraph builds eagerly (same eager-expansion shape as Domain.Locks.LockGraph); DataStructures.Graph.Contracts.Ordering.ListEdges<TNode,TWeight>. No Domain/ additions - the witness is problem-specific per ARCHITECTURE.md 17.3.
problems.notes: Baseline MinimumPathWeightByBclPriorityQueue expands (node,runLength) states on the fly with BCL PriorityQueue+Dictionary. Composed MinimumPathWeightByReduceGraph materializes the full n*k state graph and runs the repo's Dijkstra. Since each state-graph edge's weight is the fixed original edge weight regardless of state, ShortestPath.Dijkstra's fixed-weight IEdgeTopology applies directly (no hand-rolled relax loop needed, unlike the travel-time-dependent-weight problems in this repo). Verified: both strategies pass all 3 LeetCode examples (12 assertions total across both problems in this cluster's shared test run), and both benchmark arms execute cleanly via `dotnet run -c Release -- --filter ... --job Dry`.

problems.title: Minimum Time to Reach Target With Limited Power
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.ShortestPaths.ShortestPath.Dijkstra composed over a this-problem-only IEdgeTopology witness (PowerStateNode/PowerStateTopology) on the expanded (node, remainingPower) state graph PowerStateGraph builds eagerly, same shape as LC 3970's ConsecutiveRunGraph and NetworkRecoveryPathways' RecoveryNode/RecoveryTopology; DataStructures.Graph.Contracts.Ordering.ListEdges<TNode,TWeight>. No Domain/ additions.
problems.notes: Baseline MinTimeMaxPowerByBclPriorityQueue expands (node,remainingPower) states on the fly with BCL PriorityQueue+Dictionary. Composed MinTimeMaxPowerByReduceGraph materializes the full n*(power+1) state graph and runs the repo's Dijkstra. Leaving a node always costs cost[node] regardless of which outgoing edge is taken, so edge weight is fixed per state-graph edge and ShortestPath.Dijkstra's IEdgeTopology applies directly. The 'max remaining power among minimum-time paths' tie-break falls out of the state expansion for free: scan every remainingPower level target was settled at, keep smallest time then largest power. Hand-verified example 1 and 2 by tracing the state expansion; all 3 LeetCode examples pass for both strategies; both benchmark arms execute cleanly.

problems.title: Palindromic Subarray Sum
problems.skipReason: missing primitive: generic (non-char) longest-palindrome-per-center / equality-oracle over an arbitrary element type
problems.notes: Missing primitive: a generic (non-char) longest-palindrome-per-center computation or O(1) palindrome-equality oracle over an arbitrary element type. Since every nums[i] > 0, the best palindromic subarray for a fixed center is always the LONGEST palindrome centered there, so this reduces exactly to 'longest palindrome radius per center' (odd+even) plus a prefix-sum lookup - precisely what Algorithms.StringMatching.Manacher computes, and the hints' O(n log n) fallback (rolling hash + binary search) is precisely what DataStructures.RollingHash computes. Both are hardcoded to ReadOnlySpan<char>/IEqualityComparer<char> by deliberate design (confirmed in both files' own doc comments), and char is a 16-bit code unit: nums[i] can be up to 1e9 and cannot be cast to char losslessly; coordinate-compressing nums to dense rank ids only fits char's 65,536-value domain when the array's distinct-value count stays <= 65536, which LC 3985's own constraint (1 <= nums.length <= 1e5) does not guarantee - an all-distinct n>65536 input breaks that encoding for real, not hypothetically. Grepped DataStructures/ and Algorithms/ (including PrefixFunctionSearch, ZFunction, RollingHashSearch, SuffixArray/SuffixAutomaton/SuffixTree) for any generic ReadOnlySpan<T>/IReadOnlyList<T> palindrome or rolling-hash primitive; none exists. A brute-force O(n^2) expand-around-center is possible and correct but composes no existing primitive beyond plain array indexing - the same 'no reusable primitive to compose against' situation LC 11 (Container With Most Water) is already marked blocked for in this manifest, not an effort issue. Closing this gap would need a generic (ReadOnlySpan<T> + IEqualityComparer<T>) Manacher or RollingHash added to Algorithms/StringMatching or DataStructures/RollingHash - out of scope for this pass per the no-new-production-primitives instruction.

problems.title: Create Grid With Exactly K Paths I
problems.primitivesUsed: None from DataStructures/Algorithms needed - pure construction problem-specific logic (k<=4, m,n<=10 keeps it purely combinatorial). Anchors one fully-open a x b rectangle (closed-form path count C(a+b-2,a-1)) at (0,0) plus a single-width L corridor to (m-1,n-1); the one gap a plain rectangle can't cover (k=4, m=n=3) uses a hand-built double-chained-2x2 fallback. Construction exhaustively verified in Python (all m,n in 1..10, k in 1..4) against an independent DP path-count oracle before porting to C#. Two strategies (PathCountDp vs BinomialFormula) differ only in how a candidate rectangle's path count is computed.
problems.notes: (none)

problems.title: Count Valid Sequences
problems.primitivesUsed: Domain/Modular/ModularArithmetic (Inverse/Power) reused, not added. Answer = C(n-1,k-1) minus the all-odd-sequence count C((n+k)/2-1,k-1) when n+k is even (stars-and-bars complement; verified against a brute-force enumeration for n<=15). Added a problem-scoped FactorialTable witness under LeetCode/CountValidSequences/ (used by this one problem only, so per ARCHITECTURE.md 17.3/17.6 it stays in the LeetCode tier rather than Domain/), mirroring CountWaysToBuildRoomsInAnAntColony's precomputed-vs-per-call factorial split for the two strategies.
problems.notes: (none)

problems.title: Minimum Cost Path with Alternating Directions III
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms/ShortestPaths/ShortestPath.Dijkstra and DataStructures/Graph/Contracts (IEdgeTopology/IEdges/ListEdges) reused, not added. Modeled as shortest paths over state (row, col, next-action-parity), up to 2*m*n nodes with up to 5 on-the-fly edges each (wait + 4 always-legal moves; parity only decides whether the source cell's penalty is also charged). Added problem-scoped AlternatingGridNode/AlternatingGridTopology witnesses under the LeetCode folder (single-problem use) whose GetEdges never materializes an adjacency structure, matching GridShortestPath's own composition style. Model verified against all 3 official examples plus 200 random small grids against an independent brute-force DFS in Python before porting to C#. Baseline arm is a hand-rolled BCL PriorityQueue+Dictionary Dijkstra per ARCHITECTURE.md 17.5 (internals stay BCL for the textbook arm).
problems.notes: (none)

problems.title: Minimum Possible Maximum Waiting Time
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer over a bespoke private CarAssignmentState(Index,Consumed0,Gap0,Gap1) record struct. Key insight that keeps the memoized state tiny: a dispenser's fuel eligibility depends only on cumulative demand assigned to it (never timing), and each dispenser's free-time 'lead' over the next car's allowed time stays within [0, max(demand)] forever, regardless of actual timestamp magnitude - so the two-part objective (maximize served count, then minimize max wait) collapses into one lexicographic top-down recurrence. Baseline arm is the same recurrence unmemoized (plain BCL recursion), mirroring MinimumTimeToBreakLocksISolution's baseline/Memoizer pairing.
problems.notes: Verified by hand against the official Example 1 trace (demand=[6,8,4,6,5], fuel=[16,13] -> max wait 6) before coding, then confirmed via the 3 published examples in the test harness (both strategies pass) and a Release-mode Dry-job BenchmarkDotNet smoke run (no exceptions, memoized search overtakes plain recursion by Length=18).

problems.title: Count Subarrays With Even Odd Ratio I
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound (coordinate compression of the +a/-b weighted prefix sums, after rearranging x/y<=a/b into prefix[L]<=prefix[R]) + DataStructures.FenwickTree.FenwickTree<int,SumOperation<int>> (a Binary Indexed Tree) for the left-to-right count sweep - the same prefix-sum-plus-Fenwick shape CountOfRangeSumTests already uses for LC 327. Baseline arm is the textbook O(n^2) enumeration, BCL only.
problems.notes: All 3 LeetCode-published examples pass for both strategies; Release-mode Dry-job BenchmarkDotNet smoke run for Length in {200,1000} completed with no exceptions.

problems.title: Count Subarrays With Even Odd Ratio II
problems.primitivesUsed: Same rule and composition as LC 4011, at LeetCode's larger n (<=1e5) and value (<=1e9) constraints: Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound for coordinate compression + DataStructures.FenwickTree.FenwickTree<int,SumOperation<int>> for the O(n log n) sweep, with a long accumulator/return type since the count can exceed int range. Kept as its own self-contained solution class rather than referencing CountSubarraysWithEvenOddRatioISolution's code, matching this repo's existing LeetCode-tier convention that no solution folder currently depends on another problem's.
problems.notes: All 3 LeetCode-published examples pass for both strategies; Release-mode Dry-job BenchmarkDotNet smoke run for Length in {200,2000} completed with no exceptions. The O(n^2) baseline's benchmark Length is deliberately kept well under LC 4013's own 1e5 ceiling since it exists only as a correctness baseline, not a contest-scale contender.

problems.title: Peaks in Array II
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.SegmentTree.SegmentTree<Element,TOperation> (point-update, pluggable ICombineOperation) keyed by two problem-local witnesses added in the LeetCode/PeaksInArrayII folder per section 17.3: PeakGapNode (aggregate: leftmost/rightmost peak in a range, plus summed C(gap,2) subarray-pair count of every no-peak gap already inside it) and PeakGapMergeOperation (bridges two ranges' boundary peaks into one more such gap). A type-1 query reads Query(l+1,r-1) and computes total-subarrays-in-[l,r] minus no-peak-subarrays in O(log n); a type-2 update touches at most 3 leaves (index-1,index,index+1), the same 3-position fact PeaksInArray/LC3187 already relies on. Baseline arm is the textbook O((r-l)^3) enumerate-every-subarray-and-rescan, BCL only. Answers are long (a single query's count can reach ~5e9 at LC's n<=1e5 ceiling).
problems.notes: No production primitive gap: reused the existing generic SegmentTree exactly as FindXValueOfArrayII/MaximumSumOfSubsequenceWithNonAdjacentElements already do, adding only a problem-specific merge witness. The merge formula (answer = C(r-l,2) minus sum of C(gap,2) over no-peak gaps) was independently derived and hand-verified against all 3 official LeetCode examples (fetched live from leetcode.com's GitHub mirror since this is a very recent problem id with no cached statement or public solution code) before writing any code. All 10 xUnit tests pass; Release-mode Dry-job BenchmarkDotNet smoke run for Length in {30,150} completed with no exceptions, and SegmentTree already overtakes the cubic brute-force baseline by Length=150.

problems.title: Elevator Requests I
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.ShortestPaths.ManhattanHeuristic applied to DataStructures.Graph.Grids.WeightedGridNode with every node's column pinned to 0, so the 4-directional Manhattan distance collapses to the 1-D floor distance this problem asks for - the same 'reuse a heuristic purely for its distance computation' composition MinimumTimeVisitingAllPoints (LC 1266) already uses for ChebyshevHeuristic. Baseline arm is the textbook running-floor-plus-Math.Abs walk, BCL only.
problems.notes: No production primitive gap. Both LeetCode-published examples pass for both strategies. Release-mode Dry-job BenchmarkDotNet smoke run for RequestCount in {100,5000} completed with no exceptions.
